docs.t: Binding Decision 1/2026 on the dispute submitted by the Belgian SA on Vlaamse Radio-en Televisieomroeporganisatie (VRT) (Art. 65 GDPR)
docs.x: Article 65 decision on whether a complaint against the Flemish broadcaster VRT should be dismissed as an abuse of the right to complain and to mandate a not-for-profit body. Procedural: it settles when authorities may reject complaints, not any substantive processing question.

docs.t: Urgent Binding Decision 01/2023 requested by the Norwegian SA for the ordering of final measures regarding Meta Platforms Ireland Ltd (Art. 66(2) GDPR)
docs.x: Meta Platforms Ireland infringed Article 6(1) GDPR by continuing to process personal data for behavioural advertising on Facebook and Instagram under Article 6(1)(b) after the Irish SA's decisions of 31 December 2022, and by switching to Article 6(1)(f) on 5 April 2023 without a valid legal basis. The EDPB instructed the Irish SA to order Meta to cease that processing across the entire EEA, extending the Norwegian SA's provisional ban of 14 July 2023; Meta's consent proposal was not assessed. For any controller the lesson is that neither contract nor legitimate interest carries behavioural advertising built on observed behaviour, location and ad interactions, which leaves consent as the basis to design for. Topic 18: behavioural advertising ban Topics: lawful-basis, marketing, enforcement

docs.t: Binding Decision 2/2023 on the dispute submitted by the Irish SA regarding TikTok Technology Limited (Art. 65 GDPR)
docs.x: TikTok's public-by-default settings for users aged 13 to 17 between 31 July and 31 December 2020 infringed Articles 25(1), 25(2), 5(1)(c), 24(1), 13(1)(e) and 12(1) GDPR, and the EDPB additionally instructed the Irish SA to find an infringement of the fairness principle in Article 5(1)(a) because the registration and video-posting pop-ups nudged children towards public accounts. The decision binds the Irish SA and the objecting authorities and is the EDPB's clearest statement that deceptive interface design is unfair processing. Audit defaults and consent flows for child users, and expect fairness, not only transparency, to be assessed. Topic 18: children's data, TikTok Topics: children, dpia, enforcement

docs.t: Binding Decision 1/2023 on the dispute submitted by the Irish SA on data transfers by Meta Platforms Ireland Limited for its Facebook service (Art. 65 GDPR)
docs.x: Meta Platforms Ireland infringed Article 46(1) GDPR by transferring EU/EEA Facebook user data to the United States on standard contractual clauses that could not compensate for the deficiencies in US law identified by the CJEU. The EDPB instructed the Irish SA to add an administrative fine to the proposed suspension order and to order Meta to bring processing into compliance, including ceasing unlawful processing of the transferred data, in an inquiry opened on 28 August 2020. The decision binds the Irish SA and shows that a transfer impact assessment concluding that supplementary measures are ineffective must lead to suspension, not continued transfer. Transfers: Meta EUR 1.2bn Topics: transfers, enforcement

docs.t: Binding Decision 3/2022 on the dispute submitted by the Irish SA on Meta Platforms Ireland Limited and its Facebook service (Art. 65 GDPR)
docs.x: Meta Platforms Ireland cannot rely on Article 6(1)(b) GDPR for behavioural advertising on Facebook, because such advertising is objectively not necessary for the performance of the contract and users cannot be taken to expect it from a brief mention in the terms. The EDPB also confirmed infringements of Articles 12 and 13 for unclear information on processing operations and legal bases, found an additional breach of the fairness principle in Article 5(1)(a) for presenting the service in a misleading way that left users with a take-it-or-leave-it choice, instructed the Irish SA to impose a fine and required compliance within three months of the final decision. Adopted on 5 December 2022, the decision sets the position later enforced EEA-wide in Urgent Binding Decision 01/2023. Topics 10 and 18: contract is not a basis for behavioural advertising Topics: lawful-basis, marketing, enforcement

docs.t: Binding Decision 4/2022 on the dispute submitted by the Irish SA on Meta Platforms Ireland Limited and its Instagram service (Art. 65 GDPR)
docs.x: Meta Platforms Ireland cannot rely on Article 6(1)(b) GDPR for behavioural advertising on Instagram: the processing is not a core part of the contract, is objectively unnecessary for its performance and falls outside users' reasonable expectations under the Terms of Use. The EDPB upheld infringements of Articles 5(1)(a), 12(1) and 13(1)(c) for failing to give meaningful information on processing operations and legal bases, found an additional breach of the fairness principle for presenting the service in a misleading way that left users with an accept-or-delete choice, instructed the Irish SA to impose a fine and set a three-month compliance deadline. Adopted on 5 December 2022, it mirrors Binding Decision 3/2022 on Facebook, and both were extended EEA-wide by Urgent Binding Decision 01/2023. Topics 10 and 18: same, Instagram Topics: lawful-basis, marketing, enforcement

docs.t: Binding Decision 5/2022 on the dispute submitted by the Irish SA regarding WhatsApp Ireland Limited (Art. 65 GDPR)
docs.x: WhatsApp Ireland cannot rely on Article 6(1)(b) GDPR to process personal data for service improvement and security features, because processing must be objectively necessary and integral to the contracted service, judged from both the controller's and a reasonable user's perspective, and a controller cannot pick a basis that serves its commercial interests at the expense of data subject protection. The EDPB instructed the Irish SA to record the Article 5(1)(a) and 6(1) infringement and impose an administrative fine; the separate order to bring WhatsApp's privacy policy into compliance with Articles 12(1) and 13(1)(c) was made in the EDPB's earlier 2021 binding decision on WhatsApp, not this one. Any controller citing contract for improvement or analytics processing should re-evaluate that basis. Topic 15: transparency, WhatsApp Topics: lawful-basis, transparency, enforcement

docs.t: Binding Decision 2/2022 on the dispute arisen on the draft decision of the Irish Supervisory Authority regarding Meta Platforms Ireland Limited (Instagram) under Article 65(1)(a) GDPR
docs.x: Article 65 decision in the Irish authority's Meta (Instagram) inquiry into children's data: contact details of child users with business accounts were published by default and children's accounts were public by default, breaching Articles 5(1)(c), 6(1), 12(1), 24, 25 and 35 among others; the Board directed a higher fine (EUR 405 million in the final decision). Enforcement history; the substantive points on default settings and children are in the Article 25 guidance and Guidelines 05/2020.

docs.t: Decision 01/2022 on the dispute arisen on the draft decision of the French Supervisory Authority regarding Accor SA under Article 65(1)(a) GDPR
docs.x: Article 65 decision on the French authority's Accor case, requiring the fine to be reassessed for failures on objections to direct marketing, access requests, information and security. Enforcement history.

docs.t: Binding decision 1/2021 on the dispute arisen on the draft decision of the Irish Supervisory Authority regarding WhatsApp Ireland under Article 65(1)(a) GDPR
docs.x: WhatsApp Ireland's privacy notices infringed the transparency duties in Articles 12 to 14 GDPR, and the EDPB, resolving objections from several supervisory authorities, instructed the Irish Data Protection Commission to add an infringement of Article 13(1)(d) because legitimate interests were not tied to specific processing operations, to treat the table of lossy hashes of non-users' phone numbers held with associated users' numbers as personal data and extend the Article 14 infringement to it, and to reassess the fine upwards from the 30 to 50 million euro range in its draft. The decision binds the Irish authority and the concerned supervisory authorities; WhatsApp Ireland is bound by the Irish final decision adopted on its basis. Read it as the benchmark for how granular a legitimate-interests description and a non-user notice must be. Topic 15: transparency, WhatsApp Topics: transparency, enforcement Status: historical

docs.t: Urgent Binding Decision 01/2021 on the request under Article 66(2) GDPR from the Hamburg (German) Supervisory Authority for ordering the adoption of final measures regarding Facebook Ireland Limited
docs.x: Urgent binding decision refusing the Hamburg authority's request for final measures against Facebook over WhatsApp data sharing, while asking the Irish authority to investigate. Procedural precedent on Article 66 urgency.

docs.t: Decision 01/2020 on the dispute arisen on the draft decision of the Irish Supervisory Authority regarding Twitter International Company under Article 65(1)(a) GDPR
docs.x: The Board's first Article 65 decision, on the Irish authority's Twitter breach notification case, directing a higher fine. Enforcement history; the substantive point on the 72-hour clock is in Guidelines 9/2022.

docs.t: EDPB-EDPS Joint Opinion 4/2026 on the Proposal for a Cybersecurity Act 2 and the Proposal on amendments to the NIS 2 Directive
docs.x: The EDPB and EDPS back a single entry point for notifying personal data breaches alongside NIS 2 incident reports, support classifying European Digital Identity and Business Wallet providers as essential entities, and welcome supply chain measures aimed at non-technical risks. They ask legislators to spell out any large-scale personal data processing by ENISA in the basic act, to require EDPB consultation before certification schemes on security of processing are adopted, to keep certification controls configurable so they respect data minimisation, and to define safeguards for the new ransomware incident reporting, including whether a ransom was paid. NIS 2 operators should plan for combined incident and breach reporting. Topic 16 NIS2 incident windows Topics: security, breach

docs.t: EDPB-EDPS Joint Opinion 3/2026 on the Proposal for a European Biotech Act
docs.x: Joint EDPB-EDPS opinion on the proposed European Biotech Act, on the handling of genetic and health data in research and regulatory pathways. Sector legislation.

docs.t: EDPB-EDPS Joint opinion 2/2026 on the Proposal for a Regulation as regards the simplification of the digital legislative framework (Digital Omnibus)
docs.x: The EDPB and EDPS reject the narrowed definition of personal data in Article 4(1) and the new Article 41a on pseudonymisation, insist Article 22 stays a prohibition in principle on solely automated decisions, and accept legitimate interest for AI only with a mandatory three-step test, an unconditional right to object and enhanced transparency. They support raising the breach notification threshold to breaches likely to result in high risk, extending the deadline from 72 to 96 hours, the six-month bar on repeat consent requests and machine-readable consent signals, but warn that splitting the terminal equipment rules between the GDPR (personal data) and the ePrivacy Directive (other data) creates legal uncertainty and must not lower protection, and want the EDPB rather than the Commission to own DPIA lists and breach templates. Current GDPR obligations stand while negotiation continues. GDPR Digital Omnibus: report add-later item Topics: breach, ai, cookies-tracking

docs.t: EDPB-EDPS Joint opinion 1/2026 on the Proposal for a Regulation as regards the simplification of the implementation of harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Digital Omnibus on AI)
docs.x: The EDPB and EDPS accept that postponing high-risk AI obligations from 2 August 2026 to no later than 2 December 2027 (Annex III) and from 2 August 2027 to no later than 2 August 2028 (Annex I) has partly objective causes but ask legislators to consider keeping the current dates for certain duties such as transparency, retain AI literacy obligations for providers and deployers, and keep registration of Annex III systems that providers self-exempt. They support bias detection with special category data in all AI systems only under strict necessity, with data protection authorities' independence and powers preserved, involved in EU-level sandboxes and unhindered by market surveillance single points of contact. Providers should not treat the delay as settled. AI Omnibus: AI Act sections 7, 8 Topics: ai, governance

docs.t: EDPB-EDPS Joint Opinion 01/2025 on the Proposal for a Regulation on simplification measures for SMEs and SMCs, in particular the record-keeping obligation under Art. 30(5) GDPR
docs.x: The Commission's proposal of 21 May 2025 would raise the Article 30(5) record-keeping exemption from fewer than 250 employees to fewer than 750, drop the trigger for special category and criminal data, and keep records only for processing likely to result in high risk, covering an estimated 38,000 SMCs. The EDPB and EDPS accept the aim, note the missing fundamental rights assessment and ask for clarifications: recitals confirming that records are needed only for the high-risk activities themselves, that Article 9(2)(b) employment processing is in principle not high risk and that public authorities stay excluded, and a reference in Article 30(5) itself to the formal SME and SMC definitions. Until adoption, the 250-employee rule applies. Art 30 threshold history Topics: governance, controller-processor

docs.t: EDPB-EDPS Joint Opinion 02/2023 on the Proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council on the establishment of the digital euro
docs.x: Joint opinion on the proposed Regulation establishing the digital euro: the EDPB and EDPS ask for a high privacy threshold, an offline mode with cash-like privacy, no central transaction database beyond what settlement needs, and clear roles for the ECB and the payment service providers. Payments sector.

docs.t: EDPB-EDPS Joint Opinion 5/2021 on the proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Artificial Intelligence Act)
docs.x: The EDPB and EDPS welcome the risk-based approach of the AI Act proposal but call for a general ban on any use of AI for automated recognition of human features in publicly accessible spaces, a ban on social scoring by private as well as public actors, and a prohibition on inferring emotions except in narrowly regulated cases. They ask that GDPR compliance be a precondition for placing systems on the market and that data protection authorities be the national supervisory authorities. Addressed to the co-legislators in June 2021, it is a historical position; read it alongside the adopted AI Act to see which asks were taken up. AI Act history Topics: ai, biometrics Status: historical

docs.t: EDPB-EDPS Joint Opinion 04/2021 on the Proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council on a framework for the issuance, verification and acceptance of interoperable certificates on vaccination, testing and recovery
docs.x: Joint opinion on the proposed Regulation for interoperable COVID-19 vaccination, test and recovery certificates (the Digital Green Certificate): no central EU database, purpose limited to free movement, and a sunset once the pandemic ends. Historical.

docs.t: EDPB-EDPS Joint Opinion 03/2021 on the Proposal for a regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council on European data governance (Data Governance Act)
docs.x: Joint opinion on the proposed Data Governance Act. Now adopted.

docs.t: EDPB-EDPS Joint Opinion 1/2021 on standard contractual clauses between controllers and processors
docs.x: The Commission's draft standard contractual clauses for Article 28 contracts are welcomed as a strong accountability tool, subject to amendments: the scope must state clearly whether the clauses apply to processors outside the EU and how they interact with Chapter V transfer clauses, the docking clause needs a procedure for new parties, the controller and not the processor must choose the auditor, cost allocation should be deleted, and the annexes must set out each party's responsibilities with absolute clarity. Addressed to the Commission in January 2021 before it adopted the clauses. When drafting a processing agreement on the Commission's clauses, give these points the most care. Art 28 DPAs Topics: controller-processor Status: historical

docs.t: EDPB-EDPS Joint Opinion 2/2021 on standard contractual clauses for the transfer of personal data to third countries
docs.x: The draft Article 46 SCCs reinforce protection for data subjects through four modules, a docking clause and clauses on third-country law and government access requests, but the EDPB and EDPS require changes: the assessment of third-country law must rest on objective factors rather than the likelihood of access or the absence of past requests, notification of access requests must precede any response, the processor-to-controller module needs the Article 28 processor obligations and the processor-to-processor module must reflect Article 28(4), and the Commission should clarify that importers already subject to the GDPR under Article 3(2) fall outside the decision. The SCCs must be used with Recommendations 01/2020 on supplementary measures. Addressed to the Commission in January 2021; the transfer impact assessment stays with the exporter. Transfers Topics: transfers Status: historical

docs.t: EDPB-EDPS Joint Opinion 1/2019 on the processing of patients' data and the role of the European Commission within the eHealth Digital Service Infrastructure (eHDSI)
docs.x: Joint opinion on patients' data and the Commission's role in the eHealth Digital Service Infrastructure. Health sector.

docs.t: Opinion 3/2019 concerning the Questions and Answers on the interplay between the Clinical Trials Regulation (CTR) and the General Data Protection regulation (GDPR)
docs.x: Opinion on the Commission's questions and answers on the interplay between the Clinical Trials Regulation and the GDPR: consent to participate in a trial is not the GDPR lawful basis. Clinical research sector.

docs.t: Opinion 23/2018 on Commission proposals on European Production and Preservation Orders for electronic evidence in criminal matters (Art. 70.1.b)
docs.x: Opinion on the proposed e-evidence Regulation on cross-border production and preservation orders for electronic evidence. Law enforcement.

docs.t: Report of the work undertaken by the ChatGPT Taskforce
docs.x: The taskforce, set up on 13 April 2023 to coordinate national investigations into OpenAI while it had no EU establishment, records preliminary common views: web scraping for training, pre-processing, training, prompts and outputs each need a lawful basis, with OpenAI relying on legitimate interests; terms of service cannot shift GDPR responsibility to users; transparency, accuracy of probabilistic output and data subject rights must be handled by design, and technical complexity does not excuse non-compliance. OpenAI established an EU presence on 15 February 2024, bringing future cross-border processing under the one-stop-shop. Read it as the authorities' checklist for any generative AI service; the views were preliminary as of 23 May 2024. Topic 13; AI Act section 13; AI Risk tool Topics: ai, lawful-basis, enforcement Status: historical

docs.t: Report of the work undertaken by the supervisory authorities within the 101 Taskforce
docs.x: Supervisory authorities handling the 101 complaints filed on 17 August 2020 about Google Analytics and Facebook Business Tools agreed that transfers relying on the invalidated Privacy Shield after 16 July 2020 breached Chapter V, that standard contractual clauses need supplementary measures addressing the deficiencies the CJEU identified, that encryption fails where the importer holds the keys, that anonymisation after transfer is too late, and that a website operator choosing such a tool is a controller. By March 2023 eight authorities had issued decisions. Since 10 July 2023 the EU-US adequacy decision covers transfers to DPF-certified recipients, so the report now matters mainly for non-certified importers and for the controller analysis. Transfers, analytics tools Topics: transfers, cookies-tracking, controller-processor Status: historical

docs.t: Report of the work undertaken by the Cookie Banner Taskforce
docs.x: Supervisory authorities agreed a minimum common position on cookie banners: a vast majority hold that no reject option on any layer where consent is sought means no valid consent, pre-ticked boxes are invalid, a reject option hidden as a low-prominence text link is not equivalent to the accept button, deceptive colours and contrast are assessed case by case with unreadable text manifestly non-compliant, cookies claimed as essential must be shown to be so, and withdrawal must be as easy as consent without mandating a specific icon. Where Article 5(3) ePrivacy is breached, subsequent GDPR processing cannot be compliant. The positions apply on top of national ePrivacy law; test each banner against them before relying on the consent. Topic 15 cookie banners Topics: cookies-tracking, consent

docs.t: Coordinated Enforcement Action, implementation of the right to erasure by controllers
docs.x: Across 32 supervisory authorities and 764 controllers surveyed, erasure compliance is mostly rated average and fails in seven recurring ways: missing internal procedures (flagged by 17 authorities), untrained staff, thin privacy notice information (13 authorities), blanket use of Article 17(3) exceptions without documented case-by-case assessment, retention periods that controllers struggle to define per purpose (one applied the longest period to everything), no method for erasure in back-ups, and anonymisation used as a substitute for deletion. Nine authorities opened or continued formal investigations. Controllers should adopt a written erasure procedure with owners and deadlines, a data deletion matrix cross-referencing data types and retention periods, a back-up erasure method, and documented reasoning for every refusal. Topic 8 Topics: rights, enforcement

docs.t: Coordinated Enforcement Action, implementation of the right of access by controllers
docs.x: Thirty supervisory authorities examined how 1,185 controllers, from SMEs to large companies and public bodies, implement the right of access; two-thirds of participating authorities rated compliance as average to high, and larger organisations and those receiving more requests performed better. The report identifies recurring shortcomings: no documented internal procedure, inconsistent or excessive reading of the limitations, automatic reliance on exceptions, excessive formal requirements and identity checks, and limited awareness of Guidelines 01/2022. It closes with non-binding recommendations for controllers and authorities. Benchmark the access procedure against the challenges it lists and align it with Guidelines 01/2022. Topic 8 Topics: rights, enforcement

docs.t: Coordinated Enforcement Action, Designation and Position of Data Protection Officers
docs.x: The second coordinated enforcement action, run by 25 supervisory authorities across the EEA in 2023 with over 17,000 replies, finds that most DPOs report the skills, training, clearly defined tasks and independence that Articles 37 to 39 require, but identifies organisations that fail to designate a DPO where mandatory, under-resource the role, assign tasks not aligned with the GDPR or compromise independence through reporting lines. The report addresses supervisory authorities, controllers and processors, and signals awareness-raising and enforcement on these points. Check DPO designation, resourcing, reporting line and task list against the findings, and give the DPO time and budget to keep knowledge current. Readiness governance activities (Arts 37 to 39); WP243 Topics: governance

docs.t: Coordinated Enforcement Action, use of cloud-based services by the public sector
docs.x: Coordinated enforcement action on public bodies' use of cloud services: findings on DPIAs, contracts, transfers and the difficulty of negotiating with large providers. Public sector.

docs.t: EDPB Document on Coordinated Enforcement Framework under Regulation 2016/679
docs.x: Founding document of the Coordinated Enforcement Framework: how authorities pick and run an annual joint action. Institutional.

docs.t: Template for Cross-Regulatory Cooperation Agreements
docs.x: A model agreement for cooperation between data protection authorities and other regulators, such as competition and consumer protection authorities. For authorities, not controllers.

docs.t: EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework F.A.Q. for European businesses - version 2.0
docs.x: Personal data may flow from the EEA to a US company without further safeguards only while that company holds an active certification on the Data Privacy Framework List kept by the US Department of Commerce, and only companies under FTC or Department of Transportation jurisdiction can self-certify. Exporters must check the list before each transfer, fall back on standard contractual clauses or binding corporate rules if certification lapses, confirm HR Data coverage and cooperation with EU authorities before sending employee data, and still sign an Article 28 agreement with any certified processor. Version 2.0, adopted 15 January 2026, replaces version 1.0 of July 2024. Privacy Assessment DPF factor Topics: transfers, controller-processor

docs.t: EU-US Data Privacy Framework FAQ for European individuals - version 2.0
docs.x: Individuals whose data is transferred to a DPF-certified US company keep rights to notice, access, correction and deletion, and can check certification on the DPF List. Complaints go first to the company, which must respond within 45 days, then to any EEA data protection authority using the EDPB template form or to the company's independent recourse mechanism; HR Data complaints and opted-in companies go to the informal panel of EU authorities, other cases can be referred to the FTC, the Department of Commerce or the OACP. Controllers should mirror these routes in privacy notices. Version 2.0 replaces the July 2024 version. Transfers Topics: transfers, rights

docs.t: EU-US Data Privacy Framework Template Complaint Form for Submitting Complaints to EU DPAs related to the Data Privacy Framework Principles - version 2.0
docs.x: Template form for an EU resident to complain to a national authority about a US company certified under the Data Privacy Framework. Useful to individuals; controllers need only know it exists.

docs.t: EU-US Data Privacy Framework FAQ for European businesses
docs.x: Answers for businesses in the EU on the EU-US Data Privacy Framework: how transfers to certified US organisations work under the adequacy decision, what a European exporter must check before relying on it, and how the framework relates to other transfer tools. It is informational guidance for controllers and processors exporting data to the United States rather than a binding position, and it sits alongside the EDPB information note on transfers to the United States and the redress mechanism documents. This 16 July 2024 version has been superseded by the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework FAQ for European businesses, version 2.0. Superseded by version 2.0 Topics: transfers Status: superseded

docs.t: EU-US Data Privacy Framework FAQ for European individuals
docs.x: Answers for individuals in the EU on the EU-US Data Privacy Framework: how transfers to the United States work under the adequacy decision of 10 July 2023, what rights individuals have and how to seek redress. It is informational guidance for individuals rather than a binding position, and it is useful to controllers drafting privacy notices or complaint responses for transfers to certified US organisations. This 16 July 2024 version has been superseded by the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework FAQ for European individuals, version 2.0. Transfers Topics: transfers, rights Status: superseded

docs.t: Information Note on the Data Privacy Framework redress mechanism for national security purposes
docs.x: Individuals in the EU and EEA who believe their personal data transferred to the United States was unlawfully collected or processed by US national security authorities can complain through the redress mechanism created by Executive Order 14086, whatever transfer tool was used, for data transmitted after 10 July 2023: the complaint goes to their national data protection authority, which checks it and passes it via the EDPB Secretariat to the US Office of the Director of National Intelligence's Civil Liberties Protection Officer, with a right of appeal to the Data Protection Review Court within 60 days. Complaints use the EDPB template complaint form for the CLPO, and the note sits alongside rules of procedure for the mechanism and for the informal panel of EU data protection authorities that handles them. Controllers transferring data to the US under any tool should reference the mechanism in their transfer documentation and privacy notices. Transfers Topics: transfers, rights

docs.t: Information note on data transfers under the GDPR to the United States after the adoption of the adequacy decision on 10 July 2023
docs.x: From 10 July 2023 transfers to US organisations on the Data Privacy Framework List may rely on the adequacy decision without Article 46 tools or supplementary measures, while transfers to non-certified US recipients still need standard contractual clauses, binding corporate rules or another Article 46 safeguard. The note addresses controllers and processors exporting data and explains that individuals may complain to their national authority about US intelligence access without proving their data was collected. Check each US recipient against the DPF List, take the Commission's assessment into account in transfer impact assessments for non-certified recipients, and note the review cycle of one year then at least every four years. Transfers Topics: transfers

docs.x: Template complaint form and template acknowledgement of receipt for use by supervisory authorities, to harmonise how complaints are lodged across the EEA.

docs.x: Toolbox of essential data protection safeguards for enforcement cooperation between EEA data protection authorities and the data protection authorities of third countries: what an agreement or arrangement must contain before personal data is shared in an investigation. For authorities.

docs.x: Response to the Commission's request for clarification on the consistent application of the GDPR to health research. Research sector.

docs.t: Information note on data transfers under the GDPR to the United Kingdom after the transition period - update 13/01/2021
docs.x: From 1 January 2021 the UK is a third country, but under the EU-UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement transfers to UK entities are not treated as third-country transfers for an interim period ending no later than 30 June 2021, provided the UK data protection regime stays in place. Exporters should use the period to put Article 46 tools in place (standard contractual clauses, binding corporate rules, codes of conduct), consider supplementary measures, and update records and privacy notices; groups with the ICO as BCR lead authority need a new EEA lead. Addressed to GDPR controllers and processors; historical now that the interim period has ended and UK adequacy applies. Transfers Topics: transfers Status: historical

docs.t: Information note on data transfers under the GDPR to the United Kingdom after the transition period
docs.x: With the transition period ending on 31 December 2020 and no adequacy decision in place, transfers of personal data to the UK fall under Chapter V GDPR from 1 January 2021: exporters need standard contractual clauses, binding corporate rules or another Article 46 safeguard, plus supplementary measures where Recommendations 01/2020 require them, and Article 49 derogations are exceptional and read restrictively. Controllers and processors must update records of processing and privacy notices, and groups with the ICO as BCR lead authority must appoint a new EEA lead. Superseded on 13 January 2021 by the updated information note reflecting the interim provision of the EU-UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement. Transfers Topics: transfers Status: superseded

docs.t: Article 65 FAQ
docs.x: Frequently asked questions on the Article 65 dispute resolution procedure. Procedure between authorities.

docs.t: Frequently Asked Questions on the judgment of the Court of Justice of the European Union in Case C-311/18 - Data Protection Commissioner v Facebook Ireland Ltd and Maximillian Schrems
docs.x: The judgment of 16 July 2020 invalidates the Privacy Shield with immediate effect and no grace period, while standard contractual clauses and binding corporate rules remain valid only where the exporter and importer have assessed, case by case, that the law of the destination country allows an essentially equivalent level of protection, adding supplementary measures where it does not. Article 49 derogations are available but cannot become the rule, and an exporter that finds no adequate safeguards must suspend the transfer or, if it intends to keep transferring, notify its supervisory authority. Addressed to controllers and processors exporting data. The guidance on supplementary measures it promised became Recommendations 01/2020, which now carries the operational detail. Transfers Topics: transfers Status: historical

docs.x: Information note for groups whose binding corporate rules had the UK ICO as lead authority: how to move the lead to an EEA authority before the end of the Brexit transition period. Historical.

docs.x: Public leaflet on GDPR rights for individuals, with a short introduction to the Board.

docs.t: Information note on BCRs for companies which have ICO as BCR Lead Supervisory Authority
docs.x: Information note for companies whose binding corporate rules had the UK ICO as lead authority. Historical, superseded by the 2020 note.

docs.t: Information note on data transfers under the GDPR in the event of a no-deal Brexit
docs.x: Information note on transfers to the UK in the event of a no-deal Brexit. Historical.

docs.t: Position Paper on the derogations from the obligation to maintain records of processing activities pursuant to Article 30(5) GDPR
docs.x: Article 30(5) GDPR exempts organisations with fewer than 250 employees from keeping records of processing activities, but the exemption falls away if the processing is likely to result in a risk to data subjects, is not occasional, or includes special category or criminal conviction data. The WP29 reads these three conditions as alternatives: any one of them alone triggers the record-keeping duty. The duty covers only the processing that meets a condition, so a small organisation that regularly processes employee data must record that processing while occasional, low-risk activities stay outside. Small organisations should treat core processing as non-occasional and keep a record rather than rely on headcount. Readiness Article 30 activity; GDPR Omnibus note Topics: governance

docs.t: One-Stop-Shop case digest on right to object and right to erasure
docs.x: Supervisory authorities handling Article 17 and Article 21 complaints through the one-stop-shop look first at whether the controller made the right easy to exercise: 631 final decisions from 2018 to January 2026 (551 on erasure, 80 on objection) show the recurring failures are poor information on the right to object, cumbersome identity checks, internal delays, weak coordination with processors and handling errors. Most cases ended in reprimands, compliance or erasure orders or amicable settlement, with fines rare. Use the catalogue to test your own objection and erasure workflow, including marketing opt-outs and account deletion. An external SPE expert wrote it; the May 2026 update replaces the 2022 version. Topic 8; LIA objection factor Topics: rights, enforcement

docs.t: Report on the use of SPE external experts in 2025
docs.x: Administrative report on how the Board's external expert pool was used during 2025.

docs.t: One-Stop-Shop case digest on the legal basis of "legitimate interest"
docs.x: Supervisory authorities applying the Article 6(1)(f) three-step test in 67 decisions between December 2018 and June 2025 (62 one-stop-shop decisions and 5 EDPB binding decisions) accepted commercial interests only when stated precisely, frequently failed controllers at the necessity stage where a less intrusive design existed, and read data subjects' interests and reasonable expectations broadly. The common infringements were no documented assessment before processing began, vague interests such as measuring content performance, retroactive reliance on legitimate interest to keep data collected without a legal basis, and transparency gaps that stopped people objecting. Controllers relying on legitimate interest should write the assessment first, name the interest specifically and disclose it. An external SPE expert wrote the digest, which builds on Guidelines 1/2024. LIA tool Topics: lawful-basis, enforcement

docs.t: Data brokers market study
docs.x: Data brokers collect personal data from many public and private sources, aggregate it into profiles and monetise it, usually without meaningful control by the individual, and activity codes do not find them: keyword searches identified over 40 brokers and providers operating in Belgium. The study, commissioned by the Belgian supervisory authority through the SPE programme and written by an external expert, sorts them into eight types, rating personal data brokers, data pools and cleanrooms, AI platforms built on personal data and user-controlled brokers as high risk. Controllers buying enriched or third-party data should check their suppliers' sources and legal basis. Topic 18 broker data Topics: marketing, transparency, lawful-basis

docs.t: Report on International Data Protection Enforcement Cooperation
docs.x: Report on cooperation between data protection enforcement bodies internationally: mechanisms, obstacles and recommendations for authorities.

docs.t: The Digital Euro and its token-based offline modality
docs.x: Expert report on the privacy design of the digital euro's offline, token-based mode. Payments sector.

docs.t: Fundamentals of Secure AI Systems with Personal Data
docs.x: Security, data science and governance teams running AI systems on personal data get shared vocabulary and lifecycle controls from this five-module open-source training (CC BY-SA 4.0): terminology, the AI lifecycle and GDPR principles and AI Act risk tiers mapped onto AI risks; personal data management and privacy-enhancing technologies before production; secure MLOps, testing and secure processing environments; deployment, monitoring and decommissioning; and audit checklists with worked use cases. It maps seven AI risk domains against the ten privacy risks in ISO/IEC 29134:2023. An external SPE expert wrote it, submitted December 2024 and updated April 2025, and it carries no official EDPB position. Use it as a curriculum and a source of AI/ML audit questions. TPSA AI/ML supplement Topics: ai, security

docs.t: Law & Compliance in AI Security & Data Protection
docs.x: Data protection officers can map GDPR and AI Act obligations onto each stage of an AI system's life with this roughly 15-hour self-study module, commissioned through the SPE programme and completed by an external expert in December 2024, in three parts: fundamental AI and cybersecurity concepts, the lifecycle from inception to discontinuation, and advanced topics including fairness, accountability, transparency, privacy-enhancing technologies and large language models. Three hypothetical case studies (a university, a children's toy start-up and a hospital) show how the two regimes interact. It states the author's views, not the EDPB's. Use it to train a DPO team before an AI risk assessment programme. AI Risk tool Topics: ai, governance

docs.t: AI Privacy Risks & Mitigations Large Language Models (LLMs)
docs.x: Large language model systems carry privacy and data protection risks at every stage of their lifecycle, and the report sets out a risk management methodology to identify, assess and mitigate them, worked through three use cases: a customer service virtual assistant, a student progress monitoring system and a travel and schedule management assistant. It was prepared by an external expert under the Support Pool of Experts programme and does not reflect an official EDPB position. Use it as a structured template for an LLM risk assessment or DPIA, and expect supervisory authorities to have read it. Topic 13; AI Risk tool; AI Act section 10 Topics: ai, dpia

docs.t: Report on the use of SPE external experts in 2024
docs.x: Administrative report on how the Board's external expert pool was used during 2024.

docs.t: AI: Complex Algorithms and effective Data Protection Supervision
docs.x: Two reports produced for the German Federal Data Protection Authority under the Support Pool of Experts programme address how supervisory authorities can evaluate algorithmic bias with available tools and how data subjects' rights can be effectively implemented in AI systems. They are written for supervisory staff, express the external author's views rather than an EDPB position, and indicate what an authority may examine in an AI investigation. Controllers deploying AI systems can use the bias evaluation methods and the rights implementation material to prepare for supervisory scrutiny. Topic 13 Topics: ai, rights, enforcement

docs.t: One-Stop-Shop case digest on right of access
docs.x: Of 185 final one-stop-shop decisions reviewed, 52 are analysed to show how supervisory authorities apply Article 15 in practice: activity logs tied to unique identifiers are personal data, an impersonating profile is the impersonated person's data, a copy must reflect the data held at the time of the request, identity verification must be proportionate and demanding official documents exceeds necessity where alternatives suffice, and the one month deadline is often missed through unclear procedures. It was prepared by an external expert under the Support Pool of Experts programme and complements Guidelines 01/2022. Use it as a worked-example library when handling contested access requests. Topic 8 Topics: rights, enforcement

docs.t: AI Auditing
docs.x: Three deliverables prepared for the EDPB under the Support Pool of Experts programme, drawing on earlier work for the Spanish DPA, map and develop tools for evaluating the GDPR compliance of AI systems: a checklist for auditing algorithms, a proposal for Algo-scores and a proposal for AI leaflets as a transparency device. They express the external author's views and not an EDPB position, and are aimed at supervisory authorities inspecting AI systems as well as those developing and acquiring them, with reference to the AI Act. Use the checklist as a starting structure for internal AI audits, the leaflet format for transparency towards buyers and implementors, and the algo-score idea for end-user facing labels. AI Act sections 9, 10 Topics: ai, governance, transparency

docs.t: AI Risks: Optical Character Recognition and Named Entity Recognition
docs.x: Optical character recognition and named entity recognition carry specific data protection risks across procurement, development and use, and two reports prepared under the Support Pool of Experts programme list those risks with possible mitigations for each phase. They are the external author's views, not an EDPB position, and are written for the users, developers and procuring entities of such systems, with criteria for assessing likelihood and severity and for accepting residual risk. Use the risk catalogues when running a DPIA on document digitisation, redaction or entity extraction pipelines. Topic 13 Topics: ai, dpia

docs.t: Data Protection Officer training
docs.x: Training material for data protection officers, produced for the Croatian DPA under the Support Pool of Experts programme, comes in three modules: a general module, a public health sector module and an educational sector module. The material is in Croatian, the general module states it was submitted in May 2024, and it expresses the external author's views rather than an EDPB position. It is relevant to organisations designing DPO training or role-based curricula for public health and education, and to Croatian-speaking DPOs directly. Readiness governance Topics: governance

docs.t: Report on the use of SPE external experts
docs.x: Administrative report on how the Board's external expert pool was used in its first period.

docs.t: Standardised Messenger Audit
docs.x: Expert methodology for auditing messaging services against data protection requirements, for supervisory authorities.

docs.t: Report on the extraterritorial enforcement of the GDPR
docs.x: Report on enforcing the GDPR against organisations outside the EEA that fall under Article 3(2), covering representatives, service of decisions and international cooperation. For authorities.

docs.t: EDPB website auditing tool
docs.x: A free and open source tool, licensed under EUPL 1.2, lets legal and technical auditors prepare, complete and evaluate a compliance audit of a website by visiting it, and controllers and processors can run it against their own sites. It was prepared by external contractors under the Support Pool of Experts programme, is available in English and French with machine-translated German, Italian and Spanish versions, and the current release adds import and export of analyses, search, database management and full-page screenshots. Use it as the same lens a supervisory authority may apply when checking cookies, trackers and third-party requests. Topic 15; cookie scanner comparison Topics: cookies-tracking, enforcement

docs.t: One-Stop-Shop case digest on Security of Processing and Data Breach Notification
docs.x: Ninety final one-stop-shop decisions adopted between January 2019 and June 2023 show how supervisory authorities apply Articles 32, 33 and 34: a breach occurring does not by itself prove that security measures were inappropriate (a point the digest draws from the Advocate General's opinion in C-340/21), and authorities assess encryption, access controls, password policies and logging case by case across external attacks, weak internal practices and human error. Each notifiable breach (Article 33(1): any breach unless it is unlikely to result in a risk) must be notified separately even if the controller thinks it linked to others, breach documentation under Article 33(5) must be detailed enough for the authority to verify compliance, and the risk assessment decides whether affected individuals must be informed. Prepared by an external expert under the Support Pool of Experts programme; use it to calibrate breach severity and notification decisions against decided cases. Incident tool; topic 16 Topics: breach, security, enforcement

docs.x: Call for experts to join the Board's Support Pool of Experts. Administrative.

docs.t: Study on the secondary use of personal data in the context of scientific research
docs.x: Member States apply no uniform approach to the secondary use of personal data for scientific research: the GDPR does not define scientific research, national definitions and the choice between consent, public task and legitimate interests diverge, and views differ on whether a fresh legal basis is needed for secondary use. The study, commissioned by the EDPB from external researchers with substantive input from 18 countries, concludes that a legal basis is required for secondary use and recommends EDPB guidelines, codes of conduct and clarification of public interest under Article 9(2). It states its authors' views, not the Board's; treat it as a map of national divergence when designing cross-border research. Topic 11 Topics: lawful-basis, consent, other

docs.t: Legal study on government access to data in third countries - Brazil
docs.x: Brazil's 2018 General Data Protection Law mirrors the GDPR and its authority ANPD became independent by 2022, but national security, public security, defence and criminal prosecution fall outside that law, judicial orders are required under the Civil Rights Framework for the Internet, and comprehensive data protection rules for security-related access are still lacking, with the judiciary and legislature as the main oversight bodies. The externally authored study, prepared for the EDPB, does not bind the EDPB or its members and is not an adequacy finding. Exporters can cite it in transfer impact assessments for Brazil as an evidence base on the law and practice of government access, alongside their own analysis. TIA reference Topics: transfers
docs.m: Legal study by external providers · 01 April 2023

docs.t: Legal study on government access to data in third countries - Mexico and Turkey
docs.x: Mexico offers constitutional ARCO rights to all persons and a 2017 public-sector data protection law, but its 2005 National Security Law carves out national security with fewer safeguards and experts reported pressure on the independence of the authority INAI; Turkey recognises data protection as a constitutional right but exempts judicial, law enforcement and intelligence bodies from its data protection law, leaving gaps in necessity and proportionality, protection of foreigners, oversight independence and rights implementation. The study applies the Article 52(1) Charter test and does not represent the EDPB's official position. Use it as source material for transfer impact assessments involving either country. TIA reference Topics: transfers
docs.m: Legal study by external providers · 01 April 2023

docs.t: Legal study on government access to data in third countries - China, India, Russia
docs.x: Government access to personal data in China, India and Russia is subject to few effective limits: the study finds vague national security concepts, oversight that is absent or internal only, limited remedies for data subjects and, for China, no substantial protection against state access at all, with Russian intelligence agencies described as virtually unrestricted. Commissioned by the EDPB from external researchers and delivered as a final report in November 2021, it carries the authors' views rather than an EDPB position. Use it as documented, publicly available evidence in a transfer impact assessment under Recommendations 01/2020 whenever an exporter sends data to any of the three countries. TIA reference Topics: transfers

docs.t: Opinion 28/2025 regarding the European Commission Draft Implementing Decision pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2016/679 on the adequate protection of personal data by Brazil
docs.x: Brazil's LGPD is closely aligned with the GDPR and the ANPD, made a regulatory agency on 15 September 2025 with over 200 new posts and fines of up to 2% of revenue, is effective, so the EDPB supports the draft adequacy decision while asking the Commission to clarify and monitor whether the LGPD covers criminal law enforcement, the absence of an explicit high-risk DPIA duty, the commercial secrecy limit on transparency, the onward transfer exceptions in Article 33 LGPD, the breadth of national security and the 48-agency SISBIN intelligence system, and the National Council's influence over the ANPD. The Commission adopted the adequacy decision on 26 January 2026 (Decision (EU) 2026/179); exporters may rely on it within its scope, with four-yearly reviews. Adequacy opinions: the resulting decisions feed the Privacy Assessment transfer safeguards list Topics: transfers

docs.t: Opinion 26/2025 regarding the European Commission Draft Implementing Decision pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2016/679 on the adequate protection of personal data by the United Kingdom
docs.x: The UK framework as amended by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 remains aligned with the EU regime, so the EDPB supports renewing GDPR adequacy until December 2031. It asks the Commission to monitor the Secretary of State's powers to change the rules by secondary legislation, the ICO's new board structure and complaint triage, the recognised legitimate interests basis for disclosures to public authorities, the onward transfer test of protection not materially lower, relaxed automated decision-making rules, wider national security exemptions, technical capability notices affecting end-to-end encryption, bulk personal dataset authorisations and the immigration exemption. Exporters to the UK may keep relying on adequacy but should watch those points. Adequacy opinions: the resulting decisions feed the Privacy Assessment transfer safeguards list Topics: transfers

docs.t: Opinion 27/2025 regarding the European Commission Draft Implementing Decision pursuant to Directive (EU) 2016/680 on the adequate protection of personal data by the United Kingdom
docs.x: The EDPB supports extending the UK's Law Enforcement Directive adequacy for six years to 27 December 2031, reviewed within four years, while flagging that the Data (Use and Access) Act replaces the onward transfer test with a standard of protection not materially lower and drops factors such as national security rules, loosens automated decision-making with an exemption for avoiding obstruction of investigations, removes the duty to log justifications, widens national security exemptions under section 88, and gives the Secretary of State appointment powers over the restructured ICO. It asks the Commission to justify adequacy on each point. Law enforcement authorities exchanging data with UK counterparts may continue. Adequacy opinions: the resulting decisions feed the Privacy Assessment transfer safeguards list Topics: transfers, enforcement

docs.t: Opinion 06/2025 regarding the extension of the European Commission Implementing Decisions under the GDPR and the LED on the adequate protection of personal data in the United Kingdom
docs.x: The EDPB accepted a technical, time-limited six-month extension of the UK GDPR and LED adequacy decisions from 27 June 2025 to 27 December 2025, because the Data (Use and Access) Bill introduced on 23 October 2024 was not expected to pass before late spring and the amended framework could not be assessed in time. It stated that the extension was exceptional and should not in principle be prolonged again, and asked the Commission to monitor UK developments closely during the period. The extension has expired; the renewal is covered by Opinions 26/2025 and 27/2025 of 16 October 2025 on the draft decisions running to December 2031. Adequacy opinions: the resulting decisions feed the Privacy Assessment transfer safeguards list Topics: transfers Status: superseded

docs.t: Opinion 07/2025 regarding the European Commission Draft Implementing Decision pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2016/679 on the adequate protection of personal data by the European Patent Organisation
docs.x: The European Patent Organisation's Data Protection Rules of 30 June 2021, overseen by a Data Protection Officer and a Data Protection Board, resemble the EU framework closely enough for the EDPB to support the draft adequacy decision, adopted 5 May 2025, subject to clarifications: that the European Patent Office stays ultimately responsible despite delegated controllers, that onward transmissions to public authorities and non-EEA contracting states keep the protection level, that the Data Protection Board's complaint decisions become binding, and that the President's discretion to waive immunity for law enforcement requests is bounded. The Commission adopted the decision on 15 July 2025 (Decision (EU) 2025/1382); firms sending personal data to the EPO may rely on it within its scope, with four-yearly reviews. Adequacy opinions: the resulting decisions feed the Privacy Assessment transfer safeguards list Topics: transfers

docs.t: Opinion 5/2023 on the European Commission Draft Implementing Decision on the adequate protection of personal data under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework
docs.x: The EDPB welcomed that Executive Order 14086 introduces necessity and proportionality into US signals intelligence, binds the entire intelligence community and creates the Data Protection Review Court, while raising concerns about temporary bulk collection without prior independent authorisation, onward transfers, the standard non-appealable response of the redress court and the absence of specific rules on automated decision-making. It recommended that the Commission make adequacy conditional on the updated intelligence policies and procedures and closely monitor the redress mechanism. The Commission adopted the adequacy decision on 10 July 2023, so the opinion now serves as the reference for the review points. Adequacy opinions: the resulting decisions feed the Privacy Assessment transfer safeguards list Topics: transfers Status: historical

docs.t: Opinion 32/2021 regarding the European Commission Draft Implementing Decision pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2016/679 on the adequate protection of personal data in the Republic of Korea
docs.x: Korea's Personal Information Protection Act offers protection with numerous similarities to the GDPR, but the EDPB conditions its support on clarifications: the binding force of PIPC Notification No. 2021-1, the exemption of pseudonymised data from access, rectification and erasure rights, the lack of a general right to withdraw consent, onward transfers that rest on consent without disclosure of third-country risks, and unclear rules on government access and intelligence sharing. The opinion is addressed to the European Commission, which subsequently adopted the adequacy decision. Exporters relying on that decision should note the points the EDPB asked the Commission to monitor. Adequacy opinions: the resulting decisions feed the Privacy Assessment transfer safeguards list Topics: transfers Status: historical

docs.t: Opinion 14/2021 regarding the European Commission Draft Implementing Decision pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2016/679 on the adequate protection of personal data in the United Kingdom
docs.x: UK data protection law shows strong convergence with the GDPR on core principles, but the EDPB flags points the Commission must resolve or monitor: the broadly formulated immigration exemption, the UK's power to recognise third countries as adequate and its agreement with the US under the CLOUD Act, the absence of an Article 48 equivalent, bulk interception where selectors have not been examined by oversight bodies, and intelligence sharing under national security exemptions. The four-year sunset clause is welcomed as the safeguard against divergence. Addressed to the Commission, which adopted the decision; exporters to the UK should track the renewal and the areas listed for monitoring. Adequacy opinions: the resulting decisions feed the Privacy Assessment transfer safeguards list Topics: transfers Status: historical

docs.t: Opinion 15/2021 regarding the European Commission Draft Implementing Decision pursuant to Directive (EU) 2016/680 on the adequate protection of personal data in the United Kingdom
docs.x: The EDPB finds strong alignment between the UK Data Protection Act 2018 and the Law Enforcement Directive on lawfulness, purpose limitation, data quality, special categories and automated decisions, and finds the UK rules on onward transfers from law enforcement authorities essentially equivalent in principle. It asks the Commission to address onward transfers based on UK-only adequacy findings, national security access including certificates that restrict data protection duties, the independence of judicial commissioners, and the effect of the UK-US CLOUD Act agreement, and it welcomes the four-year sunset clause. Addressed to the Commission on 13 April 2021; relevant to competent authorities sharing data with UK law enforcement bodies rather than to private controllers. Adequacy opinions: the resulting decisions feed the Privacy Assessment transfer safeguards list Topics: transfers, other Status: historical

docs.t: Opinion 28/2018 regarding the European Commission Draft Implementing Decision on the adequate protection of personal data in Japan
docs.x: The Board welcomed the Supplementary Rules that Japan adopted to bridge gaps with the GDPR and called them essential to adequacy, but asked the Commission to resolve remaining concerns before finalising the decision: consent withdrawal treated as merely desirable, onward transfers losing the Supplementary Rule protections, record-keeping on data origin limited to three years, insufficient evidence that government access is essentially equivalent, and no general rules on automated decisions. It recommended review every two years rather than four and monitoring of the binding force of the PPC Guidelines. Exporters relying on the Japan adequacy decision should read it for the limits of the finding, notably on onward transfers. Adequacy opinions: the resulting decisions feed the Privacy Assessment transfer safeguards list Topics: transfers Status: historical

docs.t: Report on stakeholder event on processing of personal data to target or deliver political advertisements
docs.x: Stakeholders consulted online on 27 March 2026 (232 participants from platforms, ad tech, civil society, academia, public authorities and political entities) told the EDPB that the political advertising regulation (TTPA) leaves the definition of political advertising, the line between targeting and delivery, explicit consent and age verification unclear, that several platforms have stopped offering political advertising, and that platforms often misdescribe themselves as processors when they act as controllers. The report records those views for the EDPB's forthcoming TTPA guidelines and binds nobody. Publishers, platforms and campaigners should track the guidelines and settle controller roles in their advertising supply chain now. docs.t: Report on stakeholder event on anonymisation and pseudonymisation of 12 December 2025
docs.x: Stakeholders at the EDPB's remote event on 12 December 2025 (115 participants, mostly business associations, law firms, academia and NGOs) asked for a concrete, practical methodology for judging identifiability after the Court of Justice's ruling, especially for SMEs, and disagreed on whose perspective decides whether data is personal in controller-processor relationships and after transmission to third parties, third countries or the public. The report feeds the pseudonymisation Guidelines 01/2025 and the forthcoming anonymisation guidelines and binds nobody. Organisations relying on pseudonymised data sharing should document the re-identification risk assessment from the recipient's perspective and the legal, organisational and technical measures that support it. docs.t: EDPB Report on the public consultation on helpful templates for organisations to facilitate their GDPR compliance
docs.x: Of 82 written contributions received between 5 November and 3 December 2025 (71 from the EU and EEA, 11 from third countries), respondents most often asked for EU-level templates for records of processing activities, DPIAs, legitimate interest assessments, privacy notices, transfer impact assessments, processing agreements, breach notification forms and privacy risk assessments. The EDPB commits in its 2026–2027 work programme to produce three: a legitimate interest assessment, a record of processing activities and a privacy notice, harmonised with existing national templates, with more if time allows. Organisations, especially SMEs, should plan to align their internal forms with these once published rather than build new ones now. Templates to come Topics: governance, lawful-basis, transparency

docs.t: EDPB Work Programme 2026-2027
docs.x: The EDPB's 2026-2027 programme, adopted 11 February 2026, lists guidelines to expect on anonymisation, pseudonymisation, legitimate interest, children's data, consent or pay models, scientific research, generative AI data scraping, telemetry and diagnostic data and blockchain, EU templates for breach notifications, DPIAs, legitimate interest assessments, records of processing and privacy notices, updated DPO guidelines, updated guidelines on administrative fines, and guidance on the interplay of the GDPR with the AI Act, DMA, DSA, political advertising and AML rules, joint with other regulators for the AI Act and DMA. The 2026 coordinated enforcement action targets transparency obligations under Articles 12 to 14. Practitioners should map pending guidance against open policy decisions and prepare transparency notices for the 2026 sweep. Report: upcoming guidelines to watch Topics: governance, transparency

docs.t: Position paper on Interplay between data protection and competition law
docs.x: Data protection and competition law pursue distinct objectives but both protect the individual, as data subject and as consumer, and personal data is central to digital business models, so the two sets of authorities must coordinate. Following the CJEU judgment in Meta v Bundeskartellamt, a competition authority assessing abuse of dominance may need to examine GDPR compliance but cannot replace the competent data protection authority, and the principle of sincere cooperation makes cooperation mandatory in some cases. The paper recommends dedicated coordination teams, cooperation protocols with deadlines and information-sharing rules, and joint sector inquiries. Expect the data combination, terms of use and consent practices of dominant firms to be reviewed by both regulators. Privacy Assessment competitor-sharing factor Topics: governance, enforcement

docs.t: EDPB work programme 2026-2027 (consent or pay guidelines in preparation)
docs.x: EU. The work programme adopted at the EDPB's February 2026 plenary and announced on 12 February 2026 lists guidelines on consent or pay among the guidance the Board will deliver in the 2026-2027 cycle; the programme states no scope, but the expectation is that they extend the reasoning of Opinion 08/2024 beyond large online platforms. It binds no one and contains no rule, but it tells publishers running paid ad-free tiers that a general EDPB position covering their model is coming. Keep any consent or pay implementation aligned with Opinion 08/2024 now, including a free alternative with less intrusive advertising where feasible, and plan for a review when the guidelines are published for consultation. Topics: consent-or-pay, consent.

docs.t: EDPB-EDPS Joint Opinion 2/2026 on the Digital Omnibus proposal
docs.x: EU. The joint opinion supports a regulatory answer to consent fatigue but warns that moving the terminal equipment rules for personal data into the GDPR while non-personal data stays under the ePrivacy Directive splits one rule across two instruments, creates legal uncertainty and must not lower protection; it welcomes the six-month bar on repeat requests after a refusal in proposed Article 88a(4) and strongly supporting machine-readable preference signals in Article 88b. It asks that the Article 88a(3) exemptions be narrow: audience measurement limited to aggregated data not combined across services, and any contextual advertising exemption clearly delimited. It objects strongly to the proposed narrowing of the definition of personal data and to delegating that definition to Commission implementing acts. It binds no one, but it signals how supervisory authorities will read the amended rules if adopted. Topics: browser-signals, analytics-exemption, consent.

docs.t: EDPB Recommendations 2/2025 on the legal basis for requiring the creation of user accounts on e-commerce websites
docs.x: EU. Adopted on 3 December 2025 for a public consultation that closed on 12 February 2026, the recommendations find that a mandatory account for a one-off purchase is unlikely to pass the necessity test under Article 6(1)(b) (paragraph 23), that Article 6(1)(c) applies only exceptionally (paragraph 47), and that order tracking, loyalty, future purchases and fraud prevention do not meet the Article 6(1)(f) necessity and balancing tests (paragraphs 58 to 75). Consent is not available for a compulsory step, and a guest checkout beside voluntary registration is the most efficient lawful design (paragraph 89). They address e-commerce operators. Remove forced registration from checkout and keep account features opt-in. Topics: consent, dark-patterns, other.

docs.t: Digital Omnibus proposal, COM(2025) 837, 2025/0360(COD): new GDPR Articles 88a and 88b on terminal equipment and machine-readable consent signals
docs.x: EU. The proposal moves the rules on storing and accessing personal data on terminal equipment from Article 5(3) ePrivacy into a new GDPR Article 88a, which keeps consent as the default, exempts transmission, requested services, aggregated first-party audience measurement and security, and bars a fresh consent request for the same purpose for at least six months after a refusal. A new Article 88b obliges controllers to honour automated, machine-readable consent and refusal signals once standards exist, applying from 24 months after entry into force, and requires browser providers other than SMEs to offer the feature from 48 months after entry into force. As of September 2026 the file remains in committee with no Council general approach and no trilogue. Topics: browser-signals, analytics-exemption, consent. Status: proposed.

docs.t: CJEU, Case C-654/23, Inteligo Media SA v ANSPDCP (soft opt-in and free accounts)
docs.x: EU. The Court held that an email address collected when a user opens a free account giving access to extra articles and a daily newsletter, on a site whose model steers users to paid subscriptions, is obtained in the context of the sale of a product or service within Article 13(2) ePrivacy, so the newsletter promoting the operator's own similar services may be sent under the soft opt-in provided an opt-out was offered at collection and in every message. Where Article 13(2) governs the communication, the Article 6(1) GDPR conditions do not apply in addition. The case arose from a 9,000 euro Romanian fine. Map freemium sign-ups to the soft opt-in. Topics: email-marketing, consent. Status: decided.

docs.t: EDPB and European Commission joint guidelines on the interplay between the Digital Markets Act and the GDPR (draft for consultation)
docs.x: EU. The draft guidelines, endorsed by the EDPB and the Commission on 9 October 2025 and put to consultation until 4 December 2025, explain how a gatekeeper satisfies both the specific choice requirement of Article 5(2) DMA and the GDPR consent conditions when it combines or cross-uses personal data across core platform services, and cover data portability, app distribution and messaging interoperability. They address gatekeepers, with indirect effect on the advertisers and publishers that feed data into gatekeeper advertising systems. Use them to understand the consent flows that gatekeeper products will impose on your integrations. The final adopted version had not been located as of September 2026. Topics: consent, consent-or-pay, other. Status: proposed.

docs.t: Digital Fairness Act initiative (dark patterns, addictive design, consent fatigue)
docs.x: EU. The initiative follows the Commission's fitness check of EU consumer law and targets dark patterns, addictive design, unfair personalisation, influencer marketing and subscription cancellation, with decision fatigue from complex cookie and tracking choices cited as a pattern to address. A public consultation ran from 17 July to 24 October 2025, and the Commission work programme schedules the legislative proposal for the fourth quarter of 2026. As of September 2026 no proposal has been tabled and nothing binds anyone. Expect a consumer-law layer on top of Article 25 DSA and the GDPR for banner design, and audit interfaces now against the EDPB deceptive design categories. Topics: dark-patterns, consent. Status: proposed.

docs.t: European Commission non-compliance decision against Meta under Article 5(2) DMA (consent or pay model), fine of 200 million euro
docs.x: EU. The Commission found that Meta's binary choice between consenting to the combination of personal data for personalised advertising and paying for an ad-free subscription, introduced in November 2023, did not give users the specific choice of a service using less personal data that Article 5(2) DMA requires, and fined Meta 200 million euro for the period from March 2024, when DMA obligations became binding, to November 2024, when a revised model was introduced. Apple was fined 500 million euro in the same package. It binds only Meta, but it is the first EU-level enforcement of consent or pay. Publishers copying the model should offer a less data-intensive free option. Topics: consent-or-pay, enforcement, consent. Status: decided.

docs.t: Proposal for an ePrivacy Regulation, COM(2017) 10, 2017/0003(COD)
docs.x: EU. Tabled on 10 January 2017 to replace Directive 2002/58/EC with a directly applicable regulation on cookies, browser settings and direct marketing, the proposal reached a Council mandate on 10 February 2021 but never a trilogue agreement. The Commission's 2025 work programme of 11 February 2025 announced its withdrawal as outdated and without foreseeable agreement, the College approved the withdrawal on 16 July 2025, and it was published in the Official Journal on 6 October 2025 as C/2025/5423. It never bound anyone. The ePrivacy Directive remains the operative text and the Digital Omnibus of 19 November 2025 is the successor reform vehicle for terminal equipment rules. Topics: consent, browser-signals, other. Status: withdrawn.

docs.t: EDPB Guidelines 2/2023 on the technical scope of Article 5(3) of the ePrivacy Directive, version 2.0
docs.x: EU. The guidelines set three criteria for Article 5(3): information, whether personal or not; terminal equipment of a user, which requires a connection to a public communications network; and storage of, or gaining access to, that information. Paragraphs 47 to 63 apply them to URL and pixel tracking, local processing whose output is sent to a third party, tracking based on IP address alone, IoT reporting and unique identifiers, and find that each falls within Article 5(3) where the instruction to send information comes from code the entity distributed or, for IP-only tracking, where the address originates from the user's terminal equipment. Treat server-side tagging, link decoration, fingerprinting and pixel calls as consent events unless an exemption applies. Version 1.0 of 14 November 2023 is superseded. Topics: pixels-wiretap, strictly-necessary, consent.

docs.t: EDPB Opinion 08/2024 on valid consent in the context of consent or pay models implemented by large online platforms
docs.x: EU. Requested by the Dutch, Norwegian and Hamburg authorities, the opinion finds that in most cases a large online platform offering only a choice between behavioural advertising and a fee will not obtain freely given consent, and that platforms should consider an equivalent alternative without a fee, in particular a free version with advertising that processes less or no personal data (paragraphs 73 to 77). Any fee must not inhibit free choice (paragraph 85), and imbalance of power, lock-in and network effects weigh against validity (paragraphs 99 to 112). Authorities apply its reasoning to publishers. Model any paid alternative against the free, less intrusive option; general EDPB guidelines are in preparation. Topics: consent-or-pay, consent, cookie-walls.

docs.t: CJEU, Case C-604/22, IAB Europe v Gegevensbeschermingsautoriteit
docs.x: EU. The Court held that the TC String generated under the Transparency and Consent Framework is personal data within Article 4(1) GDPR, because combined with an identifier such as an IP address it allows the user to be identified, and that IAB Europe is a joint controller with its members for the recording of users' consent preferences in the TC String, though not for the later processing by participants unless it influences its purposes and means. It binds the framework operator and every publisher and vendor using the TCF. Treat consent strings as personal data in retention, security and rights handling, and run the current TCF version. Topics: tcf, consent, other. Status: decided.

docs.t: Digital Services Act, Regulation (EU) 2022/2065, Article 25 (dark patterns), Article 26 (advertising transparency) and Article 28 (minors)
docs.x: EU. Article 25(1) prohibits online platforms from designing or operating interfaces that deceive or manipulate users or materially distort their ability to make free and informed decisions, with Article 25(3) naming repeated choice prompts and prominence tricks as examples and Article 25(2) carving out practices covered by the GDPR or the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive. Article 26 requires each advertisement to show that it is an ad, who paid for it and the main targeting parameters, and bans ads profiled on special-category data. Article 28(2) bans profiling-based ads where the platform is reasonably certain the user is a minor. Applies from 17 February 2024; fines reach 6 per cent of turnover. Topics: dark-patterns, children, other.

docs.t: EDPB letter on the Commission's draft principles for a voluntary cookie pledge
docs.x: EU. The letter gives the Board's feedback on the Commission's draft cookie pledge principles and records that a voluntary pledge cannot be used to circumvent legal obligations, and that the validity of consent under Article 5(3) ePrivacy, Article 4(11) and Article 7 GDPR cannot be assessed in the abstract: whether a paid alternative to tracking secures free consent depends on whether a less intrusive alternative, such as contextual advertising, is also offered. It addressed the Commission, not operators. Practitioners meet it as one of the reasons the pledge is understood to have stalled and as an early statement of positions later formalised in Opinion 08/2024. Treat it as background only; the operative EDPB positions are in Opinion 08/2024 and the Cookie Banner Taskforce report. Topics: consent-or-pay, consent, other. Status: historical.

docs.t: European Commission cookie pledge initiative (draft pledging principles)
docs.x: EU. Announced on 28 March 2023 and developed through round tables and working groups, the pledge set out voluntary principles for signatories: no consent request for strictly necessary cookies, upfront disclosure that content is financed by advertising, clear presentation of the business model and the choices, a less intrusive advertising alternative, fewer repeat consent requests per tracker, no further consent requests after a business model choice, and a one-year non-solicitation period after a refusal. Draft principles were presented on 19 December 2023, to be finalised in January 2024 and put to the Consumer Summit of April 2024, but no pledge was ever signed: the Commission closed the project on 8 November 2024 with a summary and three annexes, including best practice principles and the EDPB opinion. Its ideas resurface in the Digital Omnibus six-month rule. Topics: consent, consent-or-pay, strictly-necessary. Status: historical.

docs.t: CJEU, Case C-252/21, Meta Platforms and Others v Bundeskartellamt
docs.x: EU.
