The Grand Chamber held that a competition authority may examine GDPR compliance when assessing abuse of dominance, provided it cooperates with the supervisory authorities; that collecting data from other group services and third-party sites is necessary for the contract under Article 6(1)(b) only where it is objectively indispensable to a purpose integral to the contract, and can rest on Article 6(1)(f) only where the interest was disclosed to users, the processing is strictly necessary and the balancing favours the controller; and that a dominant position does not by itself invalidate consent but is an important factor in judging whether it was freely given, with the burden on the operator. Visiting a website revealing sensitive characteristics does not make that data manifestly public. Treat contract and legitimate interest as hard to sustain for off-site tracking data used in ad personalisation. Topics: consent, consent-or-pay, health-data. Status: decided.

docs.t: Digital Markets Act, Regulation (EU) 2022/1925, Article 5(2) (consent for combining and cross-using personal data)
docs.x: EU. Article 5(2) prohibits a gatekeeper from processing third-party data for advertising through its core platform services, combining personal data across its services or with third-party data, cross-using data between services, or signing users in to other services to combine data, unless the user has been presented with a specific choice and has given GDPR-standard consent. A refused or withdrawn consent may be asked for again at most once a year. The obligation binds each designated gatekeeper six months after its designation, which for the first six gatekeepers meant 6 March 2024, with fines up to 10 per cent of worldwide turnover and 20 per cent for repeat infringements. Publishers using gatekeeper advertising products should expect the gatekeeper to surface the consent moment and align their tag configuration with it. Topics: consent, consent-or-pay, enforcement.

docs.t: EDPB Guidelines 03/2022 on deceptive design patterns in social media platform interfaces, version 2.0
docs.x: EU. The guidelines name six families of deceptive design pattern, overloading, skipping, stirring, obstructing, fickle and left in the dark, and assess each against Article 5(1)(a) fairness and transparency, Article 12 transparency, Article 25 data protection by design and default, and the Articles 4(11) and 7 consent conditions. They are written for social media providers but the assessment method transfers to any consent interface, and supervisory authorities cite them in cookie banner decisions. Use the pattern catalogue as an audit list for banner copy, colour contrast, click depth and withdrawal paths, and record the review under Article 5(2) accountability. Topics: dark-patterns, consent, reject-button.

docs.t: EDPB Report of the work undertaken by the Cookie Banner Taskforce
docs.x: EU. The report records the positions supervisory authorities share on the noyb banner complaints: a first layer with an accept button but no reject option is non-compliant (paragraphs 6 to 8); pre-ticked boxes do not create consent (paragraphs 9 to 10); a reject option hidden as a small link or outside the banner is insufficient (paragraphs 11 to 14); unreadable button contrast is manifestly misleading (paragraph 18); legitimate interest cannot ground a cookie under Article 5(3) (paragraphs 20 to 25); operators must prove and keep updated the list of essential cookies (paragraph 28); and withdrawal must be as easy as consent (paragraph 34). It sets the common enforcement baseline. Topics: reject-button, dark-patterns, strictly-necessary.

docs.t: noyb, 422 formal GDPR complaints filed against cookie banners after the warning period
docs.x: EU. After the May 2021 warning letters, noyb reported that 42 percent of the flagged violations were remedied within 30 days but 82 percent of companies had not fully stopped violating the GDPR, and filed 422 formal complaints with ten European authorities, among them 36 major sites that had resisted any change, targeting missing reject buttons, pre-ticked boxes, deceptive colours, absent withdrawal options and unsupported legitimate-interest claims. Roughly half went to the Austrian DPA. Decisions from these complaints continued to arrive in 2025 and 2026, so a banner that passed in 2021 may still be the subject of a pending case. Topics: dark-patterns, reject-button, enforcement. Status: historical.

docs.t: noyb, cookie banner campaign launch: more than 500 draft complaints to websites using unlawful banners
docs.x: EU. noyb sent draft complaints to more than 500 websites across 33 countries, generated with an automated scanner, after finding that 81 percent of scanned banners offered no reject option on the first layer, 73 percent used deceptive colours and contrasts, and 90 percent offered no simple way to withdraw consent, and announced up to 10,000 complaints over 2021. Recipients were given a month to fix their banners before formal complaints. The campaign, later routed through ten data protection authorities, is the origin of many of the national decisions on this page, including the Austrian, Swedish and Belgian ones. Topics: dark-patterns, reject-button, enforcement. Status: historical.

docs.t: EDPB Guidelines 8/2020 on the targeting of social media users, version 2.0
docs.x: EU. The guidelines apply Wirtschaftsakademie and Fashion ID to advertising: a targeter that embeds a social media pixel or plug-in jointly determines the purpose of the collection and transmission with the platform and is a joint controller for those operations, though not for what the platform does afterwards. Where targeting relies on tracking across websites, Article 5(3) consent is the only available basis, legitimate interest is excluded, and the parties need an Article 26 arrangement. They set the standard applied to social media providers and to every advertiser or publisher that installs their tags. Tie every pixel to a consent purpose, document the joint controllership split, and cover the transmission in the privacy notice. Topics: pixels-wiretap, consent, other.

docs.t: CJEU, Case C-61/19, Orange Romania SA v ANSPDCP
docs.x: EU. The Court held under Articles 4(11) and 6(1)(a) GDPR (and the equivalent Directive 95/46 provisions) that the controller must prove the data subject consented by active behaviour after receiving information in clear and plain language, and that a contract clause recording consent does not prove it where the controller pre-ticked the box, where the terms could mislead the customer about being able to contract without consenting, or where refusing required completing an extra form. The case concerned identity documents in a telecoms contract, but the reasoning applies to any consent flow. Keep the refusal path no longer than the acceptance path and retain evidence of the affirmative act. Topics: consent, dark-patterns. Status: decided.

docs.t: EDPB Guidelines 05/2020 on consent under Regulation 2016/679
docs.x: EU. The guidelines spell out the Article 4(11) and Article 7 conditions and add two positions that shape banners directly: access to a website cannot be conditioned on accepting cookies (a cookie wall does not produce freely given consent, paragraph 39), and scrolling or swiping through a page is not a clear affirmative action (paragraph 86). They also require granular purposes, a documented record, and withdrawal as easy as giving consent. They set the standard the authorities apply to every controller relying on consent, including for the GDPR processing that follows a cookie. Use them as the checklist for banner wording, button design and consent logs. They replace Article 29 Working Party Guidelines WP259 on consent. Topics: consent, cookie-walls, reject-button.

docs.t: CJEU, Case C-673/17, Bundesverband der Verbraucherzentralen v Planet49 GmbH
docs.x: EU. The Court held that consent under Article 5(3) ePrivacy, read with Article 2(h) of Directive 95/46 and Article 4(11) GDPR, is not validly given by a pre-ticked checkbox the user must deselect, and that this applies whether or not the information stored or accessed is personal data. It also held that the information the operator must give includes the duration of the cookies and whether third parties may have access to them. The ruling binds every operator setting cookies on EU users' devices and is the source of the active opt-in rule. Check that no toggle is preset to on and that the banner discloses lifetimes and third-party recipients. Topics: consent, reject-button. Status: decided.

docs.t: CJEU, Case C-40/17, Fashion ID GmbH & Co. KG v Verbraucherzentrale NRW eV
docs.x: EU. The Court held that a website operator embedding a third-party social plug-in that causes the visitor's browser to send personal data to the plug-in provider is a joint controller with that provider for the collection and disclosure by transmission, but not for the provider's subsequent processing. The operator must itself provide the information due at collection and, where consent is the basis, obtain it for the collection and transmission it controls. It binds every site that embeds a third-party pixel, plug-in or script that fires before consent. Gate every third-party tag behind consent, name the recipient in the notice, and agree the Article 26 allocation with the vendor. Topics: pixels-wiretap, consent, other. Status: decided.

docs.t: EDPB Opinion 5/2019 on the interplay between the ePrivacy Directive and the GDPR
docs.x: EU. The opinion holds that where the ePrivacy Directive particularises the GDPR the specific rule prevails, so where Article 5(3) requires consent for storing or accessing information on a device, no other Article 6 GDPR basis can replace it, and the later processing of the personal data collected still needs its own GDPR basis. It also confirms that the GDPR one-stop-shop and consistency mechanism do not extend to ePrivacy enforcement, which stays with the national authority each Member State designates. Adopted under Article 64(2), it states the reading the supervisory authorities apply to every operator. Expect parallel national enforcement of cookie rules without a lead authority, and never justify a tracking cookie on legitimate interest. Topics: consent, enforcement, other.

docs.t: General Data Protection Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Articles 4(11), 6, 7 and 25 and Recital 30
docs.x: EU. Article 4(11) defines consent as freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, shown by a statement or clear affirmative action, and Article 7 adds the burden of proof, separability, and withdrawal as easy as giving consent. Recital 30 names cookie identifiers and IP addresses as identifiers that may make a person identifiable, so tracking data is personal data and Article 6 requires a legal basis for what follows collection. Article 25 requires privacy by design and by default, applied by regulators to default banner settings. Applies from 25 May 2018 to processing in the context of an EU establishment and, under Article 3(2), to controllers elsewhere that offer goods or services to people in the Union or monitor their behaviour there (residence or citizenship alone is not the test); fines reach 20 million euro or 4 per cent of turnover. Topics: consent, dark-patterns, other.

docs.t: CJEU, Case C-582/14, Patrick Breyer v Bundesrepublik Deutschland (dynamic IP addresses)
docs.x: EU. The Court held that a dynamic IP address recorded by a website operator is personal data in relation to that operator where it has legal means to obtain from the access provider the additional information needed to identify the visitor, and that national law cannot limit the legitimate interest ground so as to exclude retention of that data to keep the site working and defend it against attacks. It binds every operator logging visitor IP addresses, and Recital 30 GDPR and EDPB Guidelines 2/2023 build on it. Treat IP-based analytics, fraud checks and server logs as personal data processing with a stated legal basis and retention period. Topics: other, analytics-exemption. Status: decided.

docs.t: ePrivacy Directive 2002/58/EC as amended by Directive 2009/136/EC, Article 5(3) and Article 13
docs.x: EU. Article 5(3) permits the storing of information, or the gaining of access to information already stored, in a user's terminal equipment only with consent given after clear and comprehensive information, with exceptions for transmission of a communication and for storage or access strictly necessary for a service explicitly requested by the user. Article 13(1) requires prior consent for automated calls, fax and email marketing, and Article 13(2) sets the soft opt-in for email marketing of own similar products to existing customers. The rules bind anyone placing cookies, pixels or scripts on EU users' devices, whatever the sender's location. Map every tag against the two exemptions and keep the consent record. Topics: consent, strictly-necessary, email-marketing.

docs.t: EDPB, article 65 binding decision requiring the Belgian DPA to examine a noyb cookie banner complaint against VRT on the merits
docs.x: Belgium. In a dispute resolution decision adopted on 28 May 2026 under article 65(1)(a) GDPR, the EDPB rejected the Belgian DPA's dismissal, as an abuse of rights under articles 77 and 80(1), of a cookie banner complaint that noyb lodged with the Austrian DPA on behalf of an individual against the Belgian public broadcaster, and instructed the Belgian DPA as lead authority to assess the complaint on its merits and submit a new draft decision under article 60(3). The decision closes the Belgian route of dismissing NGO-backed model complaints; cross-border banner complaints will be decided on substance. Topics: enforcement, dark-patterns. Status: decided.

docs.t: Bundesverwaltungsgericht (Austria), W171 2303402-1: ORF.at must give accept and reject buttons equal prominence
docs.x: Austria. The Federal Administrative Court upheld an October 2024 DSB decision, originating in noyb's August 2021 campaign against 422 websites, that the public broadcaster's banner used deceptive design by colouring the Accept button and leaving Reject less prominent, leading to unintended consent in breach of transparency and freely given consent. ORF must redesign the banner so that both buttons receive equal prominence. This is the first Austrian court ruling on button colour and contrast; Austrian-facing sites should remove visual hierarchy between the two first-layer options. Topics: dark-patterns, reject-button. Status: decided.

docs.t: CNIL, Deliberation 2026-042: recommendation on tracking pixels in emails
docs.x: France. The recommendation, adopted on 12 March 2026 and published on 14 April 2026, states that open-tracking pixels in emails require consent under article 82, with two exemptions: security measures that help authenticate the user, and measuring individual open rates for deliverability, limited to what is needed to adapt or stop sending to inactive recipients. Both exemptions cover only emails the recipient asked for or that relate to a service they requested, such as transactional messages (order confirmations, password resets, account alerts) and messages they consented to receive; pixel consent is separate from consent to receive the email itself, although one consent can cover direct marketing and the pixel purposes connected to it. Senders must clearly inform recipients about pixels and let them withdraw consent as easily as they gave it, for example through a footer link. For addresses collected before publication, senders had three months to inform recipients and give them an easy objection route. Email platforms and marketing teams should reconfigure open tracking to consent-gated operation. Topics: email-marketing, pixels-wiretap, consent.

docs.t: CNIL, 3.5 million euro fine for transmitting loyalty-member data to a social network and for eleven cookies placed before choice
docs.x: France. The CNIL fined an unnamed retailer 3.5 million euros for sending loyalty members' email addresses and phone numbers to a social media platform for targeted advertising since February 2018 without a valid legal basis (article 6 GDPR) and without adequate information or rights handling (articles 12 and 13), for weak password rules (article 32), for a missing impact assessment (article 35), and under article 82 because eleven consent-requiring cookies were written before any choice and were neither deleted nor stopped from being read after refusal, affecting more than 10.5 million people. Customer-matching uploads to ad platforms need their own legal basis, separate from the cookie banner. Topics: pixels-wiretap, consent, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: CNIL, American Express Carte France fined 1.5 million euros for cookies placed on arrival and read after refusal
docs.x: France. The CNIL fined American Express Carte France 1.5 million euros under article 82 after January 2023 inspections of americanexpress.com/fr-fr showed cookies placed on arrival before any choice, advertising cookies still placed after refusal, and previously placed cookies read after consent was withdrawn. The CNIL noted that the rules were well known from its long-running action plan, and reduced the penalty because the company came into compliance during the proceedings. A mid-sized fine for a national subsidiary shows the CNIL is now enforcing beyond the largest platforms. Topics: consent, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens, more than 200 websites warned over misleading cookie banners; three quarters corrected, enforcement against the rest
docs.x: Netherlands. The AP announced that, since it began structural checks in April 2025, it had warned more than 200 websites about their cookie banners, that about three quarters had already adjusted them, and that it was now taking enforcement steps against those that had not. Its position is that tracking cookies may be placed only with voluntary consent given on the basis of clear and correct information, and that the simplest way to respect users' choice is not to use tracking software at all, so no banner is needed. Organisations serving Dutch users should treat an AP warning as the last step before a formal investigation. Topics: dark-patterns, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: BfDI recognises the first consent management service under the EinwV (Consenter)
docs.x: Germany. On 17 October 2025 the Federal Commissioner (BfDI) recognised the first service under the Einwilligungsverwaltungsverordnung, the PIMS Consenter from Law & Innovation Technology GmbH, and entered it in the public register required by section 13 EinwV. Recognition makes the section 19 EinwV duties concrete for any German digital service that chooses to integrate the service: stored end-user settings must be honoured, and users without stored settings must be told which service the provider uses and that settings can be made there. Consent platforms operating in Germany should decide whether to interoperate with recognised services and document that decision. Topics: browser-signals, consent.

docs.t: CNIL, Google LLC and Google Ireland fined 325 million euros for cookies at account creation and adverts inserted between Gmail emails
docs.x: France. The CNIL fined Google LLC 200 million euros and Google Ireland Limited 125 million euros for placing advertising cookies during Google account creation without valid, informed consent (article 82 of the French Data Protection Act) and for displaying adverts between emails in the Gmail Promotions and Social tabs without prior consent (article L.34-5 of the Postal and Electronic Communications Code), affecting more than 74 million accounts and 53 million users respectively. Both companies must comply within six months under a penalty of 100,000 euros per day of delay. Account sign-up flows are cookie consent flows and the same banner standard applies. Topics: consent, email-marketing, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: CNIL, Infinite Styles Services (SHEIN) fined 150 million euros for cookies placed without consent
docs.x: France. The CNIL fined SHEIN's Irish subsidiary 150 million euros under article 82 because shein.com, visited by around 12 million people in France each month, placed cookies before consent, kept reading them after refusal or withdrawal, and used two incomplete banners that omitted the advertising purpose and the third parties involved. The company fixed the site during the procedure, so no injunction was issued, but the fine stands at the upper end of the CNIL's cookie sanctions. Withdrawal must stop both writing and reading of existing cookies. Topics: consent, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: Bundesverwaltungsgericht (Austria), DerStandard pay or okay: DSB decision confirmed, consent must be granular
docs.x: Austria. The Federal Administrative Court confirmed the DSB's 2023 finding that derstandard.at did not obtain valid consent under its pay-or-okay model (subscription priced at 9.90 euros per month) because users could only consent or refuse globally, whereas the GDPR requires the option to consent separately to distinct processing purposes; the DSB had not objected to the model as such. The court allowed an appeal to the Supreme Administrative Court on the novel question. Austrian publishers using consent-or-pay must offer per-purpose consent inside the tracked option and should expect a referral to the CJEU. Topics: consent-or-pay, consent. Status: under appeal.

docs.t: Datatilsynet and Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, joint guidance on the use of cookies and similar technologies
docs.x: Denmark. The two Danish authorities issued one guidance document, with a supplementary annex of practical advice and an accompanying podcast, covering both the cookie order and the data protection rules that often apply in parallel: the cookie order requires consent before cookies are placed, and the GDPR governs the processing that follows, including any statistics or advertising. The guidance goes through the main rules of each regime, gives practical advice and examples, and flags the typical pitfalls. Danish-facing sites should re-check banners against it, in particular the treatment of statistics cookies. Topics: consent, analytics-exemption.

docs.t: Brussels Market Court, judgment 2022/AR/292 on IAB Europe's appeal against decision 21/2022
docs.x: Belgium. Applying the CJEU's judgment in C-604/22 of 7 March 2024, the Market Court ruled with full jurisdiction that the TC String is personal data and that IAB Europe is joint controller for processing of user preferences within the TCF, confirmed the infringements and the 250,000 euro fine, but annulled the Belgian DPA's decision 21/2022 for procedural reasons and rejected the DPA's finding that IAB Europe is controller for processing occurring entirely within the OpenRTB protocol. Publishers and vendors relying on TCF signals remain individually responsible for a valid legal basis and transparency; the framework alone does not deliver compliance. Topics: tcf, consent, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: Integritetsskyddsmyndigheten (IMY), three cookie banner decisions: reprimands for Warner Music Sweden, ATG and Aller Media
docs.x: Sweden. Investigating complaints channelled through the EDPB cookie banner taskforce, IMY reprimanded Warner Music Sweden (October 2024) for not adequately informing users of the right to withdraw consent (articles 6 and 7(3) GDPR), ATG (December 2024) for not making withdrawal as easy as consent and for misleading banner design that hindered informed and voluntary consent, and Aller Media (April 2025) for processing without a legal basis by citing legitimate interest for cookie data without a documented balancing test (article 6(1)(f)). IMY noted that the Post and Telecom Authority (PTS) alone supervises the Electronic Communications Act's cookie rules, while IMY supervises the subsequent GDPR processing. Swedish-facing sites need a documented basis for post-consent processing, not only a banner. Topics: dark-patterns, consent, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: CNIL, Deliberation 2025-024: recommendation on mobile applications (amended version)
docs.x: France. The recommendation, first adopted on 18 July 2024 (Deliberation 2024-061) and replaced by the amended version adopted in Deliberation 2025-024 of 27 March 2025 and published on 8 April 2025, sets the CNIL's expectations for each actor in the mobile chain (publisher, developer, SDK provider, operating system and store), including how consent for trackers and permissions must be collected in-app under article 82 and the GDPR. The 2025 amendments are targeted corrections and clarifications, shown in an annotated version, including the roles of publisher and SDK provider in one SDK example. Apps distributed in France should map SDKs against it and treat it as the yardstick for CNIL app inspections. Topics: consent, other.

docs.t: Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens, five cookie banner investigations closed after corrections (deceptive banners)
docs.x: Netherlands. The Dutch DPA reported that all five organisations it investigated in 2024, across finance, media and hospitality, broke the law through hidden reject buttons, pre-ticked boxes and cookies placed before or despite refusal, and that all five corrected their banners after its intervention. The AP restated its rules: ask permission clearly without tricks that make saying no difficult, place no tracking cookies without consent, and rely on the exemption only for strictly necessary functional cookies. It announced systematic checks of around 10,000 Dutch websites, with warnings before fines. Dutch-facing sites should expect a warning letter and a short window to fix the first layer. Topics: reject-button, dark-patterns, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: Germany, Einwilligungsverwaltungsverordnung (EinwV): regulation on recognised consent management services
docs.x: Germany. The regulation (BGBl. 2025 I Nr. 32), in force since 1 April 2025 under section 26(2) TDDDG, defines the requirements a consent management service must meet to be recognised (user-friendly and competition-neutral procedures, switching, security concept, a public register under section 13) and names the recognising authority. Integration by digital service providers is voluntary (section 18(1)), but a provider that integrates a recognised service must respect the stored settings and point users to them when asking for consent (section 19), and browsers should not suppress or alter the signal (section 17). The provider stays responsible for GDPR consent validity (section 1(2)). Topics: browser-signals, consent.

docs.t: Verwaltungsgericht Hannover, judgment 10 A 5385/22: a reject all button on the first layer is mandatory
docs.x: Germany. The administrative court upheld an order by the Lower Saxony data protection commissioner against a publisher, holding that where a banner offers Accept all it must offer an equally visible Reject all on the same layer, that repeating the banner to pressure users and highlighting the accept option violate the requirement of freely given consent, and that information on third-party partners, transfers outside the EU and revocation must be immediately visible. The judgment is the first German administrative court decision on banner design and backs supervisory orders under section 25 TDDDG. Treat nudging patterns as grounds for a binding order, not only a fine. Topics: reject-button, dark-patterns, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: UODO, bulletin 03/2025: the Polish DPA's position on cookie consent and banners
docs.x: Poland. The Polish supervisory authority's March 2025 bulletin states that consent to cookies must be voluntary, informed, unambiguous and preceded by an active user action, that pre-ticked boxes are invalid, that withdrawing consent must be as easy as giving it, that cookie walls which block access to a site unless cookies are accepted are incompatible with the GDPR, and that clear pre-consent information on data, recipients and purposes is required; it relies on EDPB Guidelines 05/2020, the EDPB cookie banner task force report and the CJEU judgments in Planet49 (C-673/17) and Orange Romania (C-61/19). The bulletin applies the GDPR consent standard to banners directly and notes that not every article in it states the authority's official position. Topics: consent, cookie-walls, dark-patterns.

docs.t: Spain, Ley 34/2002 (LSSI), article 22.2: consent for storage devices on terminal equipment
docs.x: Spain. Article 22.2 LSSI allows a service provider to store or access information on a recipient's terminal only after the recipient has consented on the basis of clear and complete information about the purposes, exempts storage strictly necessary for transmission or for a service the user requested, and permits consent to be expressed through appropriate browser or application settings where technically possible. It binds providers established in Spain and non-EU providers that direct their services at Spain. The consolidated text was last updated on 23 January 2025 and the AEPD enforces it as a leve infringement, which becomes grave on repeat offences within three years. Topics: consent, strictly-necessary.

docs.t: CNIL, formal notices to website publishers over misleading cookie banners
docs.x: France. The CNIL served formal notices on several publishers whose banners made the refusal option smaller, paler or buried in text, repeated the accept option several times while offering refusal once in unclear wording, or left too little visual separation between the refusal link and surrounding text, giving each one month to comply. The notices restate that refusing must be as simple as accepting and that information must be clear and complete. Use the listed patterns as a design checklist: contrast, size and wording of the refuse control are now enforcement criteria in France. Topics: dark-patterns, reject-button, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: Garante, provvedimento n. 670: warning and compliance order after Guardia di Finanza cookie inspections of e-commerce sites
docs.x: Italy. Under a 2021 protocol, the Garante delegated online checks of a sample of e-commerce operators to the Guardia di Finanza's privacy unit; on the inspected shop the banner offered OK and No grazie but no cookie policy existed and no cookie categories were disclosed, so consent could not be specific or informed. The Garante found breaches of articles 4(11), 5, 7, 12, 13, 24 and 25 GDPR and article 122 of the Code, issued a warning under article 58(2)(b) and ordered a compliant banner with an information layer, without a fine because the operator had partly remediated. Italian sweeps target small sites and turn on documentation, not only buttons. Topics: consent, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: Germany, TDDDG section 25 (Telekommunikation-Digitale-Dienste-Datenschutz-Gesetz, formerly TTDSG): protection of privacy in terminal equipment
docs.x: Germany. Section 25(1) TDDDG permits storing information on, or accessing information already stored in, an end user's terminal only with consent given on the basis of clear and comprehensive information, and requires that information and consent meet the GDPR standard. Section 25(2) exempts storage or access whose sole purpose is transmitting a message over a public network, or which is strictly necessary for a digital service the user has expressly requested. The provision applies to any provider of digital services reaching German users, irrespective of whether personal data is involved. The act was renamed from TTDSG to TDDDG on 14 May 2024 with the section unchanged. Topics: consent, strictly-necessary.

docs.t: AEPD, Guia sobre el uso de las cookies (May 2024 edition)
docs.x: Spain. The current guide applies article 22.2 LSSI together with the GDPR and LOPDGDD: a reject option must sit at the same layer and with the same visibility as accept, consent should be renewed at most every 24 months, cookie walls are lawful only with clear notice and a genuinely equivalent alternative that need not be free, and access to legally guaranteed rights cannot be blocked. A May 2024 section transposes EDPB Opinion 08/2024: large platforms will in most cases not obtain valid consent from a binary pay-or-consent choice and should consider a free alternative such as contextual advertising. It is the reference for AEPD sanction procedures in Spain. Topics: reject-button, consent-or-pay, cookie-walls.

docs.t: BayLDA, press release on automated checks of cookie banners on 350 websites and 15 apps
docs.x: Germany. The Bavarian State Office for Data Protection Supervision announced that in a partly automated sweep it had checked more than 350 Bavarian websites and 15 apps, finding that almost all apps ran consent-requiring processes before any consent and that about 350 websites failed the requirement, tested by its automated banner tool, that the option to withhold consent appear on the first layer alongside Accept all. Operators were given the opportunity to respond and fix their sites, and the BayLDA said it would extend the tool to further consent platforms. Expect scripted first-layer checks from German state authorities and design banners to pass them without human review. Topics: reject-button, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: Oberlandesgericht Koeln, judgment 6 U 80/23: accept and reject options in a cookie banner must be equivalent
docs.x: Germany. The OLG Koeln held that a banner offering Accept, Settings and an X labelled Accept and close in the corner on the first layer, and only Save or Accept all on the second, gave users no rejection option equivalent to the consent option on either layer, and that pairing the X with Accept and close was misleading and intransparent, so the consent is invalid under section 25 TTDSG. The claim was brought by a consumer association against a weather portal; the judgment (6 U 80/23, 19 January 2024) is not final. Site operators in Germany face civil injunctions from competitors and associations, not only regulators, for asymmetric banners; give both options the same layer and weight. Topics: reject-button, dark-patterns. Status: decided.

docs.t: CNIL, Yahoo EMEA fined 10 million euros for ignoring cookie refusals and tying withdrawal to loss of email access
docs.x: France. The CNIL fined Yahoo EMEA Limited 10 million euros under article 82 because yahoo.com continued to place advertising cookies after users refused them, and because Yahoo Mail users who wanted to withdraw cookie consent were told they would lose access to their mailbox, which the CNIL treated as a consent that was not freely given. The case followed 27 complaints. Withdrawal must be possible without penalty to the core service, and a refusal must be honoured technically, not just displayed. Topics: consent, cookie-walls, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: AEPD, press release: cookie guide updated to the EDPB deceptive design guidelines, compliance by 11 January 2024
docs.x: Spain. The AEPD announced that its cookie guide now incorporates EDPB Guidelines 03/2022 on deceptive design: accept and reject actions must be presented in a prominent place and format, rejection cannot be harder than acceptance, access may be conditioned on consent only where an alternative access route exists (which need not be free), and personalisation chosen by the user is technical while personalisation decided by the publisher needs an accept or reject choice. Sites were given until 11 January 2024 to comply. The July 2023 text has since been replaced by the May 2024 edition of the guide. Topics: reject-button, dark-patterns, cookie-walls. Status: superseded.

docs.t: CNIL, Criteo fined 40 million euros for retargeting without proof of consent (upheld by the Conseil d'Etat, decision no. 482872)
docs.x: France. The CNIL fined Criteo 40 million euros for failing to demonstrate under article 7(1) GDPR that its publisher partners had collected valid consent for its tracker, for incomplete information that disclosed only personalised advertising and not the reuse of the data to configure and improve its targeting algorithms (articles 12, 13 and 15), for treating erasure requests by merely stopping personalised ads while keeping the identifiers and training on the data (article 17) and for joint-controller contracts missing required terms on rights, breach notification and impact assessments (article 26). An adtech vendor must audit partner consent, not merely contract for it: the Conseil d'Etat held that contracting the duty to partners does not relieve the controller of holding the proof. On 4 March 2026 it rejected Criteo's appeal in full, holding that pseudonymous identifiers tied to browsing data are personal data because the volume and precision of the information recouped for one identifier make at least some users identifiable without disproportionate effort. Topics: consent, tcf, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: DSK, Beschluss zur Bewertung von Pur-Abo-Modellen auf Websites
docs.x: Germany. The German authorities accept consent-or-pay (Pur-Abo) models on websites only where the paid alternative gives fundamentally the same service at a market-standard price, consent for the tracked version meets every GDPR requirement including granular consent per materially distinct purpose, and the paid version stores or reads only what is strictly necessary for the chosen service. Blanket consent covering materially different purposes is invalid; only closely related purposes may be bundled. Publishers using Pur-Abo models in Germany should separate advertising, measurement and personalisation consents and audit the paid path for tracking; the EDPB's April 2024 opinion adds stricter conditions for large platforms. Topics: consent-or-pay, consent.

docs.t: Datatilsynet, guidance on the use of cookie walls (four criteria) following two decisions
docs.x: Denmark. Datatilsynet published four criteria for lawful cookie walls after two decisions: one publisher was found compliant because its paid alternative was substantially equivalent and reasonably priced, another non-compliant because the service offered against consent was not substantially similar to the paid one. The criteria require a reasonable alternative for visitors who refuse, a price that does not make the choice illusory, consent requested only for purposes needed to fund the free path (statistics and personalisation need separate consent), and only strictly necessary processing on the paid path. Both publishers received orders on statistical purposes. Topics: cookie-walls, consent-or-pay.

docs.t: AEPD, PS/00393/2022: Infinity Ecom fined 10,000 euros, including 5,000 euros for non-essential cookies placed without consent
docs.x: Spain. The AEPD fined an online shop 5,000 euros under article 22.2 LSSI and 5,000 euros under article 13 GDPR after finding Shopify, Klaviyo, Pinterest, Google and Meta cookies (for example _shopify_y, _gcl_au and _fbp) placed before any consent, with no working consent mechanism or granular panel and a privacy policy missing the controller's identity. The amounts are small but the reasoning is routine: named third-party cookies observed before choice are enough for a sanction. Small merchants on hosted platforms should verify that platform and plugin tags are actually gated by the banner. Topics: consent, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: CNIL, Deliberation SAN-2022-027: TikTok fined 5 million euros for a banner without an equivalent refuse option
docs.x: France. The CNIL fined TikTok Information Technologies UK Limited and TikTok Technology Limited 5 million euros because, between May 2020 and June 2022, tiktok.com let users accept cookies in one click but refuse only through several clicks, and because neither the banner nor the consent tool adequately described cookie purposes, in breach of article 82. The CNIL weighed the number of French users, including minors, and its earlier public warnings on easy refusal. Sites with young audiences should expect no leniency on banner symmetry. Topics: reject-button, children, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: CNIL, Deliberation SAN-2022-023: Microsoft Ireland Operations fined 60 million euros for cookies on bing.com
docs.x: France. The CNIL fined Microsoft Ireland Operations Limited 60 million euros because bing.com wrote an advertising cookie to the terminal before any consent and offered no first-layer button to refuse cookies, while acceptance took one click, in breach of article 82. An injunction required consent to be collected on arrival at bing.com before any write used for advertising fraud detection, within three months, backed by 60,000 euros per day of delay. The case confirms that a cookie used for both fraud detection and advertising still needs consent. Search engines and other high-traffic services operating in France are treated as within the CNIL's direct reach. Topics: reject-button, consent, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: DSK, Orientierungshilfe fuer Anbieter:innen von Telemedien (OH Telemedien 2021), version 1.1
docs.x: Germany. The joint guidance of the German federal and state data protection authorities, first adopted in December 2021 and revised by the 104th DSK in December 2022, reads section 25 TTDSG (now TDDDG) as requiring consent for any storage or access on the terminal regardless of personal data, limits the strictly necessary exemption to functional necessity rather than economic need, and treats a first layer with accept all but no equally accessible reject as invalid consent. It rules out legitimate interest as a substitute for the section 25 standard and refuses to label reach measurement as necessary per se. German supervisory audits, including the BayLDA's, apply it. Topics: reject-button, strictly-necessary, consent.

docs.t: Belgian DPA, decision 85/2022: Roularta Media Group fined 50,000 euros after the cookie sweep of 20 press sites
docs.x: Belgium. In its first thematic investigation the Belgian DPA's Inspection Service examined the 20 most visited Belgian news sites for cookie use, consent and transparency, and fined Roularta 50,000 euros for cookies placed before consent, statistics cookies treated as exempt from consent, pre-ticked partner choices, a disclaimer for third-party cookies, deficient information, excessive cookie lifetimes and ineffective withdrawal on two of its sites, with an order to comply within three months. A parallel decision of 16 June 2022 fined Rossel 50,000 euros for similar practices on three sites. Publishers in Belgium should expect sector-wide sweeps with technical evidence and orders addressed to each violation. Topics: consent, enforcement, dark-patterns. Status: decided.

docs.t: CNIL, first evaluation criteria for cookie walls and paywalls
docs.x: France. The CNIL sets out when conditioning access on consent can still yield free consent: a real and equitable alternative must exist, a paid alternative must be reasonably priced (the CNIL sets no threshold but encourages publishers to publish their pricing analysis), consent must be requested only for trackers needed to monetise the free path, and the paid path may carry only strictly necessary trackers, with separate consent for third-party content. The criteria are applied case by case to publishers serving French users. Document the pricing rationale and audit the paid path for stray advertising or analytics tags. Topics: cookie-walls, consent-or-pay.

docs.t: Belgian DPA (APD/GBA), decision 21/2022 on IAB Europe and the Transparency and Consent Framework
docs.x: Belgium. The Litigation Chamber found that the TC String generated under the TCF is personal data, that IAB Europe is a controller for it, and that the framework breached the GDPR on legal basis, transparency, security and accountability; it fined IAB Europe 250,000 euros and gave two months to submit an action plan, which it approved on 11 January 2023. The decision passed the one-stop-shop consistency process and was endorsed by all concerned authorities. On 14 May 2025 the Market Court annulled decision 21/2022 on procedural grounds while confirming its findings and the fine in its own judgment. Topics: tcf, consent, enforcement. Status: superseded.

docs.t: Conseil d'Etat, decision no. 449209: Google's 100 million euro cookie fine confirmed
docs.x: France. The Conseil d'Etat held that the GDPR one-stop-shop mechanism does not apply to enforcement of the ePrivacy Directive, so the CNIL was competent to sanction Google's cookie practices under article 82 without going through the Irish lead authority, and that a 100 million euro fine was proportionate given Google's market share above 90 percent in France, 47 million affected users and the advertising revenue involved. It also refused a preliminary reference to the CJEU. Any operator serving French users should expect direct CNIL enforcement regardless of where its EU establishment sits. Topics: enforcement, consent. Status: decided.

docs.t: Landgericht Muenchen I, judgment 3 O 17493/20 on Google Fonts embedded from Google servers
docs.x: Germany. The court held that loading Google Fonts from Google's servers transmits the visitor's dynamic IP address to Google without consent, which infringes the general right of personality under section 823(1) BGB and article 6(1)(a) GDPR, and awarded 100 euros in non-material damages plus an injunction. The judgment triggered a wave of warning letters in Germany and is the reference for treating third-party resource loads as data transfers needing a legal basis. Self-host fonts, maps and scripts or gate them behind consent; a banner covering cookies alone does not address the IP transfer. Topics: consent, transfers. Status: decided.

docs.t: Austrian Datenschutzbehoerde, decision on Google Analytics and EU-US transfers (noyb model complaint 101)
docs.x: Austria. In the first decision on noyb's 101 complaints after Schrems II, the DSB held that an Austrian website's use of Google Analytics transferred personal data (identifiers, IP address, browser data) to the United States in breach of Chapter V GDPR, because the standard contractual clauses and Google's supplementary measures could not prevent access by US intelligence services under FISA 702. The reasoning was adopted by other authorities in 2022 and drove the move to consent-gated or EU-hosted analytics. The EU-US Data Privacy Framework adopted in July 2023 changed the transfer basis, but the analysis of what analytics tags actually send remains the practical checklist. Topics: transfers, analytics-exemption, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: UOOU (Czech Republic), cookies only with consent from 1 January 2022 (amendment to the Electronic Communications Act)
docs.x: Czech Republic. The Czech DPA explains that the amendment to Act No. 127/2005 on Electronic Communications, effective 1 January 2022, removed the ambiguity that had let operators read the law as opt-out: website operators may collect visitors' data through cookies only on the basis of demonstrable consent (opt-in), with an exception only for technical cookies necessary for transmission and for providing the service, including security. Consent through pre-set browser settings or a statement that staying on the site means consent is not valid, and the controller must be able to prove consent. Czech-facing sites should present layered information and per-purpose choices. Topics: consent, strictly-necessary.

docs.t: CNIL, Deliberation SAN-2021-023: Google fined 150 million euros because refusing cookies took more clicks than accepting
docs.x: France. The CNIL fined Google LLC 90 million euros and Google Ireland Limited 60 million euros because google.fr and youtube.com offered a one-click accept button but required several clicks to refuse all cookies, which the CNIL held discourages refusal and invalidates consent under article 82. An injunction required a refusal mechanism as simple as acceptance within three months, backed by 100,000 euros per day of delay. The decision is the CNIL's clearest statement that refusing must be as simple as accepting, which in practice means a reject all control on the first layer. The CNIL later closed the injunction after Google added a reject all button. Topics: reject-button, dark-patterns, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: CNIL, Deliberation SAN-2021-024: Facebook Ireland fined 60 million euros over the refusal path on facebook.com
docs.x: France. The CNIL fined Facebook Ireland Limited 60 million euros under article 82 because facebook.com let users accept cookies in one click but required several clicks to refuse, and because the button ending the refusal path was labelled Accept cookies, which misled users about what they were doing. An injunction with a penalty of 100,000 euros per day required a refusal mechanism as simple as acceptance within three months. Button labels on the refusal path must say what they do, and the CNIL has since closed the injunction. Topics: reject-button, dark-patterns, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: CNPD (Luxembourg), updated guidelines on cookies and other tracking devices
docs.x: Luxembourg. The CNPD published an updated set of guidelines, in French, for operators of websites and applications on the use of cookies and other tracking devices, distinguishing essential cookies that need no consent from non-essential cookies that require prior informed consent, and accompanied by a practical fact sheet for the public and for operators. The guidelines are the CNPD's stated reference for compliance in Luxembourg and are aligned with the CJEU and EDPB positions. Operators established in Luxembourg, including many EU headquarters of platforms, should map their banners to the guidelines' categories. Topics: consent, strictly-necessary.

docs.t: Traficom, guidance on cookies and other information stored on users' terminal devices (service providers)
docs.x: Finland. Following Helsinki Administrative Court rulings of 8 April 2021 that confirmed Traficom as the competent authority for cookie consent questions, the agency's guidance under section 205 of the Act on Electronic Communications Services (917/2014) states that consent for non-essential cookies cannot be given through browser settings, continued use or pre-ticked toggles, must be as easy to refuse as to give and as easy to withdraw, and that legitimate interest is not a basis for storing on the terminal. Only cookies whose sole purpose is transmitting a communication or that are necessary for a service the user has requested (session login, shopping basket, language choice, load balancing) are exempt. The page records updates through 23 April 2026 and enforcement decisions against major Finnish providers for setting consent-requiring cookies without valid consent. Topics: consent, reject-button, strictly-necessary.

docs.t: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali, Linee guida cookie e altri strumenti di tracciamento (provvedimento n. 231)
docs.x: Italy. The guidelines, published in the Gazzetta Ufficiale on 9 July 2021 with six months to comply, apply article 122 of the Italian Privacy Code: scrolling is not consent, cookie walls are unlawful unless an equivalent alternative exists, closing the banner with the X (top right, graphically equal to the accept control) must leave default settings in place, the banner may be re-presented only after at least six months or a material change, and analytics cookies escape consent only with IP truncation and no cross-site combination. Every site addressing Italian users must follow them; the Garante cites them in each cookie warning and fine. Topics: consent, cookie-walls, analytics-exemption.

docs.t: AEPD, PS/00032/2020: Iberia fined 30,000 euros for a banner with no way to refuse cookies
docs.x: Spain. The AEPD imposed the maximum 30,000 euro fine for a leve infringement of article 22.2 LSSI under article 39.1.c because Iberia's banner used unclear wording, cookies were installed on the first visit, the second layer did not identify third-party cookies or their retention periods, and there was no genuine way to refuse: users could only accept or open the settings, where cookies had to be rejected group by group behind a cookie wall. The AEPD also found that the compliance changes Iberia claimed had not been implemented until after proceedings began, and confirmed the fine on reconsideration. A banner without an easy reject option reaches the top of the leve scale in Spain. Topics: reject-button, cookie-walls, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: CNIL, Deliberation SAN-2020-012: Google LLC and Google Ireland fined 100 million euros for cookies on google.fr
docs.x: France. The CNIL fined Google LLC 60 million euros and Google Ireland Limited 40 million euros under article 82 for placing advertising cookies on google.fr before any user action, for a banner that did not explain purposes or how to refuse, and for an opposition mechanism that left one cookie active. An injunction carried a penalty of 100,000 euros per day of delay. Cookie rules fall outside the GDPR one-stop shop, so the CNIL acts directly against non-French controllers. The Conseil d'Etat upheld the decision on 28 January 2022. Topics: consent, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: CNIL, Deliberation SAN-2020-013: Amazon Europe Core fined 35 million euros for cookies on amazon.fr
docs.x: France. The CNIL found that more than 40 advertising cookies were written to French users' terminals on arrival at amazon.fr, whether from the home page or from third-party advertisements, and that the banner text (offer and improve our services) described neither the advertising purpose nor the means of refusal, in breach of article 82. The fine was 35 million euros with a three-month injunction backed by 100,000 euros per day. Landing pages reached from advertising links need the same banner as the home page. The Conseil d'Etat confirmed the sanction on 27 June 2022 (decision no. 451423). Topics: consent, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: CNIL, Deliberation 2020-091: guidelines on cookies and other trackers (article 82 of the French Data Protection Act)
docs.x: France. The guidelines restate article 82 of the loi Informatique et Libertés: reading or writing on a user's terminal requires prior, free, specific, informed and unambiguous consent, continued browsing is not consent, and refusing trackers must be as easy as accepting them. They apply to every operator addressing users in France, including third parties whose trackers a site loads, and exempt only trackers strictly necessary for the service or for audience measurement under narrow conditions. Keep proof of consent available at any time, and treat the July 2019 guidelines they replace (Deliberation 2019-093) as superseded. Topics: consent, reject-button, analytics-exemption.

docs.t: CNIL, Deliberation 2020-092: recommendation on practical arrangements for cookies and other trackers
docs.x: France. The recommendation gives the CNIL's expected banner design: a first layer that names every purpose, gives access to the full list of controllers behind consent-requiring trackers, and offers an accept action and a refuse action of equal effort, with a refusal remembered so that the user is not asked again at each visit. It applies to every organisation using trackers as defined in the 2020 guidelines, web and mobile first, and is the reference the CNIL uses in its cookie fines. Build banners to it, log consent and refusal, and re-ask no more often than the recommended six-month rhythm. Topics: consent, reject-button, dark-patterns.

docs.t: Conseil d'Etat, decision no. 434684 on the CNIL's 2019 cookie guidelines (cookie walls)
docs.x: France. The Conseil d'Etat annulled the CNIL's general ban on cookie walls in its July 2019 guidelines because a soft-law instrument cannot impose an absolute prohibition, while confirming the requirements of purpose-specific consent, easy refusal and withdrawal, recommended retention periods and information on consent-exempt trackers. The ruling binds the CNIL and frames how French regulators assess walls: freedom of consent is judged case by case. Practitioners can operate a wall in France only where a genuine alternative exists, and the CNIL's May 2022 criteria now set the test. Topics: cookie-walls, consent. Status: decided.

docs.t: Bundesgerichtshof, judgment I ZR 7/16 (Cookie-Einwilligung II, Planet49)
docs.x: Germany. Following the CJEU's judgment in C-673/17, the BGH held that section 15(3) TMG had to be read in conformity with article 5(3) of the ePrivacy Directive, so cookies for advertising and market research require active consent and a pre-ticked checkbox does not provide it. The same judgment found consent to telephone advertising invalid where the user faced an onerous opt-out list of partner companies. The ruling ended the German opt-out reading for non-essential cookies and was later codified in section 25 TTDSG (now TDDDG) from 1 December 2021. Topics: consent, dark-patterns. Status: decided.

docs.t: Data Protection Commission, Guidance note on cookies and other tracking technologies
docs.x: Ireland. Applying Regulation 5(3) of the ePrivacy Regulations 2011 (S.I. 336 of 2011), the DPC states that storing or accessing information on a device requires consent after clear information, that pre-ticked boxes and sliders set to on are not consent following Planet49, that rejecting must be as easy as accepting, that analytics cookies need consent even if first-party aggregated analytics are a low enforcement priority, and that consent should be re-affirmed no later than six months after it is recorded. Only communications and strictly necessary cookies (for example shopping-basket session cookies) are exempt. It remains the operative Irish standard for banner design. Topics: consent, analytics-exemption, strictly-necessary.

docs.t: Data Protection Commission, Report on the use of cookies and other tracking technologies (cookie sweep)
docs.x: Ireland. The DPC surveyed a selection of Irish websites across media and publishing, retail, food ordering, insurance, sport and the public sector between August and December 2019 to examine how controllers obtain consent for cookies and other tracking technologies, and found that advertising technology and tracking were core to many of the business models examined, with widespread non-compliance. The report was published alongside the DPC's guidance note and framed the DPC's stated intention to examine consent practices. Use it to understand which practices the DPC flagged, then apply the guidance note as the operative rules. Topics: consent, enforcement. Status: historical.

docs.t: Hellenic DPA, Recommendations 1/2020 on compliance of controllers with the electronic communications legislation for trackers
docs.x: Greece. Issued after the authority found widespread non-compliance by Greek website operators, the recommendations under Law 3471/2006 require prior consent for every tracker not technically necessary, including third-party analytics such as Google Analytics, with a two-month grace period. Accepting and refusing must take the same number of clicks from the same layer, withdrawal must be as easy as consent, access may not be restricted for refusal, buttons and fonts should share size, emphasis and colour, and the storage period of a refusal must equal that of an acceptance. Scrolling, continued browsing, pre-ticked boxes and browser settings are invalid. The HDPA re-invoked points C4 and C7 in its 2022 action on news websites. Topics: reject-button, cookie-walls, dark-patterns.

docs.t: Denmark, Cookiebekendtgoerelsen (BEK nr 1148 af 9. december 2011) on information and consent for storage of or access to information on terminal equipment
docs.x: Denmark. The Danish cookie order, in force since 14 December 2011, prohibits storing or accessing information on an end user's terminal without prior information and consent, and exempts storage or access that is a technical precondition for delivering a service the user requested or for transmitting communications. It applies to any website or app addressed to Danish users regardless of whether personal data is processed. The Danish Agency for Digital Government (Digitaliseringsstyrelsen) supervises the order, while Datatilsynet supervises the subsequent processing under the GDPR; the two authorities' joint guidance of May 2025 explains how the regimes interlock. Topics: consent, strictly-necessary.

docs.t: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (Commencement No. 9 and Transitional and Saving Provisions) Regulations 2026, SI 2026/1015: abolition of the Information Commissioner and transfer to the Information Commission
docs.x: United Kingdom. Made on 10 September 2026, regulation 2 commences sections 118 and 119 of the 2025 Act (with the related section 117(4)(a) amendment) on 30 September 2026: the office of Information Commissioner is abolished and its functions transfer to the Information Commission, a body corporate with non-executive and executive members, including an interim chief executive. Update references in privacy notices, DPIAs and contracts to the Information Commission after that date; no change to PECR obligations follows from the renaming. Topics: enforcement, other. Status: applies from a future date.

docs.t: ICO advice to government on potential changes to online advertising rules (PECR regulation 6 exception for low-risk advertising)
docs.x: United Kingdom. The ICO advised the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology that regulation 6 could be amended by secondary legislation, using the power in the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, to allow certain low-risk forms of online advertising to operate without consent where advertising is based on the context of the content viewed rather than a person's past activity, while intrusive tracking and profiling over time and across services would continue to require consent. It is advice to government, not law, and the ICO states that the existing PECR rules still apply and organisations must continue to comply. Keep consent for behavioural advertising and monitor for draft regulations. Topics: consent, other. Status: proposed.

docs.t: ICO Guidance on the use of storage and access technologies (final version)
docs.x: United Kingdom. The guidance explains how PECR regulation 6 and the UK GDPR apply to cookies, tracking pixels, link decoration, local storage, device fingerprinting, scripts and tags across websites, apps and connected TV, with chapters on the five exceptions, consent in practice, online advertising, cookie walls and consent or pay, and what a simple means of objecting requires. The statistical exception covers how a service is used, not who uses it; the appearance exception excludes adapting content to inferred interests; both need information and a free objection control, and legitimate interests is unavailable for non-exempt technologies. It replaces the 2024 and 2025 drafts and applies to every organisation subject to PECR. Topics: consent, analytics-exemption, strictly-necessary.

docs.t: PECR Regulation 6 (Privacy and Electronic Communications (EC Directive) Regulations 2003, SI 2003/2426), as amended by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025
docs.x: United Kingdom. Regulation 6(1) prohibits storing information, or gaining access to information stored, in a subscriber's or user's terminal equipment, subject to the exceptions in new Schedule A1; regulation 6(2) extends the prohibition to instigating storage or access and to collecting information automatically emitted by the device, which captures fingerprinting and pixels. It binds any person operating a website, app or connected service reaching UK users, not only controllers. Map every storage or access operation to one Schedule A1 exception (consent, transmission, strictly necessary, statistical, appearance, emergency) and document it. The substituted text applies from 5 February 2026 under SI 2026/82, regulation 2(w). Topics: consent, strictly-necessary, analytics-exemption.

docs.t: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, section 112 and Schedule 12: new Schedule A1 to PECR (exceptions to the storage and access prohibition)
docs.x: United Kingdom. Schedule 12 inserts Schedule A1 into PECR. Paragraph 2 permits storage or access where the user receives clear and comprehensive information and gives consent, which may be signified through browser or application settings; paragraphs 3 and 4 keep the transmission and strictly necessary exceptions; paragraph 5 covers collection solely for statistical purposes to improve the service; paragraph 6 covers adapting or enhancing a website's appearance or functionality; paragraph 7 covers emergency geolocation. Paragraphs 5 and 6 both require prior information and a simple free means of objecting; paragraph 5 additionally bars disclosure except to a party assisting with the improvements. Rely on paragraph 5 only with processor-only analytics and a live objection control. Topics: analytics-exemption, strictly-necessary, consent.

docs.t: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, section 115 and Schedule 13: PECR enforcement aligned with the Data Protection Act 2018
docs.x: United Kingdom. Schedule 13 substitutes Schedule 1 to PECR and applies the Data Protection Act 2018 enforcement toolkit to regulation 6 breaches: information, assessment, interview and enforcement notices, powers of entry and penalty notices under sections 155 to 157 as modified. The maximum penalty for a regulation 6 contravention becomes the UK GDPR higher ceiling of £17.5 million or 4 per cent of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is greater, replacing the previous £500,000 cap; the former threshold of serious contravention causing substantial damage or distress falls away. It binds every person subject to PECR. Treat tag deployment as a UK GDPR-scale liability. In force from 5 February 2026 under SI 2026/82. Topics: enforcement, consent.

docs.t: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (Commencement No. 6 and Transitional and Saving Provisions) Regulations 2026, SI 2026/82
docs.x: United Kingdom. Regulation 2 brings the PECR provisions of the 2025 Act into force on 5 February 2026, including section 112 and Schedule 12 (regulation 6 and Schedule A1 exceptions), section 115 and Schedule 13 (enforcement and penalties), and section 101 on penalty notices; regulation 3 commences further provisions on 19 June 2026. It applies to every organisation subject to PECR and the UK GDPR. Use 5 February 2026 as the date from which the statistical and appearance exceptions can be relied on and from which regulation 6 breaches attract UK GDPR-level fines; the transitional provisions govern investigations opened before that date. Topics: analytics-exemption, enforcement.

docs.t: UK GDPR Article 4(11) and Article 7: definition and conditions for consent
docs.x: United Kingdom. PECR consent means consent as defined in the UK GDPR: a freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous indication by statement or clear affirmative action (Article 4(11)). Article 7 requires the controller to demonstrate consent, to present the request clearly distinguishable from other matters in plain language, to allow withdrawal at any time with withdrawal as easy as giving consent, and to weigh whether access to a service is conditioned on unnecessary consent when judging whether it is freely given. It binds every controller relying on consent. Build banners so reject and withdraw match accept in effort, keep consent records, and never treat browsing or pre-ticked boxes as consent. Topics: consent, reject-button, dark-patterns.

docs.t: ICO action secures increased cookie compliance across the UK's top 1,000 websites (campaign outcome)
docs.x: United Kingdom. The ICO reports that 979 of the top 1,000 UK websites met its compliance checks at the most recent test, with 21 still failing; 415 passed without intervention and 564 improved after initially failing, following warning letters, investigations and 17 preliminary enforcement notices. The checks were whether advertising cookies were stored before the user could choose, whether rejecting was as easy as accepting, and whether cookies were placed despite refusal. The outcome covers sites reaching an estimated 80 per cent of UK internet users over 14. Expect periodic re-testing; keep the three checks in release testing so sites do not revert. Topics: enforcement, reject-button, consent. Status: decided.

docs.t: CMA decision to release Google from the Privacy Sandbox commitments
docs.x: United Kingdom. Following a consultation opened in June 2025 after Google abandoned third-party cookie deprecation in Chrome, the CMA decided on 17 October 2025 that it had reasonable grounds to believe its competition concerns no longer arose and released Google from all the 2022 commitments, ending the CMA and ICO oversight of Privacy Sandbox design. The decision concerns Google but removes the regulatory driver behind UK cookie deprecation planning. Plan on third-party cookies persisting in Chrome for UK users, keep consent-based tagging as the compliance baseline, and treat Privacy Sandbox APIs as optional rather than a mandated replacement. Topics: browser-signals, other. Status: decided.

docs.t: ICO consultation on a new chapter within the draft updated guidance on storage and access technologies (Data (Use and Access) Act exceptions)
docs.x: United Kingdom. Opened on 7 July 2025 and closed on 26 September 2025, the consultation added a chapter explaining the statistical purposes and appearance exceptions introduced by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, including the information and objection conditions and the restriction on sharing statistical data beyond processors. It was addressed to website and app operators, analytics vendors and consent management platform providers serving UK users. Its content was folded into the final guidance of 29 April 2026, which supersedes it; cite the final text rather than the draft chapter. Topics: analytics-exemption, consent. Status: superseded.

docs.t: ICO consultation on the draft updated guidance on storage and access technologies (draft that replaced the 2019 cookies guidance)
docs.x: United Kingdom. The draft, previously known as the detailed cookies guidance, widened the ICO's cookie position to all storage and access technologies, confirmed that consent must meet the UK GDPR standard, that reject must be as easy as accept, that the strictly necessary exception is judged from the user's perspective and that pixels and fingerprinting are in scope. It was open for comment until 5 pm on 21 March 2025 and was directed at every organisation deploying such technologies for UK users. Use it only to trace how the ICO's thinking developed; it was superseded by the final guidance published on 29 April 2026. Topics: consent, pixels-wiretap, strictly-necessary. Status: superseded.

docs.t: ICO Consent or pay guidance
docs.x: United Kingdom. The guidance states that consent or pay models, which offer a choice between consenting to personalised advertising, paying a fee, or leaving the service, can comply with UK data protection law where consent is freely given, assessed against four factors: power imbalance, equivalence of the core service, an appropriate fee, and privacy by design in how the choice is presented. It applies to any organisation operating or considering such a model for UK users, with additional expectations where services are likely to be accessed by children under 18 (the Children's code applies, with profiling off by default) and parental consent where consent is sought from children under 13. Document the four-factor assessment in a DPIA before launch and present both options with equal prominence. Topics: consent-or-pay, consent, children.

docs.t: ICO takes action to tackle cookie compliance across the UK's top 1,000 websites (2025 online tracking strategy)
docs.x: United Kingdom. The announcement launched the ICO's 2025 online tracking strategy with a plan to bring the UK's top 1,000 websites into compliance, having already assessed the top 200 and communicated concerns to 134 of them, setting out the expectation that they comply with the law by giving people meaningful choice. It also sets out the ICO's position on consent or pay models and further engagement with consent management platforms. It targets every operator of a high-traffic UK website and the ad tech vendors behind them. Audit banners so that non-essential advertising cookies are not set before a choice is made and rejecting is as easy as accepting. Topics: enforcement, reject-button, consent. Status: decided.

docs.t: ICO reprimand: Sky Betting and Gaming (Bonne Terre Limited) for advertising cookies without consent
docs.x: United Kingdom. The ICO found that between 10 January and 3 March 2023 Bonne Terre Limited, trading as Sky Betting and Gaming, processed personal data through advertising cookies and shared it with ad tech companies before visitors could accept or reject them, in a way that was not lawful, transparent or fair, and issued a reprimand; the company made changes in March 2023. The same announcement reported that 52 of 53 warned top-100 websites had made changes, leaving 99 of the top 100 either offering a meaningful choice or making improvements. It applies to any operator whose tags fire before consent. Verify tag sequencing on first page load and block ad tech calls until consent is recorded. Topics: enforcement, consent, tcf. Status: decided.

docs.t: ICO and CMA joint position paper: Harmful design in digital markets (online choice architecture and cookie choices)
docs.x: United Kingdom. The joint paper identifies design practices that could break data protection law, including failing to give an equal choice between accept all and reject all cookies, overly complicated privacy controls, leading language steering data sharing, bundled choices and default settings that give less control. It applies to every organisation designing online interfaces for UK consumers; the ICO warns it will act against businesses that deliberately and persistently design unfairly, and the CMA warns that businesses standing in the way risk action from either regulator. Use the paper as the UK benchmark for banner and preference-centre design. Topics: dark-patterns, reject-button, consent.

docs.t: CMA acceptance of Google's Privacy Sandbox commitments (investigation into Google's Privacy Sandbox browser changes)
docs.x: United Kingdom. On 11 February 2022 the CMA accepted binding commitments under which Google would design and test the Privacy Sandbox with the CMA and the ICO before any final decision to remove third-party cookies from Chrome, would not self-preference its own ad tech and would limit its use of data, with a monitoring trustee appointed in March 2022. The commitments bound Google but set the timeline for every publisher and vendor planning for cookie deprecation in the UK. Google announced in July 2024 that it would retain third-party cookies with a user choice and in April 2025 that no prompt would ship. The CMA released the commitments on 17 October 2025. Topics: browser-signals, other. Status: superseded.

docs.t: ICO Guidance on the use of cookies and similar technologies (2019 detailed cookies guidance)
docs.x: United Kingdom. Version 1.0 of 3 July 2019 set the ICO's post-GDPR cookie position: PECR consent means GDPR consent, continuing to browse is not consent, pre-ticked boxes and default-on sliders are invalid, analytics cookies are not strictly necessary and need consent, non-essential cookies must not be set before consent, third parties must be named, and cookie walls are acceptable only in limited circumstances. It applied to every operator of a website or app used from the UK and still appears in audit checklists and vendor documentation. It has been superseded by the Guidance on the use of storage and access technologies of 29 April 2026, which reflects the statistical exception for analytics. Topics: consent, analytics-exemption, cookie-walls. Status: superseded.

docs.t: noyb and the Norwegian Consumer Council, complaint against Schibsted's pay or okay model with the Norwegian DPA
docs.x: Norway. noyb filed a complaint with Datatilsynet, in cooperation with the Norwegian Consumer Council, alleging that Schibsted's requirement that readers of vg.no either accept tracking for personalised advertising or pay 49 NOK a month produces consent rates near 99 percent although only about 3 percent of users want to be tracked, so consent is not freely given under Articles 5(1), 6(1) and 7 GDPR. The complaint records that 64 consumers contacted the Consumer Council about the model between 28 April and 2 June 2026 and that Schibsted rolled the model out on its Swedish sites first. The complaint is pending; Nordic publishers should expect the first consent-or-pay decisions on news sites under the GDPR to come from this case. Topics: consent-or-pay, consent. Status: proposed.

docs.t: FDPIC Factsheet on the use of cookies and similar technologies (for internet users)
docs.x: Switzerland. The factsheet, published on 31 March 2026, is the FDPIC's awareness document for internet users and complements rather than replaces the operator-facing Guidelines of 6 October 2025. It explains what cookies do, encourages data-minimalist use, warns against blanket acceptance of all cookies and points users to opt-in and opt-out controls and their rights of control and choice. It creates no obligations for operators but signals the FDPIC's expectation that refusal and withdrawal controls are easy to find and use. Use it to anticipate the complaints the FDPIC will receive and to test that the refusal path on Swiss-facing sites works as the factsheet describes. Topics: consent, other.

docs.t: FDPIC Guidelines on data processing using cookies and similar technologies, version 1.1
docs.x: Switzerland. Version 1.1 of 6 October 2025 replaces version 1.0 of 22 January 2025 and sets out how the FDPIC supervises cookies, pixels and similar technologies under the FADP, the Data Protection Ordinance and Article 45c TCA: necessary cookies need information only; other non-essential cookies justified by overriding interests need information and a mandatory opt-out; express consent is required for sensitive data, high-risk profiling, any profiling by federal bodies and unexpected uses that seriously intrude, including paid access for multiple embedded advertising third parties and location profiling. Banners must not use pre-ticked boxes or dark patterns; cookie paywalls need a proportionate price. The guidelines themselves state only the Article 45c TCA fine of up to CHF 5,000; the general FADP penalty regime separately allows fines of up to CHF 250,000. Topics: consent, dark-patterns, consent-or-pay.

docs.t: Datatilsynet (Norway), guidance on consent for cookies and other tracking technologies: ten practical rules
docs.x: Norway. Applying ekomloven section 3-15, the guidance sets ten rules for a valid banner: clear information in the consent box, full information behind it, no conditioning of access on consent, per-purpose choice, no pre-ticked boxes or acceptance by passivity, refusal without extra clicks, no hiding or de-emphasising the reject option, plain wording on buttons, easy withdrawal, and internal control of what the site sets. It states that other GDPR bases can almost never replace consent for the subsequent processing of cookie data. The current version, updated in April 2025, replaces the 2023 guidance that first demanded an equal reject option. Topics: reject-button, dark-patterns, cookie-walls.
