docs.t: Norway, Lov om elektronisk kommunikasjon (ekomloven) section 3-15: cookies require GDPR-standard consent
docs.x: Norway. The new Electronic Communications Act of 13 December 2024, in force from 1 January 2025, replaces the 2003 act and provides in section 3-15 that storing or accessing information on a user's equipment is prohibited unless the user has been informed of what is processed, the purpose and who processes it, and has given consent meeting the GDPR's requirements; exemptions cover transmission and storage strictly necessary for an information-society service the user expressly requested. Browser settings no longer count as consent in Norway. Datatilsynet and Nkom share supervision: Nkom decides scope and exemptions, Datatilsynet decides information and consent validity. Topics: consent, strictly-necessary.

docs.t: Norway: Electronic Communications Act (ekomloven) section 3-15 on cookies and similar technologies, with Nkom and Datatilsynet joint supervision
docs.x: Norway. The new ekomloven, in force from 1 January 2025, provides in section 3-15 that use of cookies and similar technologies requires consent valid under the GDPR: voluntary, specific, informed, unambiguous, given by active action, documented and easily withdrawable, replacing the former section 2-7b under which browser default settings counted as consent. Supervision is shared by Nkom and Datatilsynet from the same date. It binds every operator of a website or app directed at users in Norway, whether or not established there. Retire any reliance on browser settings for Norwegian traffic and apply the same opt-in banner standard as under the EU rules, with the Norwegian regulators as enforcement contacts. Topics: consent, browser-signals, enforcement.

docs.t: Norway Datatilsynet guidance page on cookies and information capsules (informasjonskapsler)
docs.x: Norway. Datatilsynet's cookie page states that consent to cookies must be GDPR-valid consent, so that browser settings alone do not suffice, and explains the interaction between the cookie rule in ekomloven and the personal data rules in personopplysningsloven and the GDPR, both of which apply at once. It is addressed to Norwegian website and app operators and to foreign operators serving Norwegian users. Read it together with Nkom's page on section 3-15, since the Datatilsynet page still cites the former section 2-7b and Nkom as sole supervisor; the operative rule since 1 January 2025 is section 3-15 with joint supervision. Topics: consent, other.

docs.t: Turkey: KVKK Guideline on Cookie Practices (Çerez Uygulamaları Hakkında Rehber)
docs.x: Turkey. The Personal Data Protection Authority's guideline, in its July 2025 edition, applies Law No. 6698 to cookies: cookies strictly necessary for a service the user requested, and first party analytics, may be used without explicit consent under Article 5(2), while social plugin tracking and online behavioural advertising cookies require explicit consent under Article 5(1), with information duties under Article 10 met through a cookie policy and banner, and cross-border transfers through cookies subject to Article 9. It applies to data controllers processing personal data through cookies on websites and web applications. Provide a banner with equally prominent accept, reject and preferences buttons, granular explicit opt-in for non-essential cookies, no consent inferred from mere site use, and a cookie policy listing each cookie, purpose, type and duration. Topics: consent, strictly-necessary, transfers.

docs.t: Federal Act on Data Protection (FADP, SR 235.1), revised text
docs.x: Switzerland. The revised FADP entered into force on 1 September 2023 without a transition period. Article 6 requires that consent, where relied on, is voluntary and informed, and express for sensitive personal data and for high-risk profiling, which Article 5 defines as profiling entailing a high risk to personality or fundamental rights; Article 19 imposes a duty to inform at collection, including the countries of any disclosure abroad. Article 60 provides criminal fines of up to CHF 250,000 against the responsible individual for wilful breaches of the information duties. It binds private controllers and federal bodies; tracking needs consent only where it reaches sensitive data or high-risk profiling. Topics: consent, other.

docs.t: Turkey: Personal Data Protection Board decision on Amazon Turkey (cookies and marketing without explicit consent), decision no. 2020/173
docs.x: Turkey. The Board found that Amazon Turkey processed personal data through cookies and sent marketing communications without obtaining explicit consent and without adequate information, in breach of Articles 4, 5, 10 and 12 of Law No. 6698, and that it also transferred data abroad without valid explicit consent under Article 9. It imposed administrative fines totalling TRY 1,200,000: TRY 1,100,000 under Article 18(1)(b) for the Article 12 failure to take the technical and organisational measures that would have prevented processing without explicit consent, and TRY 100,000 under Article 18(1)(a) for failing to inform users about the cookies, and it ordered the company to bring its privacy notice, terms and cookie notice into line and report back. The decision binds the addressee and sets the Board's position for all controllers using cookies on Turkish users. It remains the reference enforcement precedent that the 2022 Guideline on Cookie Practices later codified; treat cookie consent in Turkey as an opt-in explicit consent regime. Topics: enforcement, consent, email-marketing. Status: decided.

docs.t: Telecommunications Act (TCA, SR 784.10), Article 45c: data on external equipment
docs.x: Switzerland. Article 45c permits the processing of data on external equipment by means of transmission using telecommunications techniques, which covers setting and reading cookies and similar identifiers, only where users are informed about the processing and its purpose and are informed that they may refuse it, or where the processing is for telecommunications services and charging purposes. It binds every operator of a website or app reaching users in Switzerland; the FDPIC applies it cumulatively with the FADP, reads the refusal requirement as a mandatory opt-out control, and cites a fine of up to CHF 5,000 under Article 53 TCA. Provide the notice and a refusal control before any non-necessary cookie is set. Topics: consent, strictly-necessary, other.

docs.t: SB 690 (2025-2026), amendment of Cal. Penal Code 637.2 for pen register and trap and trace claims against websites and apps
docs.x: California. SB 690 passed the Assembly 66 to 0 on 28 August 2026, the Senate concurred 39 to 0, and the enrolled bill went to the Governor on 4 September 2026. As enrolled it amends only section 637.2 to remove the private right of action for section 638.51 pen register and trap and trace claims arising from website, online application and mobile application conduct, vests enforcement in the Attorney General, applies to pending claims commenced on or after 1 January 2025 and would operate from 1 January 2027. Sections 631 and 632 are untouched. Keep prior-consent gating for session replay, chat and pixels; the wiretap theory survives whatever the Governor decides. Topics: pixels-wiretap, enforcement. Status: proposed.

docs.t: Variety Media, LLC v. Superior Court, No. B350578 (Cal. Ct. App., 2d Dist., Div. 3), tentative opinion on CIPA section 638.51
docs.x: California. In a tentative opinion issued on 21 August 2026 before argument on 25 August 2026, the Court of Appeal indicated that section 638.51 can reach internet communications but that collecting a visitor's IP address alone does not state a pen register claim, because an IP address identifies the source of a communication whereas a pen register captures information identifying the destination of an outgoing communication; it proposed sustaining the demurrer with leave to amend. The ruling is not final and may change. It applies to website operators sued under the pen register theory. Watch for the final opinion and note that referrer and destination metadata may still support amended claims. Topics: pixels-wiretap. Status: under appeal.

docs.t: Delete Act (SB 362), Cal. Civ. Code 1798.99.86, accessible deletion mechanism
docs.x: California. Section 1798.99.86 required the California Privacy Protection Agency to establish, by 1 January 2026, a free mechanism through which a consumer submits a single verifiable request that every registered data broker delete their personal information. From 1 August 2026 each data broker must access the mechanism at least every 45 days, delete within 45 days of receipt, direct service providers and contractors to do the same, and undergo an independent compliance audit every three years from 1 January 2028. It binds registered data brokers. Process an unverifiable request as an opt-out of sale or sharing, and check whether tracking vendors in the stack are themselves registered brokers. Topics: sale-sharing, other.

docs.t: NetChoice, LLC v. Bonta, No. 25-2366 (9th Cir.), California Age-Appropriate Design Code Act (AB 2273)
docs.x: California. The Ninth Circuit affirmed the preliminary injunction against the Act's data use restrictions (Cal. Civ. Code 1798.99.31(b)(1) to (4)) and its dark patterns prohibition ((b)(7)) on vagueness grounds, but vacated the injunction covering the statute as a whole, the coverage definition and the age estimation requirement, and remanded, leaving the severability of the notice-and-cure provision unresolved. The Act applies to businesses providing online services likely to be accessed by children under 18. Treat the age estimation, high-privacy default settings, child-readable notices and tracking-signal provisions as potentially enforceable while the district court proceedings continue, and keep the earlier injunction history in mind when reading vendor claims. Topics: children, dark-patterns. Status: decided.

docs.t: California Privacy Protection Agency, Order of Decision against Ford Motor Company
docs.x: California. The agency's board found that Ford required consumers to complete email verification before it would process a request to opt out of sale or sharing, treated unverified requests as expired and so failed to process dozens of opt-outs within the statutory timeframe; the decision states that unnecessary friction in the opt-out process violates the CCPA. Ford must pay $375,703, process the unverified requests, audit tracking technologies on its website and honour opt-out preference signals including Global Privacy Control. It binds Ford. Remove every confirmation step between the click and the suppression of tags; verification belongs to access and deletion requests, not opt-outs. Topics: dark-patterns, opt-out-signals, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: California Privacy Protection Agency, Order of Decision against PlayOn Sports
docs.x: California. The agency found that the ticketing and streaming platform forced users to accept tracking before they could buy tickets or use the site, directed consumers to Network Advertising Initiative and Digital Advertising Alliance opt-out pages instead of providing its own opt-out, failed to recognise opt-out preference signals and gave insufficient privacy notice. PlayOn must pay $1.10 million, conduct risk assessments and scan its tracking technologies. It binds PlayOn but rules out cookie walls and industry opt-out pages as CCPA compliance. Never condition access on accepting tracking, and operate the opt-out yourself. Topics: cookie-walls, opt-out-signals, children. Status: decided.

docs.t: People v. The Walt Disney Company (Disney DTC and ABC Enterprises), California Attorney General CCPA settlement
docs.x: California. The Attorney General alleged that Disney applied an opt-out toggle only to the streaming service and device in use rather than the whole account, that its webform opt-out did not stop sales through third-party ad tech code embedded in its platforms, that connected TV apps had no in-app opt-out, and that a Global Privacy Control signal was limited to the device even when the consumer was logged in. Disney paid $2.75 million, the largest CCPA settlement to date, and must honour opt-outs across every linked device and service. It binds Disney. Propagate opt-outs and GPC signals from the browser to the authenticated account and every property tied to it. Topics: opt-out-signals, sale-sharing, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: California Privacy Protection Agency, Delete Act enforcement against unregistered data brokers (Rickenbacher Data and S&P Global)
docs.x: California. The agency fined Rickenbacher Data LLC (Datamasters) $45,000 and S&P Global, Inc. $62,600 for failing to register as data brokers under the Delete Act, the former for reselling lists of people with conditions such as Alzheimer's disease and addiction. The registration duty binds any business that sells personal information about consumers with whom it has no direct relationship, which can include vendors that build audiences from website tracking. Both companies must register and implement compliance auditing. Check whether any audience, enrichment or identity partner meets the data broker definition before the 1 August 2026 DROP processing obligations apply. Topics: sale-sharing, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: CCPA Updates, Cybersecurity Audits, Risk Assessments, ADMT and Insurance Regulations (approved text, effective 1 January 2026)
docs.x: California. Approved by the Office of Administrative Law on 22 September 2025, the amended regulations took effect on 1 January 2026. Section 7025(c)(6) now requires a business to display whether it has processed a consumer's opt-out preference signal, replacing the earlier permissive wording. Risk assessments are required for processing that presents significant risk, including selling or sharing personal information, with documentation due to the agency by 1 April 2028; ADMT obligations apply from 1 January 2027; cybersecurity audits are staggered from 1 April 2028 by revenue. It binds all CCPA businesses. Add the signal-status indicator to the banner and log selling and sharing through cookies in the risk assessment. Topics: opt-out-signals, browser-signals, sale-sharing.

docs.t: California Privacy Protection Agency, Delete Request and Opt-out Platform (DROP)
docs.x: California. DROP opened to Californians on 1 January 2026 and consolidates deletion and opt-out requests to more than 600 registered data brokers in a single submission verified through the California Identity Gateway. Data brokers began processing requests on 1 August 2026, status updates may take up to 90 days, and ongoing deletion is required every 45 days. It binds registered data brokers and is operated by the agency under the Delete Act. Failure to process carries fines of $200 per request per day. Confirm whether any advertising or enrichment partner is registered and build the 45-day retrieval cycle into vendor contracts. Topics: sale-sharing, enforcement.

docs.t: California Invasion of Privacy Act, Cal. Penal Code 631 (wiretapping), with 632 and 638.51 (pen register and trap and trace)
docs.x: California. Section 631(a) makes it an offence to tap a line or to read the contents of a communication in transit without the consent of all parties, or to aid another in doing so; section 638.51 prohibits installing a pen register or trap and trace device without a court order; section 637.2 gives a private right of action. Plaintiffs plead session replay, chat and pixel vendors under 631 and IP or device capture under 638.51. It applies to any website reachable from California. Obtain prior consent before any recording or third-party capture loads; later consent does not cure it. SB 690, awaiting the Governor, would remove the private action under 638.51. Topics: pixels-wiretap, consent.

docs.t: People v. Jam City, Inc., California Attorney General CCPA settlement
docs.x: California. The Attorney General alleged that the developer of 21 mobile games provided no in-app method to opt out of the sale or sharing of personal information and sold or shared the data of users aged 13 to 15 without the affirmative opt-in consent required by section 1798.120(c). Jam City paid $1.4 million in civil penalties and must add in-app opt-out methods and obtain opt-in consent before selling or sharing the data of users aged 13 to 15. It binds Jam City but confirms that in-game ad tech sharing is a sale or share. Provide the opt-out inside the app, not only on a website, and age-screen neutrally. Topics: children, sale-sharing, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: AB 566, California Opt Me Out Act (Chapter 465, Statutes of 2025), Cal. Civ. Code 1798.136
docs.x: California. Chaptered on 8 October 2025, the act adds section 1798.136 to the Civil Code and requires a business that develops or maintains a browser to include a setting, easy for a reasonable person to locate and configure, that lets the consumer send an opt-out preference signal. The California Privacy Protection Agency may adopt implementing regulations, and browser developers are not liable for violations by businesses receiving the signal. The obligation is operative from 1 January 2027 and binds browser vendors, not website operators. Expect signal volumes to rise sharply after that date and size opt-out handling accordingly. Topics: opt-out-signals, browser-signals. Status: applies from a future date.

docs.t: California Privacy Protection Agency, Stipulated Final Order against Tractor Supply Company
docs.x: California. The agency found that a Do Not Sell webform did not actually stop sale or sharing through third-party tracking technologies, that opt-out preference signals were not honoured until July 2024, that the privacy policy had not been updated since November 2021 and omitted how signals are processed, that job applicants received no CCPA notice and that third-party contracts lacked required terms. Tractor Supply paid $1,350,000, must scan its digital properties for tracking technologies quarterly, honour opt-out signals, and obtain annual officer certification for four years. It binds Tractor Supply. Prove that a webform opt-out and a GPC signal both suppress every tag, not just the cookie table. Topics: opt-out-signals, sale-sharing, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: Gutierrez v. Converse Inc., No. 24-4797 (9th Cir.)
docs.x: California. The Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment against a plaintiff who alleged that Salesforce's chat software on a retailer's website violated CIPA section 631(a), finding no evidence from which a jury could conclude that Salesforce made an unauthorised connection with a telephone wire or read messages in transit. A concurrence went further and reasoned that the section's reference to telegraph or telephone wires does not reach internet communications. The unpublished memorandum applies to operators deploying third-party chat and similar vendors. Keep evidence of what the vendor's software actually accesses or reads, since the plaintiff's inability to show that Salesforce read her messages, rather than merely being capable of doing so, was fatal to the claim. Topics: pixels-wiretap. Status: decided.

docs.t: People v. Healthline Media LLC, California Attorney General CCPA settlement
docs.x: California. The Attorney General alleged that Healthline kept sharing data with advertisers after consumers opted out, ignored Global Privacy Control signals, ran a consent banner that did not actually disable tracking cookies, lacked required contract terms with third parties and breached the purpose limitation principle by sending article titles that revealed diagnoses to advertisers. Healthline paid $1.55 million and must stop disclosing data that links a consumer to an article title suggesting a diagnosis, audit third-party contracts and maintain accurate disclosures. It binds Healthline but is the first purpose limitation enforcement under the CCPA. Strip page titles and URLs that reveal health conditions from ad tech payloads. Topics: health-data, pixels-wiretap, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: California Privacy Protection Agency, Order against Todd Snyder, Inc.
docs.x: California. The agency found that the retailer's privacy portal was misconfigured so that opt-out requests, including those sent through its cookie banner, were not processed for 40 days, that it demanded more information than necessary for privacy requests, and that it required identity verification before opting consumers out of sale or sharing. Todd Snyder paid $345,178 and must correctly configure its opt-out mechanisms and train employees. It binds Todd Snyder, but the agency stated that a business remains responsible for its consent management vendor's failures. Test the banner and the downstream tag suppression after every release, and keep evidence of the tests. Topics: consent, enforcement, opt-out-signals. Status: decided.

docs.t: California Privacy Protection Agency, Stipulated Final Order against American Honda Motor Co.
docs.x: California. The agency's first enforcement order found that Honda required excessive personal information and identity verification before honouring opt-out requests, offered a cookie management tool that did not present accept and decline choices in an equal way, obstructed authorised agents and shared consumer data with ad tech companies without CCPA-compliant contracts. Honda paid $632,500 and must simplify request handling, consult a user experience designer on its privacy request methods, train staff and revise contracting. It binds Honda but applies the symmetry rule in regulation section 7004 to cookie banners generally. Make Reject All as prominent as Accept All and never verify identity for an opt-out. Topics: dark-patterns, reject-button, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: California Consumer Privacy Act as amended by the CPRA, Cal. Civ. Code 1798.100 et seq. (sections 1798.120, 1798.135, 1798.155)
docs.x: California. Section 1798.120 gives consumers the right to direct a business not to sell or share their personal information. Section 1798.135(a) requires a clear and conspicuous homepage link titled Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information plus a Limit the Use of My Sensitive Personal Information link, or one consolidated link; 1798.135(b) lets a business omit the links if it honours an opt-out preference signal. Section 1798.120(c) requires opt-in under 16; section 1798.155 sets fines of up to $2,500 per violation and $7,500 for intentional violations or those involving the data of consumers known to be under 16, amounts the California Privacy Protection Agency adjusts for inflation ($2,663 and $7,988 from 1 January 2025). Route ad tech sharing, the link and the signal to one suppression path. Current text as amended by AB 3286. Topics: sale-sharing, opt-out-signals, children.

docs.t: CCPA Regulations, Cal. Code Regs. Title 11, Division 6, Chapter 1 (final text of 29 March 2023)
docs.x: California. The 2023 text established the operative rules behind the statute: section 7004 bans dark patterns and requires symmetry in choice, so declining must take no more steps than accepting; sections 7013 to 7015 govern the Do Not Sell or Share link, the Limit the Use link and the Alternative Opt-out Link; section 7025 makes opt-out preference signals mandatory to process; section 7026 governs opt-out requests. It binds every business subject to the CCPA and its service providers and contractors. Use it to understand the reasoning behind current enforcement. Superseded as a document by the consolidated regulations text approved on 22 September 2025 and effective 1 January 2026. Topics: dark-patterns, opt-out-signals, sale-sharing. Status: superseded.

docs.t: Cal. Code Regs. Title 11, section 7025, Opt-Out Preference Signals
docs.x: California. Section 7025(b) requires a business that sells or shares personal information to process any opt-out preference signal sent in a commonly used format such as an HTTP header field or JavaScript object, and 7025(c) requires it to treat the signal as a valid opt-out for that browser or device and any consumer profile associated with it, including pseudonymous profiles, without demanding extra information. Section 7025(e) and (f) let a business drop the Do Not Sell or Share link only if it processes the signal frictionlessly: no fee, no changed experience, no pop-up or other interstitial content. It binds every CCPA business. Read Global Privacy Control before any tags fire. Under 7025(c)(6) displaying the signal's processing status is optional, so check the CPPA's updated regulations for any change from 1 January 2026. Topics: opt-out-signals, browser-signals.

docs.t: People v. Sephora USA, Inc., California Attorney General CCPA settlement
docs.x: California. The first public CCPA settlement found that allowing third-party tracking software on a website and app in exchange for advertising and analytics services is a sale of personal information, that Sephora failed to disclose the sale, ignored Global Privacy Control signals and did not cure within the 30-day period. Sephora paid $1.2 million and must state in its privacy policy that it sells data, honour GPC, align service provider contracts with the CCPA and report to the Attorney General. It binds Sephora but signals the position taken against every business using ad tech cookies. Treat GPC as an opt-out request from the first page load. Topics: opt-out-signals, sale-sharing, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: Javier v. Assurance IQ, LLC, No. 21-16351 (9th Cir.)
docs.x: California. The Ninth Circuit held that CIPA section 631(a) requires the prior consent of all parties to a communication, so consent obtained after a session replay vendor has already begun recording does not defeat the claim, and reversed dismissal of a complaint alleging that ActiveProspect's TrustedForm recorded a website visitor's interactions before he agreed to the site's privacy policy. The memorandum is unpublished and not precedential. It applies to any operator whose recording, chat or form-capture vendor loads before consent. Delay session replay and similar scripts until an affirmative consent event, and keep a record of the consent timestamp. Topics: pixels-wiretap, consent. Status: decided.

docs.t: Federal Trade Commission Act, Section 5, 15 U.S.C. 45
docs.x: United States (federal). Section 5 of the FTC Act, 15 U.S.C. 45, empowers the Commission to prevent unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce, and it is the legal basis for every federal tracking-pixel, health-data and dark-pattern case on this page: a privacy policy or consent interface that misstates what tags do is deceptive, and sharing sensitive data without consent in a way consumers cannot avoid is unfair. It binds virtually every company in United States commerce, with exemptions for common carriers and certain non-profits. Write cookie disclosures so that every statement about tags and data sharing is literally true; the FTC needs no state privacy statute to act. Topics: dark-patterns, pixels-wiretap, enforcement.

docs.t: FTC v. Kochava Inc., stipulated final order banning sale of sensitive location data
docs.x: United States (federal). The Commission sued the data broker in the District of Idaho on 29 August 2022 under the unfairness prong of Section 5, alleging that it sold geolocation data from hundreds of millions of mobile devices that could track visits to reproductive health clinics, places of worship and shelters. The stipulated order, approved 2 to 0, prohibits Kochava and its subsidiary Collective Data Solutions from selling, licensing or sharing sensitive location data without affirmative express consent, and requires a sensitive location programme, consent verification, disclosure of recipients on request and scheduled deletion. It binds Kochava. Treat precise location collected through SDKs as sensitive data requiring opt-in. Topics: health-data, consent, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: FTC Policy Statement on COPPA and age verification technologies
docs.x: United States (federal). Adopted 2 to 0, the statement announces that the Commission will not bring COPPA enforcement against an operator that collects personal information solely to verify age, provided the data is used only for that purpose, deleted promptly afterwards, not disclosed to third parties without written assurances, explained in clear notice to parents and children, secured reasonably and gathered through a reasonably accurate method. It remains in effect until final rule amendments on age verification are published or it is withdrawn, and the Commission intends to open a rule review. It applies to all COPPA operators. Age gates can use verification data without triggering consent if those conditions are met. Topics: children, consent.

docs.t: Salazar v. Paramount Global, No. 25-459 (U.S. Supreme Court), definition of consumer under the Video Privacy Protection Act
docs.x: United States (federal). The Supreme Court granted certiorari on 26 January 2026 on whether a person who subscribes to a non-audiovisual offering such as an email newsletter is a consumer under the Video Privacy Protection Act. The Sixth Circuit in Salazar v. Paramount and the D.C. Circuit in Pileggi require the goods or services to be audiovisual; the Second Circuit in Salazar v. NBA and the Seventh Circuit in Gardner v. Me-TV read consumer broadly. The decision will fix the class of plaintiffs able to sue over pixel disclosures of video viewing. Until judgment, do not send video titles with user identifiers to advertising platforms. Topics: pixels-wiretap. Status: under appeal.

docs.t: Popa v. Microsoft Corp., No. 24-14 (9th Cir.)
docs.x: United States (federal). In a published opinion the Ninth Circuit affirmed dismissal for lack of Article III standing of wiretapping and intrusion claims based on Microsoft's Clarity session replay tool, which captured mouse movements, clicks, keystrokes, URLs and product browsing on a retailer's website. The court held that recording ordinary website interactions does not resemble a harm traditionally recognised at common law and is not highly offensive, comparing it to a shop assistant watching which aisles customers visit. The underlying claims were brought under Pennsylvania's wiretapping statute, not California's CIPA, but the standing reasoning binds federal courts across the Ninth Circuit and is now cited to dismiss session-replay claims generally. Keep sensitive fields masked and avoid capturing health, financial or identity data. Topics: pixels-wiretap. Status: decided.

docs.t: Solomon v. Flipps Media, Inc., No. 23-7597 (2d Cir.), Video Privacy Protection Act and the Meta Pixel
docs.x: United States (federal). The Second Circuit adopted the ordinary person standard for personally identifiable information under the Video Privacy Protection Act and held that a Meta Pixel transmission of a Facebook ID together with an encoded video title is not PII, because an ordinary person could not use that code to identify a consumer's viewing habits without specialised knowledge. Dismissal was affirmed and the Supreme Court denied certiorari on 8 December 2025. It binds federal courts in New York, Connecticut and Vermont and deepens a split with circuits applying a broader reasonable foreseeability test. Pixel exposure on video pages remains live elsewhere, and the Supreme Court is reviewing who counts as a consumer. Topics: pixels-wiretap. Status: decided.

docs.t: Children's Online Privacy Protection Rule, 16 CFR Part 312, 2025 final amendments
docs.x: United States (federal). Published in the Federal Register on 22 April 2025, effective 23 June 2025 and with a compliance date of 22 April 2026 for most provisions, the amended rule requires operators to obtain separate verifiable parental consent before disclosing children's personal information to third parties, including for targeted advertising, limits retention to what is reasonably necessary for a specific purpose, adds biometric and government identifiers to personal information, confines persistent identifiers collected under the support for internal operations exception to those activities, and requires neutral age screening on mixed audience sites. It binds operators of child-directed services and those with actual knowledge. Behavioural advertising to children now needs a separate consent. Topics: children, consent.

docs.t: HHS Office for Civil Rights, Use of Online Tracking Technologies by HIPAA Covered Entities and Business Associates
docs.x: United States (federal). First issued on 1 December 2022 and revised in 2024, the bulletin states that regulated entities must configure tracking technologies on user-authenticated pages so that vendors use and disclose protected health information only as the Privacy Rule permits, with a business associate agreement in place, and that information entered on unauthenticated pages such as appointment schedulers or symptom checkers is also PHI. On 20 June 2024 the Northern District of Texas vacated the part treating an IP address combined with a visit to a page about a health condition as PHI; HHS is evaluating its next steps. It binds HIPAA covered entities and business associates. Keep ad tech off portals. Topics: health-data, pixels-wiretap.

docs.t: FTC Health Breach Notification Rule, 16 CFR Part 318, 2024 final amendments
docs.x: United States (federal). Approved 3 to 2 and effective 60 days after Federal Register publication, the amended rule clarifies that a breach of security includes an unauthorised disclosure, not only a hacking incident, adds definitions of covered health care provider and health care services or supplies so that health apps and connected devices are covered as personal health record vendors, allows electronic notice, and requires notice to the Commission at the same time as consumers for breaches affecting 500 or more people, within 60 calendar days of discovery. It binds vendors of personal health records and related entities outside HIPAA. Sharing health data with an advertising pixel without authorisation is a notifiable breach. Topics: health-data, pixels-wiretap.

docs.t: FTC and HHS joint letters to hospital systems and telehealth providers on online tracking technologies
docs.x: United States (federal). The Federal Trade Commission and the HHS Office for Civil Rights sent joint letters to approximately 130 hospital systems and telehealth providers warning that the Meta Pixel, Google Analytics and similar technologies on websites and apps may impermissibly disclose sensitive health data to third parties, citing HIPAA for covered entities and the FTC Act and Health Breach Notification Rule for everyone else. The letters reference the HHS bulletin of December 2022. They apply to health providers and to non-HIPAA health businesses alike. Inventory every tag on pages where users schedule appointments, search symptoms or log in, and remove those without a business associate agreement or consent. Topics: health-data, pixels-wiretap.

docs.t: United States v. Easy Healthcare Corp. (Premom), FTC enforcement action
docs.x: United States (federal). The Commission alleged that the Premom fertility app shared health data with AppsFlyer and Google through advertising and analytics SDKs, and sent device identifiers, precise location and social media data to the China-based analytics firms Umeng and Jiguang, contrary to privacy policy promises, and failed to notify users under the Health Breach Notification Rule. Easy Healthcare pays a $100,000 civil penalty plus $100,000 to Connecticut, the District of Columbia and Oregon, is barred from sharing health data for advertising, must obtain affirmative consent for other sharing, seek deletion by recipients and limit retention. It binds Easy Healthcare. Audit mobile SDKs with the same rigour as web pixels. Topics: health-data, pixels-wiretap, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: In the Matter of BetterHelp, Inc., FTC consent order
docs.x: United States (federal). The Commission alleged that the online counselling platform disclosed email addresses, IP addresses and intake questionnaire answers to Facebook, Snapchat, Criteo and Pinterest for advertising, including building lookalike audiences from people who had sought therapy, despite promising not to share health data. The order, finalised on 14 July 2023 by a 3 to 0 vote, requires $7.8 million in consumer refunds, bans sharing health data for advertising and retargeting, requires affirmative express consent before any disclosure to third parties, and mandates a privacy programme, deletion by recipients and a retention schedule. It binds BetterHelp. Match every pixel event against the promises in the privacy policy before it fires. Topics: health-data, pixels-wiretap, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: United States v. GoodRx Holdings, Inc., FTC enforcement action under Section 5 and the Health Breach Notification Rule
docs.x: United States (federal). The Commission's first Health Breach Notification Rule action alleged that GoodRx shared users' prescription medications and health conditions with Facebook, Google, Criteo and other advertising platforms through pixels and identifiers, used the data to build targeted advertising audiences, and never notified users of the unauthorised disclosures. GoodRx paid a $1.5 million civil penalty and is permanently barred from disclosing health information for advertising, must obtain affirmative express consent for other sharing, direct third parties to delete the data, limit retention and avoid dark patterns when seeking consent. It binds GoodRx but sets the template for every health-adjacent site. Treat pixel disclosures of health data as reportable breaches. Topics: health-data, pixels-wiretap, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: FTC staff report, Bringing Dark Patterns to Light
docs.x: United States (federal). The staff report groups dark patterns into four categories: misleading consumers and disguising advertisements, making subscription cancellation difficult, burying terms and hiding fees, and tricking consumers into sharing data through privacy choices designed to steer them toward the option that gives away the most personal information, including default settings that share viewing activity with third parties behind an easily missed notice. It is guidance on how the Commission reads Section 5 and applies to any consumer-facing interface. Use it as the design checklist for consent banners: equal weight for accept and decline, no pre-selected sharing, and no interface that treats closing a pop-up as consent. Topics: dark-patterns, consent.

docs.t: Connecticut Public Act 25-113 (SB 1295), amendments to the Connecticut Data Privacy Act
docs.x: Connecticut. From 1 July 2026 the Act lowers the applicability threshold to controllers processing personal data of 35,000 or more consumers and covers any controller that sells personal data or processes sensitive data regardless of volume, adds neural, reproductive and gender-affirming health data to sensitive data, bars targeted advertising to or sale of data of consumers aged 13 to 17 without consent, and requires impact assessments and a right to question profiling decisions with significant effects. Opt-out preference signals must be honoured where the signal is affirmative, freely given and unambiguous. It binds controllers doing business in Connecticut. Re-run the scoping analysis, because many smaller publishers now fall inside the Act. Topics: opt-out-signals, children, sale-sharing.

docs.t: Indiana Consumer Data Protection Act, Ind. Code 24-15 (SEA 5 of 2023)
docs.x: Indiana. Effective 1 January 2026, the Act gives consumers the right to opt out of targeted advertising, sale of personal data and profiling, requires consent for sensitive data and requires a controller that sells data or engages in targeted advertising to disclose that fact and the means to opt out. It contains no universal opt-out signal requirement. It binds controllers conducting business in Indiana that process data of 100,000 or more consumers, or 25,000 with over 50 percent of revenue from sales. The Attorney General has exclusive enforcement authority, with a 30-day cure period and civil penalties of up to $7,500 per violation. A disclosed opt-out link is sufficient for Indiana. Topics: sale-sharing.

docs.t: Kentucky Consumer Data Protection Act, HB 15 of 2024 (Acts Chapter 72), KRS 367.3611 to 367.3627
docs.x: Kentucky. Signed on 4 April 2024 and effective 1 January 2026, the Act gives consumers the right to confirm processing, correct, delete, obtain a copy and opt out of targeted advertising, the sale of data or profiling, and requires consent for sensitive data. It contains no universal opt-out signal requirement. It binds persons conducting business in Kentucky that process data of 100,000 or more consumers, or 25,000 with over 50 percent of revenue from sales. The Attorney General has exclusive enforcement authority with a 30-day cure period, civil penalties of up to $7,500 per violation and a consumer privacy fund. A disclosed opt-out link meets the requirement. Topics: sale-sharing.

docs.t: Rhode Island Data Transparency and Privacy Protection Act, R.I. Gen. Laws Chapter 6-48.1
docs.x: Rhode Island. Operative from 1 January 2026, the chapter gives customers under 6-48.1-5 the right to opt out of processing for targeted advertising, sale of personal data or profiling in furtherance of solely automated decisions, exercised by secure and reliable means established by the controller and described in its privacy notice; no universal opt-out mechanism is required. It binds controllers meeting the consumer-volume thresholds. Under 6-48.1-8 the Attorney General has sole enforcement authority, there is no private right of action and no cure period, and intentional disclosure in violation of the chapter carries $100 to $500 per disclosure in addition to general commercial law remedies. Publish the opt-out method in the notice. Topics: sale-sharing.

docs.t: Maryland Online Data Privacy Act of 2024, SB 541 (Chapter 455), Md. Code Com. Law 14-4601 et seq.
docs.x: Maryland. Approved on 9 May 2024 and effective 1 October 2025, the Act gives consumers rights to opt out of targeted advertising, sale of personal data and profiling and requires controllers to honour an opt-out preference signal for these choices. It prohibits the sale of sensitive data outright, limits collection to what is reasonably necessary, and bars targeted advertising and sale of personal data to consumers the controller knows or should know are aged 13 to 17. A narrower provision on permitted-processing exceptions applies only to activity after 1 April 2026. It binds controllers processing data of 35,000 or more consumers, or 10,000 with 20 percent of revenue from sales. Suppress ad tech for known teenage users and honour Global Privacy Control for Maryland visitors. Topics: opt-out-signals, children, sale-sharing.

docs.t: California, Colorado and Connecticut joint investigative sweep on Global Privacy Control compliance
docs.x: United States (multi-state). The California Attorney General, the California Privacy Protection Agency and the Attorneys General of Colorado and Connecticut announced a coordinated investigative sweep of businesses that fail to honour Global Privacy Control, describing it as a browser setting or extension that automatically signals a request to stop selling or sharing personal information. The announcement cites the CCPA and the Colorado and Connecticut privacy laws and asks businesses to come into immediate compliance. It applies to any business selling or sharing data of residents of those states. Assume GPC processing is being tested from outside, and confirm it works across every domain and subdomain. Topics: opt-out-signals, browser-signals, enforcement.

docs.t: Minnesota Consumer Data Privacy Act, Minn. Stat. Chapter 325O (2024 Minn. Laws ch. 121, art. 5)
docs.x: Minnesota. Enacted in 2024 Minnesota Laws chapter 121 and effective 31 July 2025, the Act gives consumers rights to opt out of targeted advertising, sale of personal data and profiling, and requires controllers to honour opt-out preference signals from the same date. It adds a right to question the result of profiling and a duty to keep a data inventory. It binds controllers that process data of 100,000 or more consumers, or 25,000 with 25 percent of revenue from sales. The Attorney General enforces with civil penalties of up to $7,500 per violation and a 30-day cure period that sunsets on 31 January 2026. Recognise Global Privacy Control for Minnesota visitors. Topics: opt-out-signals, sale-sharing.

docs.t: Tennessee Information Protection Act, Tenn. Code Ann. 47-18-3201 et seq. (Public Chapter 408 of 2023)
docs.x: Tennessee. Effective 1 July 2025, the Act gives consumers the right to opt out of targeted advertising, sale of personal data and profiling and requires consent for sensitive data. It contains no universal opt-out signal requirement and provides an affirmative defence to a controller whose written privacy programme reasonably conforms to the NIST Privacy Framework. It binds controllers with more than $25 million in revenue that process data of 175,000 or more consumers, or 25,000 with over 50 percent of revenue from sales. The Attorney General enforces with a 60-day cure period and civil penalties of up to $7,500 per violation, trebled for wilful violations. Document the programme against NIST. Topics: sale-sharing.

docs.t: New Jersey Data Privacy Act, P.L.2023, c.266 (S332), N.J.S.A. 56:8-166.4 et seq.
docs.x: New Jersey. Approved on 16 January 2024 and effective 365 days later, the Act gives consumers rights to opt out of targeted advertising, sale of personal data and profiling, and requires controllers to honour opt-outs sent through a user-selected universal opt-out mechanism from six months after the effective date, that is 15 July 2025. It binds controllers that process data of 100,000 or more consumers, or 25,000 with revenue from sales. The Attorney General has sole enforcement authority, a 30-day cure notice applied only for the first 18 months after the effective date, and the Division of Consumer Affairs may adopt rules for the mechanism. Treat Global Privacy Control as an opt-out for New Jersey visitors. Topics: opt-out-signals, sale-sharing.

docs.t: Delaware Personal Data Privacy Act, 6 Del. C. Chapter 12D
docs.x: Delaware. Effective 1 January 2025, the Act gives consumers rights to opt out of targeted advertising, sale of personal data and profiling, and from 1 January 2026 controllers must allow those opt-outs through an opt-out preference signal that is consumer friendly, requires an affirmative and unambiguous choice rather than a default, and lets the controller verify residency. It binds controllers that process data of 35,000 or more consumers, or 10,000 with 20 percent of revenue from sales, with the thresholds falling to 10,000 and 5,000 on 1 January 2027. The Attorney General enforces and may demand data protection assessments. Honour Global Privacy Control for Delaware visitors and revisit scope before 2027. Topics: opt-out-signals, sale-sharing.

docs.t: New Hampshire Expectation of Privacy Act, RSA Chapter 507-H (SB 255)
docs.x: New Hampshire. Effective 1 January 2025, the chapter gives consumers rights to opt out of targeted advertising, sale of personal data and profiling, and RSA 507-H:6, V(a)(1)(B) requires controllers, not later than 1 January 2025, to accept opt-out preference signals sent through a platform, technology or mechanism that communicates the consumer's intent to opt out. It binds controllers meeting the consumer-volume thresholds. The Attorney General has exclusive enforcement authority, violations are unfair or deceptive practices under RSA 358-A:2, there is no private right of action, and the 60-day cure notice was mandatory only during 2025 and is discretionary after that. Recognise Global Privacy Control from day one for New Hampshire visitors. Topics: opt-out-signals, sale-sharing.

docs.t: Nebraska Data Privacy Act, LB 1074, Neb. Rev. Stat. 87-1101 to 87-1130
docs.x: Nebraska. Effective 1 January 2025 and modelled on the Texas statute, the Act gives consumers rights to opt out of targeted advertising, sale of personal data and profiling, and requires controllers to honour opt-out requests sent through a technology such as a browser setting, browser extension or global device setting, with no separate later date for that duty. It binds any person conducting business in Nebraska that processes or sells personal data and is not a small business, with no volume threshold. The Attorney General enforces, may issue civil investigative demands and may request data protection assessments; a 30-day cure period applies. Treat Global Privacy Control as binding for Nebraska visitors. Topics: opt-out-signals, sale-sharing.

docs.t: Iowa Consumer Data Protection Act, Iowa Code Chapter 715D
docs.x: Iowa. Enacted in 2023 Acts chapter 17 and effective 1 January 2025, the chapter requires controllers under 715D.4 to disclose clearly and conspicuously any sale of personal data or targeted advertising and how consumers can opt out, and to provide secure and reliable means for requests. It does not mandate acceptance of universal opt-out signals, and sensitive data requires notice and an opportunity to opt out rather than consent. It binds controllers meeting the consumer-volume thresholds. Under 715D.8 the Attorney General has exclusive enforcement authority, must give 90 days' written notice to cure, and may seek civil penalties of up to $7,500 per violation. Signal handling is optional here. Topics: sale-sharing.

docs.t: Montana Consumer Data Privacy Act, SB 384, Mont. Code Ann. 30-14-2801 et seq.
docs.x: Montana. Effective 1 October 2024, the Act gives consumers the right to opt out of targeted advertising, sale of personal data and profiling, and requires controllers to honour opt-out preference signals sent through a consumer-friendly platform, technology or mechanism by 1 January 2025. The Attorney General has exclusive enforcement authority, there is no private right of action, and the 60-day notice and cure requirement terminated on 1 April 2026. It binds controllers doing business in Montana that meet the consumer-volume thresholds. Route Global Privacy Control to the same opt-out as the banner and expect no cure notice before enforcement from April 2026. Topics: opt-out-signals, sale-sharing.

docs.t: New York Attorney General, Website Privacy Controls: A Guide for Business
docs.x: New York. After reviewing 13 high-traffic websites with about 75 million visitors in March 2024, the Office found privacy controls that did not work as described: marketing and advertising tags stayed active after visitors disabled them, most often because tags were uncategorised or miscategorised in the consent management tool, hard-coded outside it, or because the consent tool was not passing opt-out signals to the tag manager. The guide states that New York's consumer protection law requires privacy representations to be truthful, warns that Accept All buttons must not imply cookies deploy only on click, and asks for equal-weight accept and decline options. It applies to any business serving New York consumers. Topics: consent, dark-patterns, reject-button.

docs.t: Colorado Attorney General, Universal Opt-Out Mechanism list and Colorado Privacy Act Rules, 4 CCR 904-3
docs.x: Colorado. The Department of Law maintains the public list of recognised universal opt-out mechanisms under C.R.S. 6-1-1306(1)(a)(IV) and Rule 5.07 of the Colorado Privacy Act Rules, 4 CCR 904-3, Part 5. Global Privacy Control is the only mechanism on the list, and controllers must honour it from 1 July 2024 as an opt-out from sale and from targeted advertising; the list does not exclude other mechanisms that meet the rules. It binds every controller subject to the Act. Implement GPC as a header and JavaScript signal, and treat a signal received while a consumer is logged in as applying to the account. Topics: opt-out-signals, browser-signals.

docs.t: Texas Data Privacy and Security Act, Tex. Bus. & Com. Code Chapter 541 (HB 4)
docs.x: Texas. Effective 1 July 2024 and enforced by the Attorney General's Consumer Protection Division, the Act gives consumers the right to opt out of targeted advertising, sale of personal data and profiling, and from 1 January 2025 section 541.055(e) requires controllers to honour targeted advertising and sale opt-outs sent through a technology such as a browser setting, browser extension or global device setting. It binds any person conducting business in Texas, or producing a product or service consumed by Texas residents, that processes or sells personal data and is not a small business, with no volume threshold. A 30-day cure period applies and civil penalties reach $7,500 per violation. Honour Global Privacy Control for Texas visitors; head counts do not scope you out. Topics: opt-out-signals, sale-sharing.

docs.t: Oregon Consumer Privacy Act, ORS 646A.570 to 646A.589 (SB 619)
docs.x: Oregon. Effective 1 July 2024, the Act gives consumers rights to opt out of targeted advertising, sale of personal data and profiling, and from 1 January 2026 controllers must honour opt-out signals that meet the statute's technical requirements, with Global Privacy Control cited by the Department of Justice as an example. The Department publishes quarterly and annual enforcement reports and issued a one-year report in August 2025. It binds controllers doing business in Oregon that process data of 100,000 or more consumers, or 25,000 or more where more than 25 per cent of annual gross revenue comes from selling personal data; motor vehicle manufacturers are covered with no threshold. The notice-and-cure period ended on 1 January 2026, so treat Oregon as a signal-mandatory state with no cure right and answer Department inquiries as enforcement, not as a warning. Topics: opt-out-signals, sale-sharing.

docs.t: Washington My Health My Data Act, RCW Chapter 19.373 (HB 1155)
docs.x: Washington. Effective 31 March 2024 for regulated entities and 30 June 2024 for small businesses, RCW 19.373.030 prohibits collecting or sharing consumer health data without the consumer's affirmative consent or a necessity to provide a requested product or service, RCW 19.373.070 makes any sale of consumer health data unlawful without a separate signed authorisation, and RCW 19.373.080 bans geofencing around in-person health services. Consumer health data includes inferences drawn from non-health data. It binds any entity doing business in Washington or targeting Washington consumers; under RCW 19.373.090 a violation is a per se Consumer Protection Act breach with a private right of action. Gate pixels on health pages behind opt-in consent. Topics: health-data, consent, pixels-wiretap.

docs.t: Washington Attorney General, guidance on the My Health My Data Act
docs.x: Washington. The Attorney General's guidance states that the Act, signed on 27 April 2023, is the first privacy law to protect health data outside HIPAA, that all persons must comply with the geofencing section from 23 July 2023, non-small businesses with sections 4 to 9 from 31 March 2024 and small businesses from 30 June 2024, and that regulated entities must prominently publish a link to a consumer health data privacy policy on their homepage. It gives a retailer's pregnancy prediction score derived from purchases as an example of covered inferences. It applies to any entity in scope of the Act. Publish the separate policy link. Topics: health-data, consent.

docs.t: Utah Consumer Privacy Act, Utah Code 13-61-101 et seq. (SB 227)
docs.x: Utah. Effective 31 December 2023, the Act gives consumers under 13-61-201 the right to opt out of targeted advertising and the sale of personal data, requires a clear notice of that right, and requires only notice and an opportunity to opt out, rather than consent, before processing sensitive data. It contains no universal opt-out signal requirement and no right to opt out of profiling. It binds controllers with $25 million or more in annual revenue that also meet the consumer-volume thresholds. The Attorney General enforces on referral from the Division of Consumer Protection, with a 30-day cure period and penalties of up to $7,500 per violation. A conventional opt-out link suffices. Topics: sale-sharing.

docs.t: Colorado Privacy Act, SB 21-190, C.R.S. 6-1-1301 et seq.
docs.x: Colorado. Signed on 7 July 2021 and effective 1 July 2023, the Act gives consumers the right to opt out of targeted advertising, sale of personal data and certain profiling, and C.R.S. 6-1-1306(1)(a)(IV) requires controllers to honour opt-outs sent through a universal opt-out mechanism meeting the Attorney General's technical specifications, with that duty operative from 1 July 2024. It binds controllers doing business in Colorado that process data of 100,000 or more consumers a year, or 25,000 with revenue from sales. The 60-day cure period expired on 1 January 2025. Recognise Global Privacy Control as an opt-out from targeted advertising, not only from sale. Topics: opt-out-signals, sale-sharing.

docs.t: Connecticut Data Privacy Act, Conn. Gen. Stat. 42-515 et seq. (Public Act 22-15)
docs.x: Connecticut. Effective 1 July 2023, the Act grants rights to opt out of targeted advertising, sale of personal data and profiling, and from 1 January 2025 every controller subject to it must honour opt-out preference signals sent by consumers. Violations are enforceable by the Attorney General under the Connecticut Unfair Trade Practices Act with civil penalties of up to $5,000 per wilful violation, alongside injunctive relief, restitution and disgorgement; the Attorney General publishes annual enforcement reports. It binds controllers meeting the consumer-volume thresholds. Map the banner's opt-out to both targeted advertising and sale, and honour Global Privacy Control without a confirmation step. Amended by Public Act 25-113 from 1 July 2026. Topics: opt-out-signals, sale-sharing.

docs.t: Virginia Consumer Data Protection Act, Va. Code 59.1-575 to 59.1-584
docs.x: Virginia. Effective 1 January 2023, the Act gives consumers the right under 59.1-577 to opt out of targeted advertising, sale of personal data and profiling in furtherance of decisions that produce legal or similarly significant effects, requires under 59.1-578(D) a clear and conspicuous disclosure of that processing and of the manner in which a consumer may opt out where a controller sells data or engages in targeted advertising, and requires consent for sensitive data. It does not require controllers to honour universal opt-out signals. It binds persons conducting business in Virginia or targeting its residents that control or process data of 100,000 or more consumers, or 25,000 with over 50 percent of gross revenue from the sale of personal data. The Attorney General enforces with a 30-day cure period and civil penalties of up to $7,500 per violation. Offer an explicit opt-out link covering cookie-based targeted advertising. Topics: sale-sharing, consent.

docs.t: Exposure draft, Privacy Amendment (Personal Data Protection) Bill 2026 (tranche 2 reforms)
docs.x: Australia. The Attorney-General's Department released the tranche 2 exposure draft, with the Bill and an accompanying consultation paper, in 2026. It would define consent as voluntary, informed, current, specific and unambiguous, extend collection to information generated or inferred, give identifiers and location or behavioural data as examples of information that is personal where reasonably linkable, make precise geolocation tracking data sensitive, add a fair and reasonable test weighing the child's best interests, require consent before trading personal information, and retain a simple opt-out from direct marketing, including online behavioural advertising based on personal information, while keeping flexibility for ad-supported services. It is not law. Model banner changes now against the proposed standard. Topics: consent, consent-or-pay, sale-sharing. Status: proposed.

docs.t: Bill C-36, Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act
docs.x: Canada. Bill C-36 would enact the Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act to replace Part 1 of PIPEDA, keeping a meaningful consent standard in plain language with expanded exceptions for business activities, research and de-identification, confirming that de-identified information remains personal information, requiring particular attention to children's information, and creating administrative penalties of up to the greater of $10 million or 3 percent of global revenue, with offences up to the greater of $25 million or 5 percent. It received first reading in the House of Commons on 15 June 2026 and has not progressed further. Track the bill, but change nothing in consent flows until it passes. Topics: consent, children, enforcement. Status: proposed.

docs.t: PPC Guidelines on the Act on the Protection of Personal Information (General Rules edition), section 2-8 on personally referable information
docs.x: Japan. The Commission's general guidelines, first issued in November 2016 and last partially revised in June 2026, define personally referable information as information that does not identify an individual by itself but can identify one when combined with other data, and explain the Article 31 confirmation and record-keeping duties when such information is provided to a third party that will treat it as personal data. They bind no one directly but state the standard the Commission applies in supervision. Use section 2-8 to decide, for each tag on the site, whether the recipient will link the identifier to a person and therefore whether the recipient's consent must be confirmed first. Topics: consent, sale-sharing.

docs.t: Commissioner-initiated investigations into Medmate Australia and Monash IVF (tracking pixels), AICmr 40 and 41
docs.x: Australia. The Privacy Commissioner determined on 11 June 2026 that a telehealth provider and a fertility provider breached APP 3.3 by collecting sensitive health information through third-party tracking pixels without consent, APP 5.1 by failing to notify, and APP 7.1 by using sensitive information for direct marketing without consent. Monash IVF ran seven pixels from 30 July 2012 to 9 December 2024 and Medmate from April 2021 to 9 December 2024; neither ran a privacy impact assessment, and the argument that data sent straight to a platform was not collected was rejected. The determinations bind the two entities. Remove or gate pixels on any page revealing a health topic. Topics: pixels-wiretap, health-data, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: OAIC exposure draft of the Children's Online Privacy Code
docs.x: Australia. The draft Code, released on 31 March 2026 for consultation to 5 June 2026, would apply to APP entities providing social media, relevant electronic services or designated internet services likely to be accessed by children, other than health services. It requires collection, use and disclosure to be consistent with the child's best interests, and limits direct marketing to children: non-sensitive information may be used only with consent and consistently with the child's best interests, while sensitive information may be used only if it was collected from the child or a person with parental responsibility, an opt-out mechanism is offered, and the use is consistent with the child's best interests. It also requires age-appropriate notices and a deletion right. The final Code must be registered by 10 December 2026. Inventory trackers on child-accessible services now and plan to disable advertising and profiling cookies for those audiences. Topics: children, consent. Status: proposed.

docs.t: Vietnam Personal Data Protection Law (Law 91/2025/QH15), successor to Decree 13/2023/ND-CP
docs.x: Vietnam. The Law, passed on 26 June 2025 and in force from 1 January 2026, carries forward the consent standard of Decree 13/2023/ND-CP (in force from 1 July 2023): consent must be voluntary, specific, informed and given per purpose, and silence is not consent. It adds fines of up to 5 percent of the previous year's revenue for unlawful cross-border transfers and up to ten times the revenue gained from unlawful sale of personal data, in each case the higher of that figure and VND 3 billion, and requires social network and online service providers to offer a do-not-track option and opt-outs for cookies and tracking. It binds domestic and foreign controllers processing Vietnamese residents' data. Present cookie consent per purpose and provide a working tracking opt-out. Topics: consent, opt-out-signals, enforcement.

docs.t: Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 (consent notice, Consent Managers, verifiable parental consent, phased commencement)
docs.x: India. The Rules, notified as G.S.R. 846(E) on 13 November 2025, bring the Act into force in phases measured from publication in the Official Gazette: the Data Protection Board provisions (rules 17 to 21) at once, the Consent Manager registration rule after twelve months in November 2026, and the remaining rules, including consent notices, children's verifiable consent and breach notification, after eighteen months in May 2027. They prescribe the content of a consent notice, the registration conditions for Consent Managers, and the methods for verifying a parent's identity and age. They bind every data fiduciary within the Act's scope. Schedule the consent banner rebuild and children's age-assurance design for completion before the eighteen-month date and plan integration with registered Consent Managers. Topics: consent, children, other. Status: applies from a future date.

docs.t: Israel Protection of Privacy Law 5741-1981 as amended by Amendment 13
docs.x: Israel. Amendment 13, in force from 14 August 2025, modernises the 1981 law by widening the definitions of personal and sensitive data, requiring that a request for information state whether provision is mandatory, the purposes, recipients and rights, giving the Privacy Protection Authority powers to audit, order and impose administrative fines, and extending duties to outsourced holders processing data for a controller. Direct marketing databases remain subject to the database registration and opt-out rules. Practitioners should present cookie notices with the statutory disclosure items and maintain an easy opt-out from direct marketing profiles built from tracking data. Topics: consent, enforcement.

docs.t: PPC Guidelines Q&A on the APPI (updated edition)
docs.x: Japan. The Commission's consolidated Q&A, last updated on 1 July 2025, answers practical questions under the guidelines, including how cookies and advertising identifiers are treated, when browsing data becomes personally referable information, what form the recipient's consent must take under Article 31, and how the providing business may confirm and record that consent. It binds no one but reflects the Commission's supervisory reading and is cited in inspections. Keep the Q&A numbers for cookies and Article 31 in the tag governance file, and use its examples to set the consent wording that advertising partners must show before matching identifiers to user accounts. Topics: consent, sale-sharing.

docs.t: Privacy Act 1988 (Cth), Australian Privacy Principles 3, 5, 6, 7 and 8 (Compilation No. 103)
docs.x: Australia. The compilation in force from 10 June 2025 defines personal information as information about an identified or reasonably identifiable individual, defines consent as express or implied, requires consent to collect sensitive information (APP 3.3), notification at or before collection (APP 5), use and disclosure only for the primary purpose or with consent (APP 6), a simple means of opting out of direct marketing (APP 7) and reasonable steps for overseas disclosures (APP 8). It binds APP entities, broadly organisations with annual turnover above $3 million and all health service providers. Map every pixel and cookie to these principles and obtain express consent before any tracker can capture sensitive information. Topics: consent, health-data, transfers.

docs.t: Mexico Ley Federal de Protección de Datos Personales en Posesión de los Particulares (2025)
docs.x: Mexico. The new federal law, published on 20 March 2025 and in force from 21 March 2025, replaces the 2010 statute, moves supervision from INAI to the Secretaría Anticorrupción y Buen Gobierno, keeps tacit consent for non-sensitive data where the privacy notice is provided and the person does not object, requires express consent for sensitive and financial data (written for sensitive data), and subjects transfers to third parties to the consent form that applies to the data concerned, with the statutory exceptions for group companies, legal requirements and contracts in the person's interest. The privacy notice must be available before collection, and the regulations continue to require disclosure of cookies, web beacons and similar technologies and how to disable them. It binds private-sector controllers in Mexico. Keep the cookie disclosure in the notice and offer an objection route. Topics: consent, other.

docs.t: Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA), s. 6.1 and Schedule 1 Principle 4.3
docs.x: Canada. PIPEDA requires knowledge and consent for the collection, use and disclosure of personal information (Schedule 1, Principle 4.3), and s. 6.1 makes consent valid only where it is reasonable to expect the individual understands the nature, purpose and consequences of the processing. It binds organisations that collect personal information in the course of commercial activity, including foreign operators with a real and substantial connection to Canada. Treat identifiers set by cookies and tracking pixels as personal information, decide whether express or implied consent fits each purpose, and document that analysis; Bill C-36 would replace Part 1 of PIPEDA if enacted. Topics: consent, other.

docs.t: Regulations on Network Data Security Management (State Council Decree 790), Articles 21, 22 and 42
docs.x: China. Published on 30 September 2024 and in force from 1 January 2025, the regulations require network data handlers to publish processing rules in a prominent place, to collect only what is necessary, to obtain separate consent for sensitive information and parental consent for children under 14, and not to repeat a consent request after refusal. Article 42 requires platform providers that push information by automated decision-making to offer an easy-to-understand, easy-to-reach switch to turn off personalised recommendation and to let users delete their tags. They bind network data handlers processing Chinese individuals' data. Remove repeated consent prompts and place the personalisation switch within the first layer of settings. Topics: consent, opt-out-signals, children.

docs.t: Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024 (No. 128, 2024)
docs.x: Australia. The first tranche of Privacy Act reform received assent on 10 December 2024. It creates a statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy from 10 June 2025, requires the OAIC to register a Children's Online Privacy Code by 10 December 2026, requires privacy policies to disclose automated decision-making from 10 December 2026, gives the Commissioner infringement and compliance notice powers from 11 December 2024, and adds tiered civil penalties. It binds all APP entities. Update privacy policies for the automated decision-making disclosure before the deadline, and plan for the Children's Code where a service is likely to be accessed by children. Topics: children, enforcement, other.

docs.t: OAIC guidance: Tracking pixels and privacy obligations
docs.x: Australia. The Commissioner explains that a third-party pixel collects IP address, location, URLs and transaction data and sends it to an advertising platform, engaging APP 1, 3, 5, 6, 7 and 8. Organisations must understand the pixel before deployment, review the provider's terms, run a privacy impact assessment, configure it to collect the minimum, avoid site-wide placement, prevent capture of sensitive information without express opt-in consent, notify users through banners or notices covering the pixel providers and any overseas recipients, and offer a simple opt-out from targeted advertising. It applies to every APP entity using pixels. Treat the list as a pre-deployment checklist and revisit it at each review cycle. Topics: pixels-wiretap, health-data, consent.

docs.t: Indonesia Law No. 27 of 2022 on Personal Data Protection
docs.x: Indonesia. The law, enacted on 17 October 2022 with a two-year transition that ended on 17 October 2024, requires explicit consent, in writing or recorded form, as the primary basis for processing, requires that a consent request be presented clearly and separately from other matters and be withdrawable, and gives data subjects rights to object to profiling and automated decisions, with administrative fines of up to 2 percent of annual revenue. A dedicated supervisory authority and implementing regulations were still being established after the transition ended. It binds controllers in Indonesia and foreign controllers whose processing has legal effect there. Run advertising and analytics cookies on explicit, separately presented consent. Topics: consent, enforcement.

docs.t: ANPD Guia orientativo: Hipóteses legais de tratamento de dados pessoais, legítimo interesse
docs.x: Brazil. The guide sets out how the ANPD expects controllers to rely on legitimate interest under Article 7, IX and Article 10 of the LGPD: a documented balancing test covering the legitimacy of the interest, the necessity of the processing, the impact on data subjects and their legitimate expectations, with a model assessment in the annex. Legitimate interest cannot be used for sensitive data and has restricted use in the public sector. It applies to any controller invoking the basis, including for analytics or necessary cookies. Complete and retain a balancing test before setting any cookie without consent, and provide transparency and an objection route for the processing. Topics: analytics-exemption, strictly-necessary, consent.

docs.t: Commission d'accès à l'information, Lignes directrices 2023-1 sur les critères de validité du consentement
docs.x: Quebec. The Commission's guidelines set eight criteria for valid consent under the public and private sector Acts: manifest, free, informed, given for specific purposes, granular, understandable, temporary, and presented separately from any other information when requested in writing. Consent is not free where refusal takes disproportionate effort compared with acceptance or where visual emphasis such as colour or font size steers the choice, and implied consent requires a genuine opportunity to refuse. The guidelines bind no one directly but state how the Commission will assess consent in investigations. Design banners with equal accept and refuse paths, one purpose per toggle, and a separate consent request for each tracker category. Topics: consent, dark-patterns, reject-button.

docs.t: Act respecting the protection of personal information in the private sector (Law 25 amendments), s. 8.1 and s. 9.1
docs.x: Quebec. Section 8.1, in force since 22 September 2023, requires an enterprise collecting personal information through technology that can identify, locate or profile a person to inform the person first of that technology and of the means available to activate those functions, which the Commission d'accès à l'information reads as requiring such functions to be off by default and switched on only by the individual. Section 9.1 requires the highest confidentiality settings by default but excludes cookies from that specific rule. The Act binds every enterprise handling Quebec residents' information. Configure analytics, advertising and geolocation trackers as opt-in for Quebec visitors and describe the activation controls in the banner. Topics: consent, strictly-necessary, other.

docs.t: Personal Information Protection Act (PIPA), as amended with effect from 15 September 2023
docs.x: South Korea. The amended Act, in force from 15 September 2023, unifies the rules for online service providers and other controllers, requires consent to collect personal information unless another basis applies, requires separate consent for marketing and third-party provision, requires the privacy policy to describe the installation, operation and refusal of automatic collection devices such as cookies, adds a right to refuse automated decisions, and raises the penalty surcharge under Article 64-2 to up to 3 percent of total sales, calculated net of sales unrelated to the violation. It binds domestic and foreign operators processing Korean residents' data. Provide granular opt-in consent for behavioural advertising cookies, keep the cookie section of the privacy policy current, and expect PIPC audits of consent screens. Topics: consent, enforcement.

docs.t: Saudi Arabia Personal Data Protection Law (Royal Decree M/19 as amended by M/148) and Implementing Regulations
docs.x: Saudi Arabia. The PDPL, amended by Royal Decree M/148 of 5/9/1444 AH (March 2023) and in force 720 days after publication under Article 43, requires a lawful basis for processing, consent that can be withdrawn at any time (Article 5), and a privacy policy made available before collection (Article 12), and its Implementing Regulations allow direct marketing only with the data subject's consent, with the sender identified and a way to stop the messages that is as easy as giving consent (Article 29). Fines reach SAR 5 million and may be doubled for a repeat violation (Article 36), with the competent authority supervising, and parties outside the Kingdom processing residents' data are bound (Article 2). Treat advertising cookies as consent-based and include a marketing opt-out in the banner's second layer. Topics: consent, email-marketing.

docs.t: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, sections 6, 9 and the Schedule
docs.x: India. The Act, assented to on 11 August 2023, requires consent that is free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous with a clear affirmative action, limited to necessary data and withdrawable with the same ease (section 6), manageable through a registered Consent Manager. Section 9 requires verifiable parental consent for anyone under 18 and prohibits tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising directed at children; the Schedule sets penalties up to INR 250 crore for security failures and INR 200 crore for children's obligations. It binds data fiduciaries processing digital personal data in India or serving India, phased in under the 2025 Rules. Remove behavioural tracking from services used by minors. Topics: consent, children, enforcement. Status: applies from a future date.

docs.t: Telecommunications Business Act, Article 27-12 (external transmission rule) and MIC guidance
docs.x: Japan. The 2022 amendment to the Telecommunications Business Act, in force from 16 June 2023, requires operators of messaging services, social networks, search services and websites delivering news or information to inform users before a browser or app sends user information to an external party, by notice or easily accessible publication, by consent, or by an opt-out. The disclosure must state the information sent, the recipient and the purpose of use.
