Information necessary to deliver the service and identifiers sent to the operator itself are exempt; e-commerce sites and personal blogs are outside scope. Publish an external transmission page listing every third-party tag, recipient and purpose, linked from the banner. Topics: consent, strictly-necessary, other.

docs.t: Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 and NDPC General Application and Implementation Directive 2025
docs.x: Nigeria. The Act, signed on 12 June 2023, establishes the Nigeria Data Protection Commission in place of the Data Protection Bureau, requires consent that is freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous with the controller bearing the burden of proof, gives a right to object to direct marketing, and empowers the Commission to impose penalties of up to the greater of NGN 10 million and 2 per cent of annual gross revenue for controllers of major importance (the greater of NGN 2 million and 2 per cent for others). The Commission's General Application and Implementation Directive of 2025 adds detailed rules on consent design, cookie notices and privacy policies. It binds controllers in Nigeria and foreign controllers processing the data of data subjects in Nigeria. Deploy a consent banner with a documented consent log and a marketing objection route. Topics: consent, enforcement.

docs.t: Enunciado CD/ANPD nº 1/2023 on the processing of children's and adolescents' personal data
docs.x: Brazil. The statement interprets Article 14 of the LGPD to allow children's and adolescents' data to be processed under any legal basis in Articles 7 and 11, not only specific parental consent, provided the best interest of the minor prevails and is assessed in each case. It binds the ANPD's own enforcement posture and applies to any controller handling minors' data, including operators of sites and apps used by children. Do not rely on it to run behavioural advertising cookies on child-directed services; document a best-interest assessment for any tracker on such services, and default to no tracking where the assessment is unclear. Topics: children, consent.

docs.t: Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI), Article 2(7) and Article 31 (personally referable information)
docs.x: Japan. Since the 2020 amendment took effect on 1 April 2022, Article 31 prohibits a business from providing personally referable information, such as cookie identifiers and browsing history that do not identify a person on their own, to a third party expected to link it to an identified individual, unless the business has confirmed that the recipient obtained the individual's consent and recorded that confirmation. The consolidated English text is current to 1 April 2023. It binds every business handling personal information, including foreign operators serving Japanese users. Where a pixel or SDK sends identifiers to an advertising platform that matches them to accounts, verify and record the platform's consent first. Topics: consent, sale-sharing, pixels-wiretap.

docs.t: OAIC guidance: Direct marketing (APP 7)
docs.x: Australia. The guidance confirms that APP 7 covers targeted online marketing whenever personal information is used or disclosed to deliver it, alongside email and post, while communications covered by the Spam Act 2003 and the Do Not Call Register Act 2006 sit outside APP 7. Organisations must provide a simple means of opting out, draw attention to it in each communication where practicable, and stop using or disclosing the information within a reasonable period after a request. It applies to organisations covered by the Privacy Act. Link the advertising toggle in the banner to a working suppression mechanism so that an opt-out from targeted advertising is honoured across ad platforms. Topics: email-marketing, opt-out-signals, consent.

docs.t: PIPC sanctions Meta for refusing service to users who declined behavioural data collection
docs.x: South Korea. The Commission fined Meta KRW 6.6 million, for making acceptance of behavioural information collection for customised advertising a condition of using the service, finding under article 39-3(3) of the Act that behavioural information gathered from third-party sites and apps is not the minimum personal information necessary to provide the service. The decision binds the company and states the Commission's position that access to a social network cannot be conditioned on advertising consent. Do not deploy cookie walls or consent-or-leave designs for Korean users, and keep the service usable when advertising consent is withheld. Topics: cookie-walls, consent, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: Resolução CD/ANPD nº 4/2023, Regulamento de dosimetria e aplicação de sanções administrativas
docs.x: Brazil. The regulation sets the method by which the ANPD calculates the sanctions in Article 52 of the LGPD, classifying infractions as light, medium or serious, applying a percentage of revenue within the 2 percent and R$50,000,000 ceilings, and listing aggravating and mitigating factors such as recurrence, good faith, cooperation and adoption of a compliance programme. It binds every processing agent subject to LGPD sanctions, which became applicable on 1 August 2021. Since the first fine in July 2023 the authority has applied it consistently. Keep evidence of consent design, records of processing and remediation steps to support the mitigating factors if a cookie complaint escalates. Topics: enforcement.

docs.t: ANPD Guia orientativo: Cookies e proteção de dados pessoais
docs.x: Brazil. The guide classifies cookies as necessary or non-necessary, first or third party, session or persistent, and pairs them with legal bases: consent for non-necessary cookies and legitimate interest for necessary ones, with legitimate interest unsuitable for behavioural profiling and advertising. A first-layer banner must offer a reject option as visible as the accept button and a link to the cookie policy, a second layer must give per-category choices with non-necessary cookies off by default, and pre-ticked boxes, hidden refuse buttons, missing revocation and cookie walls are listed as non-compliant. It is advisory but states how the authority reads the LGPD. Use it as the specification for Brazilian banners. Topics: consent, reject-button, cookie-walls.

docs.t: PIPC sanctions Google and Meta for collecting behavioural information without consent
docs.x: South Korea. The Commission imposed penalty surcharges of KRW 69.2 billion on Google and KRW 30.8 billion on Meta for collecting users' behavioural information from third-party websites and apps and using it for customised advertising without clearly informing users or obtaining consent, finding that Google hid the setting behind a default-on option and that Meta buried the disclosure in its terms. The decision binds the two companies and set the largest surcharges under the Act at the time. Corrective orders required an easy, clear consent screen for third-party behavioural data. Treat any cross-site behavioural data flow into Korean advertising accounts as requiring separate, explicit consent presented outside the terms of service. Topics: consent, enforcement, dark-patterns. Status: decided.

docs.t: Bill C-27, Digital Charter Implementation Act, 2022 (Consumer Privacy Protection Act)
docs.x: Canada. Bill C-27 would have replaced Part 1 of PIPEDA with the Consumer Privacy Protection Act, adding a statutory consent standard, a business-activities exception, rules for de-identified data, administrative penalties and a tribunal, together with the Artificial Intelligence and Data Act. It died on the Order Paper when Parliament was prorogued on 6 January 2025 after committee study but before third reading. Practitioners still meet references to the CPPA in vendor documentation and privacy programmes. Treat those references as historical and map obligations to PIPEDA as it stands and to Bill C-36, which the government tabled on 15 June 2026 as the successor. Topics: consent, other. Status: historical.

docs.t: Joint investigation into location tracking by the Tim Hortons app (PIPEDA Findings 2022-001)
docs.x: Canada. The federal, Quebec, Alberta and British Columbia commissioners found that the app collected granular location data every few minutes while closed, contrary to statements that collection occurred only when the app was open, and that the data was gathered for targeted advertising but never used for that purpose, so consent was invalid and the collection lacked an appropriate purpose. The finding binds the operator and signals the offices' approach to tracking statements generally. The company was told to delete the location data, build a privacy management programme with impact assessments, and report within nine months. Align every tracking statement in a banner or policy with what the code actually does. Topics: consent, enforcement, pixels-wiretap. Status: decided.

docs.t: Personal Data Protection Act B.E. 2562 (2019), sections 19, 23 and 82 to 90
docs.x: Thailand. The Act, fully in force since 1 June 2022 after two deferrals, requires consent under section 19 to be explicit, in writing or electronic form, requested separately from other matters in a clear and accessible format without deceptive conditions, and withdrawable as easily as it was given, and section 23 requires a privacy notice before or at collection. Administrative fines reach THB 5 million and criminal penalties include imprisonment of up to one year for certain sensitive-data offences. It binds controllers in Thailand and foreign controllers offering goods or services to people in Thailand. Use a separate, granular cookie consent screen and keep necessary cookies outside the consent request. Topics: consent, dark-patterns, enforcement.

docs.t: Provisions on the Management of Algorithmic Recommendations in Internet Information Services, Articles 17, 18 and 21
docs.x: China. The provisions, in force from 1 March 2022, require algorithmic recommendation providers to offer users an option not targeted at their personal characteristics or a convenient way to turn the recommendation service off, to let users select or delete the user tags used for recommendations, to protect minors from harmful or addictive content, and not to use algorithms to apply unreasonable differential prices or transaction conditions based on user characteristics. They bind providers of algorithmic recommendation services to users in China. Implement a tag management screen and a global personalisation switch, and record the state of the switch with the same rigour as cookie consent. Topics: opt-out-signals, children, dark-patterns.

docs.t: UAE Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 on the Protection of Personal Data
docs.x: United Arab Emirates. The federal PDPL, effective 2 January 2022, requires consent that is clear, specific, informed and withdrawable unless another basis applies, and gives data subjects a right to object to processing for direct marketing and to automated decision-making, with the UAE Data Office as regulator. It applies to controllers in the UAE outside the financial free zones, which run their own regimes, and to foreign controllers processing UAE residents' data. Executive regulations that would set detailed consent mechanics and penalties have not been issued, so obligations are applied from the law's text. Run advertising cookies on opt-in consent and offer an objection route for profiling. Topics: consent, other.

docs.t: Personal Information Protection Law (PIPL), Articles 13, 14, 24 and 66
docs.x: China. Article 13 lists the lawful bases, with consent first and no legitimate-interest basis, and Article 14 requires consent given voluntarily and explicitly on the basis of full information, refreshed when purpose, method or categories change. Article 24 requires that information push or commercial marketing based on automated decision-making be accompanied by an option not targeted at personal characteristics or a convenient way to refuse, and Article 66 allows fines up to RMB 50 million or 5 percent of the prior year's turnover for serious violations. It binds handlers in China and foreign handlers targeting individuals in China. Offer a visible non-personalised mode and a one-step refusal of personalised advertising. Topics: consent, opt-out-signals, enforcement.

docs.t: ACCC Digital advertising services inquiry, final report
docs.x: Australia. The competition regulator's final report, released on 28 September 2021, found competition in ad tech ineffective because of opacity across the supply chain and the data advantage of the largest intermediary, and made six recommendations, including that the leading provider explain publicly how it uses first-party data in ad tech, sector-specific rules allowing data separation or access remedies, and transparency standards backed by mandatory rules if voluntary measures fail. It binds no one but frames how the ACCC assesses consent and data flows in advertising, complementing its 2019 platforms inquiry call for opt-in consent. Expect Australian regulators to read consent strings and data-sharing settings as competition evidence too. Topics: sale-sharing, consent, other. Status: decided.

docs.t: Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA), sections 11, 18, 69 and 107 to 109
docs.x: South Africa. POPIA commenced on 1 July 2020 with a grace period ending 30 June 2021. Section 11 requires a lawful basis such as consent or legitimate interest, section 18 requires notification of the purpose and source of collection, and section 69 prohibits direct marketing by electronic communication unless the data subject has consented or is an existing customer marketed with similar products, with an opt-out in every message; the Information Regulator may impose administrative fines of up to R10 million. The Act binds responsible parties domiciled in South Africa or using means there. Treat advertising cookies that feed electronic direct marketing as needing opt-in consent, and document legitimate-interest reliance for analytics. Topics: email-marketing, consent, enforcement.

docs.t: Provisions on the Scope of Necessary Personal Information for Common Types of Mobile Apps
docs.x: China. Issued on 12 March 2021 and effective from 1 May 2021, the provisions define for 39 common app types the personal information necessary for basic functions, from location for navigation to phone number for social platforms, and state that an app must not refuse basic services because a user declines to provide non-necessary personal information; news, browser and utility apps need no personal information for basic use. They bind app operators and are enforced through CAC and MIIT app checks. Map every SDK and tracker to the necessary-information list for the app's category and keep advertising and analytics collection strictly optional. Topics: strictly-necessary, consent, cookie-walls.

docs.t: Personal Data Protection Act 2012, Parts 4 and 9A (consent, deemed consent by notification, legitimate interests, financial penalties)
docs.x: Singapore. The Act requires consent, or deemed consent, before collecting, using or disclosing personal data, and the 2020 amendments in force from 1 February 2021 added deemed consent by notification, available only after an assessment shows no likely adverse effect and a reasonable opt-out period is given, and a legitimate interests exception that cannot be used for direct marketing. Financial penalties of up to 10 percent of annual turnover in Singapore or S$1 million, whichever is higher, apply from 1 October 2022. It binds organisations processing data in Singapore. Use deemed consent by notification only for low-risk cookies with a documented assessment, and obtain express consent for behavioural advertising. Topics: consent, analytics-exemption, enforcement.

docs.t: PDPC Advisory Guidelines on the PDPA for Selected Topics, chapter on online activities (cookies and behavioural targeting)
docs.x: Singapore. The Commission's guidelines state that consent is not required for cookies needed to provide the service the user requested, that deemed consent may cover other cookies where the user voluntarily provides data with knowledge of the purpose, that behavioural targeting using personal data requires consent with a clear explanation of the purpose, and that IP addresses and device identifiers are personal data when they can identify an individual alone or with other data. They bind no one directly but state how the Commission assesses complaints. Classify each cookie as necessary, deemed-consent or express-consent, keep a written justification, and present advertising cookies as an opt-in choice. Topics: consent, strictly-necessary, analytics-exemption.

docs.t: GB/T 35273-2020, Information security technology: Personal information security specification
docs.x: China. The recommended national standard, published on 6 March 2020 and implemented on 1 October 2020, sets the detailed practice that regulators and app stores use to assess personal information handling: separate consent for each business function, no bundling of functions, personalised display marked as such with a way to opt out, restraints on third-party SDK data collection with contractual and technical controls, and privacy policy templates. It is voluntary in form but is the reference in CAC, MIIT and TC260 app assessments. Audit every embedded SDK against the standard's third-party access clauses and label personalised advertising content as required. Topics: consent, opt-out-signals, other.

docs.t: Measures for Determining Illegal Collection and Use of Personal Information by Apps (App违法违规收集使用个人信息行为认定方法)
docs.x: China. Issued jointly by the CAC, MIIT, Ministry of Public Security and SAMR, the measures list six categories of violation used in app enforcement: no privacy policy or one not shown at first launch or reachable within four clicks, unclear purpose, method and scope, collection before or after refusal of consent including default consent and inducement, collection of unnecessary data or refusal of service when non-essential data is declined, unauthorised sharing with third parties through embedded code or servers, and missing deletion, correction and complaint channels. They bind app operators in China and drive the CAC's periodic public naming of apps. Test the app against each category before release. Topics: consent, dark-patterns, enforcement.

docs.t: Kenya Data Protection Act 2019 and Data Protection (General) Regulations 2021 (direct marketing)
docs.x: Kenya. The Act, in force from 25 November 2019, requires a lawful basis including consent that is express, unequivocal, free, specific and informed, and the General Regulations of 2021 permit direct marketing only with consent or to existing customers who have not opted out, and require the opt out route to be visible, easy and free of charge. The Office of the Data Protection Commissioner enforces with penalties of up to KES 5 million or 1 percent of annual turnover, whichever is lower, and has issued determinations against operators for unsolicited marketing. It binds controllers in Kenya and those processing Kenyan residents' data. Treat advertising cookies as consent-based and honour marketing opt-outs across channels. Topics: consent, email-marketing.

docs.t: Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais (Law 13.709/2018), Articles 7, 8 and 52
docs.x: Brazil. Article 7 lists ten legal bases, including consent (item I) and legitimate interest (item IX), and Article 8 requires consent in writing or by another means demonstrating the data subject's will, in a highlighted clause when written, with the burden of proof on the controller and revocation available at any time. Article 52 allows fines of up to 2 percent of revenue in Brazil, capped at R$50,000,000 per infraction, plus daily fines, publication and blocking. It binds any processing of data of individuals located in Brazil or carried out in Brazil. Pair each cookie category with a legal basis, record consent events, and keep refusal as easy as acceptance. Topics: consent, enforcement.

docs.t: OPC, OIPC Alberta and OIPC British Columbia, Guidelines for obtaining meaningful consent
docs.x: Canada. The three commissioners set seven principles for consent that is meaningful under PIPEDA and the Alberta and British Columbia PIPAs: emphasise key elements, let individuals control the level of detail, offer clear yes or no options for non-essential collection, be innovative, consider the consumer perspective, make consent dynamic, and be accountable. Express consent is required for sensitive information, for uses outside reasonable expectations, and where a meaningful residual risk of significant harm remains. The guidelines have been applied by the offices since 1 January 2019. Build layered notices and just-in-time prompts into consent flows, and keep records that demonstrate the process meets each principle. Topics: consent, dark-patterns.

docs.t: Cybersecurity Law, Article 22 and Article 41
docs.x: China. Article 22 requires providers of network products and services with functions that collect user information to tell users and obtain their consent, and Article 41 requires network operators to collect and use personal information lawfully, properly and only as necessary, to publish their collection and use rules, to state purpose, method and scope, and to obtain consent. The law, in force since 1 June 2017, binds network operators in China and is the basis on which the Cyberspace Administration inspects apps and websites for undisclosed collection. Keep a published collection rule for every site and SDK and make sure the banner text matches the collection actually performed. Topics: consent, other.

docs.t: PIPC and KCC Guideline on personal information protection in online customised advertising (behavioural information)
docs.x: South Korea. The guideline, issued by the KCC on 7 February 2017 and moved to the PIPC on 5 August 2020, treats online behavioural information as protected data, requires advertising businesses and the media operators hosting them to disclose the items collected, the collection method, the purpose and how users can exercise control, prohibits generating or using sensitive information from behavioural data without consent, bans collecting behavioural information for advertising from services whose main users are children under 14, and requires an easy control, with a direct control on the advert itself for third-party advertising. It is guidance and binds no one directly, but the Commission applied its standard in the September 2022 sanctions against Google and Meta. In January 2024 the Commission announced a policy plan to revise it. Publish a behavioural information notice and an opt-out that works across advertising partners. Topics: consent, opt-out-signals, children.

docs.t: Colombia Statutory Law 1581 of 2012 and Decree 1377 of 2013 (prior, express and informed authorisation)
docs.x: Colombia. Law 1581 requires prior, express and informed authorisation from the data subject before personal data is collected, and Decree 1377 allows that authorisation to be given by unequivocal conduct but never by silence, with the controller bearing the burden of proof. The Superintendencia de Industria y Comercio enforces the law and has sanctioned operators for collecting data through websites without valid authorisation, with fines of up to 2,000 monthly minimum wages. It binds controllers in Colombia and foreign controllers subject to Colombian law by treaty. Use an affirmative consent action for non-essential cookies, record the authorisation, and publish the treatment policy the law requires. Topics: consent, enforcement.

docs.t: Philippines Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act 10173) and NPC guidelines on consent
docs.x: Philippines. The Act defines consent as a freely given, specific, informed indication of will evidenced by written, electronic or recorded means, requires a privacy notice before collection, and its implementing rules give data subjects a right to object to processing for direct marketing and profiling. The National Privacy Commission's guidelines on consent state that consent may not be bundled, that non-response or implied consent is not consent, and that withdrawal must be as easy as giving it, and the Commission has ordered operators to fix non-compliant consent interfaces. It binds controllers in the Philippines and those processing Filipino residents' data. Use an affirmative cookie consent action and an accessible withdrawal control. Topics: consent, dark-patterns.

docs.t: OPC Guidelines on privacy and online behavioural advertising
docs.x: Canada. The Commissioner accepts opt-out consent for online behavioural advertising under PIPEDA only where the practice is explained clearly and outside the privacy policy, the opt-out is offered at or before collection, takes effect immediately and persists, no sensitive information is used, children and child-directed sites are not tracked, and data is destroyed or de-identified promptly. Tracking that a user cannot decline, such as zombie cookies or device fingerprinting, must not be used for advertising. It applies to any organisation tracking Canadian users across sites. Configure banners and ad-preference tools to meet each condition, and treat opt-in as required where a condition cannot be met. Topics: consent, children, other.

docs.t: Argentina Personal Data Protection Law 25.326, Articles 5, 6 and 27
docs.x: Argentina. Law 25.326 requires free, express and informed consent, in writing or by an equivalent means, before personal data is processed unless an exception applies (Article 5), requires notice of purpose and recipients (Article 6), and lets any person ask at any time for the removal or blocking of their name from advertising databases, with access to those records free of charge (Article 27). The Agency of Access to Public Information enforces it with fines that remain low under the current scale; a replacement bill with turnover-based fines has been pending since 2023. It binds controllers in Argentina and those using means there. Present advertising cookies as opt-in and provide a no-cost objection route for marketing profiles. Topics: consent, opt-out-signals.

docs.t: California AB 566, the Opt Me Out Act (browser opt-out preference signal)
docs.x: California. AB 566, signed on 8 October 2025, amends the CCPA to require a business that develops or maintains a web browser to include a setting that lets a consumer send an opt-out preference signal to businesses the consumer interacts with through the browser, easy to locate and configure, with an explanation of how the signal works and its intended effect. It operates from 1 January 2027, with a safe harbour for compliant browser makers when a website fails to honour the signal, and the California Privacy Protection Agency may adopt regulations. It binds browser developers; businesses already must honour such signals under the CCPA regulations, so expect more signals from 2027. Topics: opt-out-signals, browser-signals. Status: applies from a future date.

docs.t: W3C Global Privacy Control (GPC) specification, Working Draft
docs.x: Standards. The Global Privacy Control specification, a W3C Working Draft of 17 September 2026 from the Privacy Working Group (First Public Working Draft 21 November 2024), defines a Sec-GPC request header with the value 1, a navigator.globalPrivacyControl boolean, and an optional /.well-known/gpc.json resource by which a site declares that it honours the signal. The signal expresses a request not to sell or share personal data and has legal effect only where a law gives it one; the draft notes that at least four US states recognise it. A draft is not law; read the header and the DOM property and treat them as opt-out requests wherever a state law applies. Topics: opt-out-signals, browser-signals. Status: proposed.

docs.t: IAB Multi-State Privacy Agreement (MSPA), Fifth Amended and Restated
docs.x: United States (federal). The MSPA is a springing contract among signatories that governs personal information flows for selecting and delivering digital advertising under US state privacy laws; the Fifth Amended and Restated version took effect on 4 June 2026, after a March 2026 revision prompted by California's Healthline and Honda enforcement actions. First parties must now process under the US National Approach, an earlier state-specific approach surviving only for signatories from before 2026 until 31 December 2026, and downstream participants must read and honour signals and verify that counterparties are signatories. The National Approach means treating every user as a resident of all covered states. It is a private contract, not law; publishers using it work with the GPP US National string. Topics: sale-sharing, opt-out-signals.

docs.t: IAB Europe TCF Policies (current version 2026-05-29.5.0.b)
docs.x: Standards. The TCF Policies are the contractual rulebook behind the TC String, defining purposes, features and legal bases and setting CMP, vendor and publisher obligations. CMPs must generate consent signals only on a clear affirmative action, resolve conflicting signals before transmission, implement publisher restrictions and resurface the interface when IAB Europe notifies material policy changes; vendors must respect signals in real time and stop processing if a signal cannot be verified; publishers may use only compliant CMPs and vendors. The Policies bind registered participants by contract and are not law, although the Belgian APD and the Brussels Market Court examined earlier versions; check which version your CMP implements. Topics: tcf, consent.

docs.t: Brussels Market Court judgment of 7 January 2026 annulling the TCF action plan validation
docs.x: Belgium. The Market Court annulled the APD decision of 11 January 2023 validating IAB Europe's TCF action plan, finding that the APD had built on a decision already found unlawful, had assumed a joint controllership extending to downstream OpenRTB processing that the May 2025 judgment rejected, and had not heard IAB Europe on the intervening CJEU developments. The APD must reassess the plan on the narrower TC String scope after giving IAB Europe the opportunity to take position. The action plan measures already built into TCF v2.2 (consent only for advertising purposes, clearer disclosures, vendor transparency) stay in place, and the 1 March 2026 TCF v2.3 deadline was unaffected. Topics: tcf, enforcement. Status: decided.

docs.t: European Commission acceptance of Meta's DMA commitments on personalised advertising choice
docs.x: EU. On 8 December 2025 the European Commission announced Meta's commitment under the Digital Markets Act to give EU users of Facebook and Instagram, from January 2026, a choice between sharing all their data for fully personalised advertising and sharing limited data for an experience with more limited personalised advertising, following the Commission's April 2025 non-compliance decision on the earlier consent-or-pay model. The commitment binds Meta and changes what signals its advertising systems hold for EU users. Advertisers running the Meta Pixel and Conversions API remain responsible for their own website consent under the ePrivacy rules and the GDPR, and should verify that pixel events fire only after that consent. Topics: consent-or-pay, pixels-wiretap, enforcement.

docs.t: Google Privacy Sandbox: update on plans for Privacy Sandbox technologies (API retirement)
docs.x: Standards. On 17 October 2025 Google announced the retirement of thirteen Privacy Sandbox technologies, including the Topics API, Protected Audience, Attribution Reporting, Private Aggregation and Shared Storage, SelectURL, Related Website Sets, IP Protection, On-Device Personalization, Protected App Signals and the SDK Runtime, to be phased out through the normal Chrome and Android processes without fixed dates. CHIPS and FedCM continue, and Google will pursue an interoperable attribution standard at the W3C. Google keeps its current approach to third-party cookie choice in Chrome. It is a vendor announcement, not law; remove Sandbox-specific purposes from consent flows once the APIs stop shipping. Topics: browser-signals, other.

docs.t: BfDI recognition of consent management services under section 26 TDDDG
docs.x: Germany. The BfDI runs the recognition procedure under section 26 TDDDG and sections 10 to 13 EinwV: it reviews an application, sends a draft decision to the applicant and the Land supervisory authorities with four weeks for comments, requires a security concept and independence from companies with a financial interest in consent data, and keeps a public register. The first recognition, of the service Consenter operated by Law & Innovation Technology GmbH, was granted on 17 October 2025. Recognition means the service meets the ordinance, not that any consent it stores is valid for a given site; German publishers should decide how to treat its signals alongside their own banner. Topics: consent, browser-signals.

docs.t: IAB Europe TCF v2.3 and the mandatory disclosed vendors segment
docs.x: Standards. TCF v2.3, released on 19 June 2025, makes the disclosedVendors segment of the TC String mandatory so that a vendor can tell whether it was disclosed to the user, resolving earlier ambiguity in legitimate interest signalling. CMPs had to update by 28 February 2026 without re-surfacing the interface; vendors must read and act on the segment from 1 March 2026, after which a new TC String without it is invalid. TC Strings created before the deadline remain valid until users refresh their choices. The change binds TCF-registered CMPs and vendors by contract, not law; confirm that your CMP's TC Strings carry the segment and that each vendor's ID bit is set. Topics: tcf, consent.

docs.t: Microsoft Advertising consent mode requirement for UET
docs.x: Standards. Microsoft Advertising announced on 31 March 2025 that from 5 May 2025 advertisers must pass user consent signals for site visits from the EEA, the UK and Switzerland, through consent mode on the Universal Event Tracking tag or Microsoft pixels (an ad_storage parameter set to granted or denied), through the IAB TCF, or through a tag manager integration. Without a signal, advertising performance for those visitors is affected because the data is not used for optimisation. It is a platform requirement, not law; map the CMP's advertising category to ad_storage so that the tag fires only after consent. Topics: consent-mode, pixels-wiretap.

docs.t: Google Privacy Sandbox: next steps for Privacy Sandbox and tracking protections in Chrome
docs.x: Standards. On 22 April 2025 Google confirmed that Chrome will not roll out a new standalone prompt for third-party cookies; users keep the existing choice in Chrome's Privacy and Security settings, and Incognito continues to block third-party cookies by default. Google also committed to launch IP Protection in Incognito in the third quarter of 2025 and to publish an updated roadmap for the Sandbox APIs. It is a vendor decision, not law. Third-party cookies therefore remain readable in Chrome for most users, and the consent banner remains the operative control over them under the ePrivacy rules. Topics: browser-signals, other.

docs.t: Global Privacy Control reference site and adoption record (globalprivacycontrol.org)
docs.x: Standards. The GPC reference site records the signal's origin and adoption: native support in Brave, DuckDuckGo and Firefox and in browser extensions, adoption as a W3C Privacy Working Group work item in November 2024, and, as of 15 January 2025, guidance from California, Colorado, Connecticut and New Jersey treating GPC as a binding opt-out, with eight further state laws permitting opt-outs through universal mechanisms. It cites the California CCPA regulations' requirement to honour user-enabled global privacy controls. The site is maintained by the signal's proponents and is not law. Use it to track which browsers send the signal and which states enforce it. Topics: opt-out-signals, browser-signals.

docs.t: Connecticut Attorney General advisory on opt-out preference signals
docs.x: Connecticut. The Connecticut Attorney General advised that from 1 January 2025 controllers under the Connecticut Data Privacy Act must treat browser-based opt-out preference signals, in practice Global Privacy Control, as binding opt-out requests for the sale of personal data and targeted advertising, including where the signal conflicts with an earlier choice or loyalty programme membership. Entities such as HIPAA-regulated healthcare providers are exempt. The advisory summarises statutory duties; the statute is what binds. Implement GPC recognition, document it in the privacy notice, and expect scrutiny: Connecticut, California and Colorado announced a joint investigative privacy sweep in 2025. Topics: opt-out-signals, browser-signals, enforcement.

docs.t: Google EU user consent policy
docs.x: Standards. Google's EU user consent policy requires anyone using Google advertising products with end users in the EEA, the UK and Switzerland (Switzerland added on 31 July 2024) to obtain legally valid consent for cookies or other local storage where legally required and for the use of personal data for ad personalisation, to identify every party receiving data, to keep consent records and to tell users how to revoke. Publishers must use a Google-certified CMP and advertisers with EEA traffic must send verified consent signals through TCF or consent mode. It is a contractual policy, not law, but it tracks the ePrivacy Directive and GDPR consent tests. Topics: consent, consent-mode.

docs.t: Google Privacy Sandbox: a new path for Privacy Sandbox on the web (third-party cookie reversal)
docs.x: Standards. On 22 July 2024 Google abandoned its plan to deprecate third-party cookies in Chrome and said it would instead introduce a browser-level choice that users could adjust at any time, after consultation with the UK Competition and Markets Authority and the Information Commissioner's Office. It committed to keep investing in the Privacy Sandbox APIs and to add IP Protection to Incognito. The post is a vendor announcement with no legal force, but it ended the assumption that consent for third-party cookies would become moot. Superseded by the 22 April 2025 decision not to introduce a standalone prompt and the 17 October 2025 retirement of most Sandbox APIs. Topics: browser-signals, other. Status: superseded.

docs.t: Google consent mode v2 requirement for EEA traffic
docs.x: Standards. Consent mode v2 adds the ad_user_data and ad_personalization parameters to ad_storage and analytics_storage, and Google requires the signals for EEA traffic under its EU user consent policy: from early March 2024 only end users outside the EEA are included in audiences shared with linked advertising products unless the signals are sent, and remarketing and personalisation features stop working for the affected traffic. Default states must be denied before the user acts and updated afterwards; basic mode holds tags until consent, advanced mode sends cookieless pings. It is a platform policy, not law; a CMP satisfies it by mapping its analytics category to analytics_storage and its advertising category to ad_storage, ad_user_data and ad_personalization, provided valid consent is collected where the law requires it and the tags actually respect the signals; the cookieless pings of advanced mode are a platform feature, not a legal exemption. Topics: consent-mode, consent.

docs.t: EDPB Website Auditing Tool
docs.x: EU. The EDPB Website Auditing Tool, released on 29 January 2024 under the EUPL 1.2 licence through the Support Pool of Experts, lets a data protection authority, controller or processor record a visit to a website and analyse the cookies, storage and third-party requests it triggers, with full-page screenshots, import and export of analyses and searchable databases. It is free and open source and available in English, French, German, Italian and Spanish. It is a tool rather than guidance, and the EDPB states that it does not represent an official EDPB position. Run it against your own sites before and after consent to see what a regulator would see. Topics: enforcement, consent.

docs.t: Google certified CMP requirement for ads in the EEA, UK and Switzerland
docs.x: Standards. From 16 January 2024 publishers serving personalised ads through AdSense, Ad Manager or AdMob to users in the EEA and UK must use a Google-certified CMP integrated with IAB Europe's TCF; Switzerland followed on 31 July 2024 and CTV inventory had an extension to July 2025. Traffic without a certified CMP is eligible only for non-personalised or limited ads. Certified CMPs must support Google's Additional Consent specification for non-TCF vendors, recertify annually and, since 4 October 2024, pass a check on TC String storage and retention (TCF policy check 30). Google states that certification does not check full TCF or legal compliance, so it is not a compliance opinion. Topics: tcf, consent.

docs.t: IAB CCPA Compliance Framework US Privacy String (deprecated)
docs.x: Standards. The US Privacy String of the IAB CCPA Compliance Framework encoded a single California do-not-sell choice for the advertising supply chain. IAB Tech Lab stopped maintaining it and set a deprecation date of 31 January 2024, extended from 30 September 2023, because only the Global Privacy Platform can carry the signals required by the Virginia, Colorado, Connecticut and Utah laws that took effect in 2023. It never had legal force. Superseded: replace any remaining usprivacy implementation with GPP section strings, and check that ad partners no longer read the old field as the source of truth. Topics: opt-out-signals, sale-sharing. Status: superseded.

docs.t: IAB Europe Transparency and Consent Framework v2.2
docs.x: Standards. TCF v2.2 launched on 16 May 2023 and removed legitimate interest as a legal basis for advertising and content personalisation purposes 3 to 6, replaced legal text with plain-language purpose descriptions, required vendors to declare data categories and retention periods, and obliged CMPs to show the total number of vendors on the first layer and to offer an easy route to withdrawal. It binds registered CMPs, vendors and publishers by contract, with switch-over required by 20 November 2023; it is an industry standard, not law, though the Belgian APD and the courts assessed its predecessor. TCF v2.3 of 19 June 2025 supersedes it by making the disclosed vendors segment mandatory. Topics: tcf, consent. Status: superseded.

docs.t: IAB Tech Lab TCF v2 technical specifications and implementation guidelines
docs.x: Standards. IAB Tech Lab maintains the TCF v2 technical specifications: the TC String format with its core, disclosed vendors and publisher TC segments, the CMP API through which vendors read signals, and the Global Vendor List (version 3 since v2.2). The implementation guidelines, last updated in May 2023, record the v2.2 changes (revised purpose names, retention periods, no legitimate interest for purposes 3 to 6, data categories, localised policy URLs) and the v2.3 mandatory disclosed vendor segment. They bind participants through the TCF Policies and are not law. Use them to test that your CMP exposes the API correctly and that TC Strings decode to the choices actually made. Topics: tcf, consent.

docs.t: IAB Europe TCF compliance programmes and CMP validation
docs.x: Standards. IAB Europe validates every CMP before it receives a CMP ID and a place on the CMP List, covering the interface and technical operation on web, mobile and CTV, and vets vendors through a questionnaire before Global Vendor List listing. Live installations are monitored: TC String tampering brings immediate suspension of at least four weeks and permanent suspension on a fourth offence within twelve months, and other policy breaches allow 10 business days (5 to 20 for vendors) to remedy before suspension. The programme binds registered participants by contract, not law. Run the public CMP Validator browser extension, available since May 2023, against your own deployments before an audit does. Topics: tcf, enforcement.

docs.t: IAB Tech Lab Global Privacy Platform (GPP) and the US National section
docs.x: Standards. The Global Privacy Platform is IAB Tech Lab's container for consent and opt-out signals across jurisdictions: the GPP string (specification 1.0 of 28 September 2022, CMP API 1.1 of June 2023) carries sections for IAB Europe TCF, IAB Canada TCF, the US National string (section ID 7, defined by the MSPA US National Technical Specification, version 2.0 in October 2024) and individual US state strings, and records whether a Global Privacy Control signal was received. It is a technical standard adopted by contract and by ad exchanges, not law. Publishers selling programmatic inventory to US or Canadian audiences should emit GPP in place of the deprecated US Privacy String. Topics: opt-out-signals, sale-sharing.

docs.t: Mozilla Firefox Total Cookie Protection by default and Global Privacy Control setting
docs.x: Standards. Firefox has shipped Total Cookie Protection to all desktop users by default since 14 June 2022, confining each site's cookies to a separate jar so that third-party cookies cannot follow users across sites, on top of the list-based Enhanced Tracking Protection introduced in 2018. Global Privacy Control has been available since Firefox 120 as an opt-in setting labelled 'Tell websites not to sell or share my data'; Mozilla notes that some websites may ignore it. These are browser defaults, not law. A banner cannot assume a Firefox third-party cookie is readable, and Firefox visitors sending GPC must be handled as opt-outs wherever a law recognises the signal. Topics: browser-signals, opt-out-signals.

docs.t: Apple App Tracking Transparency requirement (iOS 14.5)
docs.x: Standards. Since 26 April 2021, with iOS 14.5, iPadOS 14.5 and tvOS 14.5, apps must ask permission through the AppTrackingTransparency framework before tracking users or reading the advertising identifier; without permission the IDFA is all zeros and tracking is prohibited. Tracking means linking app data with data from other companies' apps, websites or offline properties for targeted advertising or measurement, or sharing it with data brokers; on-device linking and fraud prevention are excluded. App Store Review Guideline 5.1.2(i) forbids gating functionality or offering incentives to obtain the permission. It is a platform rule, not law, and a separate consent under the ePrivacy rules may still be needed. Topics: consent, browser-signals.

docs.t: Brave Shields default blocking and Global Privacy Control on by default
docs.x: Standards. Brave Shields blocks third-party ads, trackers and cross-site cookies on every page by default, using EasyList, EasyPrivacy, uBlock Origin and Brave's own filter lists, and randomises the browser fingerprint. Brave announced Global Privacy Control on 7 October 2020, first in the Nightly desktop channel and the Android beta, and the signal is on by default in every version that implements it, described as a way for users to assert legal privacy rights, with an option to turn it off. These are browser defaults, not law. A business that receives Sec-GPC: 1 from a Brave visitor in a state that recognises the signal must treat it as an opt-out of sale, sharing and targeted advertising. Topics: browser-signals, opt-out-signals.

docs.t: ISO/IEC 29184:2020 Online privacy notices and consent
docs.x: Standards. ISO/IEC 29184:2020, published on 2 June 2020 (edition 1, 25 pages, reviewed and confirmed in 2026), specifies controls for the content and structure of online privacy notices and for the process of obtaining, recording and withdrawing consent when personally identifiable information is collected. It is a voluntary standard: it binds no one unless adopted by contract or certification, and it does not replace the GDPR Article 7 conditions or national cookie rules. Use it as a checklist for layered notices and for the record a CMP should keep about each consent, including what the user was shown and when. Topics: consent, other.

docs.t: Apple WebKit Intelligent Tracking Prevention and full third-party cookie blocking
docs.x: Standards. Safari 13.1 and iOS and iPadOS 13.4 completed Intelligent Tracking Prevention by blocking all cross-site cookies by default, with the Storage Access API as the only exception, and by deleting all script-writable storage (cookies, IndexedDB, LocalStorage, service worker caches) after seven days without user interaction. WebKit's tracking prevention page adds that cookies set through CNAME or IP-address cloaking are capped at seven days and JavaScript cookies on landing pages reached through link decoration at 24 hours. These are engine defaults, not law. Measurement that relies on script-written first-party storage in Safari loses returning users after seven days of Safari use without interaction, whatever consent was recorded; cookies set by the server in an HTTP response are not capped unless they arrive through CNAME or IP-address cloaking. Topics: browser-signals, other.

docs.t: W3C Tracking Preference Expression (Do Not Track), Working Group Note
docs.x: Standards. Tracking Preference Expression, published as a W3C Working Group Note on 17 January 2019, defined a DNT request header whose value 1 expressed a preference not to be tracked. The Tracking Protection Working Group closed because there had not been sufficient deployment to justify further advancement and no indication of planned support among user agents, third parties and the wider ecosystem. The header still exists in some browsers but has no defined legal effect and no cookie law requires sites to honour it. Withdrawn as a standard; Global Privacy Control (W3C Working Draft) is its successor for opt-out signalling, so do not build banner logic on DNT. Topics: browser-signals, opt-out-signals. Status: withdrawn.

docs.t: Article 1: Subject Matter
docs.x: Article 1 states the purpose of the Regulation: to improve the functioning of the internal market, promote human-centric and trustworthy AI and protect health, safety and fundamental rights while supporting innovation (paragraph 1). Paragraph 2 lists what the Regulation contains: harmonised rules for placing AI systems and general-purpose AI models on the market, prohibitions of certain practices, requirements for high-risk systems and their operators, transparency rules, rules on general-purpose AI models, market surveillance and enforcement, and innovation support for SMEs, start-ups and small mid-caps. It binds everyone in scope and is the reference point for reading every later obligation. Binds: everyone. Applies from 2 February 2025.
docs.m: Chapter I: General Provisions · applies from 2 February 2025

docs.t: Article 1: Subject Matter (amended by Regulation 2026/1744)
docs.x: Point (g) of paragraph 2 was replaced so that the innovation support measures are now framed around small mid-cap enterprises (SMCs) and SMEs, including start-ups.
docs.m: Chapter I: General Provisions · applies from 2 February 2025

docs.t: Article 2: Scope
docs.x: Article 2 fixes who is caught: providers placing AI systems or general-purpose AI models on the Union market wherever established, deployers in the Union, third-country operators whose output is used in the Union, importers, distributors, product manufacturers, authorised representatives and affected persons (paragraph 1). Paragraphs 3 to 12 exclude military, defence and national security uses, scientific research, pre-market testing, purely personal use and free and open-source systems unless high-risk or caught by Articles 5 or 50. Paragraph 2 confines Annex I Section B products to Article 6(1), Article 60a and Articles 102 to 112; paragraph 13 lets the Commission limit Articles 9 to 15 and 17 to 25 by 2 August 2027. Binds: everyone. Applies from 2 February 2025.
docs.m: Chapter I: General Provisions · applies from 2 February 2025

docs.t: Article 2: Scope (amended by Regulation 2026/1744)
docs.x: Paragraph 2 was rewritten so that only Article 6(1), Article 60a and Articles 102 to 112 apply to Annex I Section B products, with Articles 57 to 59 applying only where integrated into that sectoral legislation, paragraph 7 now cross-refers to the new Article 4a, and a new paragraph 13 lets the Commission limit Articles 9 to 15 and 17 to 25 for Article 6(1) systems by delegated act.
docs.m: Chapter I: General Provisions · applies from 2 February 2025

docs.t: Article 3: Definitions
docs.x: Article 3 supplies the 70 definitions on which every later obligation depends, numbered 1 to 68 with the inserted points 14a and 14b. An AI system is a machine-based system with varying levels of autonomy that infers from input how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations or decisions (point 1); a provider develops a system or model and places it on the market under its own name (point 3); a deployer uses a system under its authority outside personal activity (point 4). Points 63 and 65 define general-purpose AI models and systemic risk, and point 49 defines a serious incident as death, serious harm to health, a serious and irreversible disruption of critical infrastructure, a fundamental rights infringement or serious harm to property or the environment. Binds: everyone. Applies from 2 February 2025.
docs.m: Chapter I: General Provisions · applies from 2 February 2025

docs.t: Article 3: Definitions (amended by Regulation 2026/1744)
docs.x: New point 14a defines SMEs by reference to Recommendation 2003/361/EC and new point 14b defines a small mid-cap enterprise (SMC) by reference to Recommendation (EU) 2025/1099.
docs.m: Chapter I: General Provisions · applies from 2 February 2025

docs.t: Article 4: AI Literacy
docs.x: Article 4 obliges providers and deployers of AI systems to take measures that support AI literacy among their staff and other persons operating the systems on their behalf, taking account of technical knowledge, experience, education, training, the context of use and the persons affected (paragraph 1). No specific level of literacy has to be guaranteed for any individual. Under paragraph 2 the Commission and Member States support providers and deployers, particularly SMEs, with practical examples published on the Article 62(3) platform, and under paragraph 3 the Board adopts recommendations on common objectives. Document role-based training now; the obligation has applied since 2 February 2025. Binds: provider, deployer, commission. Applies from 2 February 2025.
docs.m: Chapter I: General Provisions · applies from 2 February 2025

docs.t: Article 4: AI Literacy (amended by Regulation 2026/1744)
docs.x: Paragraph 1 was softened to a duty to support literacy without guaranteeing any individual level, and new paragraphs 2 and 3 add Commission, Member State and Board support duties.
docs.m: Chapter I: General Provisions · applies from 2 February 2025

docs.t: Article 4a: Processing of special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction
docs.x: Article 4a lets providers of high-risk AI systems process special categories of personal data, for bias detection and correction, under six cumulative conditions (paragraph 1, points (a) to (f)): other data including synthetic or anonymised data cannot do the job, technical limits on re-use and state-of-the-art security measures apply, access is strictly controlled and documented, the data is not passed to other parties, it is deleted once the bias is corrected or the retention period ends, and the processing record explains the necessity. Paragraph 2 extends the permission, under the same safeguards, to providers and deployers of other AI systems and deployers of high-risk systems, where strictly necessary to address biases affecting health and safety, fundamental rights or prohibited discrimination. It imposes no duty to detect bias. Binds: provider, deployer. Applies from 27 July 2026.
docs.m: Chapter I: General Provisions · applies from 27 July 2026

docs.t: Article 4a: Processing of special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction (amended by Regulation 2026/1744)
docs.x: Inserted by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744: it moves the special category data permission out of Article 10(5) into a general provision and extends it to providers and deployers of non-high-risk systems and to deployers of high-risk systems.
docs.m: Chapter I: General Provisions · applies from 27 July 2026

docs.t: Article 5: Prohibited AI Practices
docs.x: Article 5 prohibits ten AI practices (paragraph 1): manipulative techniques, exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring, criminal risk prediction based solely on profiling, untargeted scraping of facial images, emotion recognition in workplaces and education except for medical or safety reasons, biometric categorisation inferring protected characteristics, real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces for law enforcement, and the two new points (ba) and (bb). Point (h) allows real-time identification only for victim searches, imminent threats or Annex II offences carrying at least four years' custody, with prior authorisation and a fundamental rights impact assessment (paragraphs 2 to 4). Points (ba) and (bb) ban generating or manipulating non-consensual intimate imagery and child sexual abuse material from 2 December 2026. Binds: everyone. Applies from 2 February 2025 (points (ba) and (bb) from 2 December 2026).
docs.m: Chapter II: Prohibited AI Practices · applies from 2 February 2025 (points (ba) and (bb) from 2 December 2026)

docs.t: Article 5: Prohibited AI Practices (amended by Regulation 2026/1744)
docs.x: New points 1(ba) and 1(bb) and paragraphs 1a and 1b add prohibitions on AI systems generating or manipulating non-consensual intimate imagery and child sexual abuse material, applying from 2 December 2026.
docs.m: Chapter II: Prohibited AI Practices · applies from 2 February 2025 (points (ba) and (bb) from 2 December 2026)

docs.t: Article 6: Classification Rules for High-Risk AI Systems
docs.x: Article 6 sets the two routes to high-risk status: safety components of, or products under, Annex I harmonisation legislation that require third-party conformity assessment (paragraph 1), and the use cases in Annex III (paragraph 2). Paragraph 3 exempts Annex III systems that perform a narrow procedural task, improve a completed human activity, detect decision-making deviations or carry out preparatory assessments, but profiling of natural persons always stays high-risk. Providers relying on paragraph 3 must document the assessment before placing on the market and register under Article 49(2) (paragraph 4). New paragraphs 1a to 1c exclude systems limited to non-safety aspects such as user assistance unless failure endangers health and safety. Article 113(c) excepts paragraph 5, the Commission's duty to issue classification guidelines, from the deferred dates, so it applies from 2 August 2026. Binds: provider, commission. Applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I).
docs.m: Chapter III: High-Risk AI Systems · applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I)

docs.t: Article 6: Classification Rules for High-Risk AI Systems (amended by Regulation 2026/1744)
docs.x: New paragraphs 1a, 1b and 1c state that systems used only for non-safety aspects such as user assistance, performance optimisation, service efficiency, automation, convenience or quality control are not safety components unless their failure endangers health and safety, and that products assessed solely for non-safety risks such as spectrum use do not meet paragraph 1.
docs.m: Chapter III: High-Risk AI Systems · applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I)

docs.t: Article 7: Amendments to Annex III
docs.x: Article 7 empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts under Article 97 adding or modifying Annex III use cases where a system falls within an existing Annex III area and poses a risk to health, safety or fundamental rights equivalent to or greater than the listed cases (paragraph 1). Paragraph 2 lists the criteria: intended purpose, extent of use, nature of data, autonomy and human override, documented harm, magnitude and reversibility of impact, benefits and existing remedies. Paragraph 3 allows removal of a use case that no longer poses a significant risk. Providers should monitor delegated acts because Annex III can change without a new regulation. Binds: commission, provider. Applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I).
docs.m: Chapter III: High-Risk AI Systems · applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I)

docs.t: Article 8: Compliance with the Requirements
docs.x: Article 8 requires high-risk AI systems to meet the Section 2 requirements of Articles 9 to 15, read in the light of the intended purpose stated by the provider and the generally acknowledged state of the art, with the Article 9 risk management system used to verify compliance (paragraph 1). Where a product contains an AI system covered by both the Regulation and Annex I Section A harmonisation legislation, providers are responsible for full compliance with both sets of rules and may integrate the testing, reporting, information and documentation into what the sectoral legislation already requires (paragraph 2). Providers should build one integrated compliance file rather than parallel ones. Binds: provider. Applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I).
docs.m: Chapter III: High-Risk AI Systems · applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I)

docs.t: Article 9: Risk Management System
docs.x: Article 9 obliges providers to establish, implement, document and maintain a risk management system for each high-risk AI system as a continuous iterative process across the whole lifecycle (paragraphs 1 and 2). The steps are identifying known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety and fundamental rights, estimating risks under intended use and foreseeable misuse, evaluating Article 72 post-market monitoring data and adopting targeted measures so that residual risk is acceptable (paragraphs 2 to 5). Systems must be tested against predefined metrics and probabilistic thresholds before placing on the market, including Article 60 real-world testing where appropriate (paragraphs 6 to 8). Paragraph 9 protects persons under 18 and vulnerable groups. Binds: provider. Applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I).
docs.m: Chapter III: High-Risk AI Systems · applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I)

docs.t: Article 10: Data and Data Governance
docs.x: Article 10 requires high-risk AI systems trained with data to use training, validation and testing datasets that meet the quality criteria in paragraphs 2 to 4 and Article 4a(1) (paragraph 1). Governance practices must cover design choices, data origin and collection, preparation and labelling, assumptions, availability and suitability, examination for bias affecting health, safety, fundamental rights or discrimination, bias mitigation and data gaps (paragraph 2). Datasets must be relevant, sufficiently representative, as error-free and complete as possible and reflect the geographical, contextual, behavioural and functional setting of use (paragraphs 3 and 4); for systems not trained on data only testing datasets are caught (paragraph 6). Binds: provider. Applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I).
docs.m: Chapter III: High-Risk AI Systems · applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I)

docs.t: Article 10: Data and Data Governance (amended by Regulation 2026/1744)
docs.x: Paragraph 5 on processing special categories of personal data for bias detection was deleted and moved to the new Article 4a, which paragraphs 1 and 6 now cross-refer to.
docs.m: Chapter III: High-Risk AI Systems · applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I)

docs.t: Article 11: Technical Documentation
docs.x: Article 11 requires providers to draw up technical documentation before a high-risk AI system is placed on the market or put into service, keep it up to date and include at least the elements in Annex IV so that authorities and notified bodies can assess compliance (paragraph 1). SMEs, start-ups and small mid-caps may supply the elements in a simplified manner using the Commission's simplified form, which notified bodies must accept. Where the system relates to an Annex I Section A product, a single set of documentation covers both regimes (paragraph 2), and the Commission may amend Annex IV by delegated act (paragraph 3). Binds: provider, notified-body. Applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I).
docs.m: Chapter III: High-Risk AI Systems · applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I)

docs.t: Article 11: Technical Documentation (amended by Regulation 2026/1744)
docs.x: Paragraph 1 was amended so that SMEs, start-ups and small mid-caps may provide the documentation in a simplified manner using a Commission simplified form that notified bodies must accept.
docs.m: Chapter III: High-Risk AI Systems · applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I)

docs.t: Article 12: Record-Keeping
docs.x: Article 12 requires high-risk AI systems to technically allow automatic recording of events (logs) over their lifetime (paragraph 1). Logging must give traceability appropriate to the intended purpose so that Article 79(1) risks and substantial modifications can be identified, Article 72 post-market monitoring is supported and Article 26(5) deployer monitoring is possible (paragraph 2). For remote biometric identification systems under Annex III point 1(a), logs must at minimum record the start and end of each use, the reference database checked, the input data that produced a match and the persons who verified the result under Article 14(5) (paragraph 3). Providers design the logging; providers and deployers keep the logs. Binds: provider. Applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I).
docs.m: Chapter III: High-Risk AI Systems · applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I)

docs.t: Article 13: Transparency and Provision of Information to Deployers
docs.x: Article 13 requires high-risk AI systems to be designed so that their operation is sufficiently transparent for deployers to interpret and use the output appropriately (paragraph 1), and to ship with instructions for use that are concise, complete, correct and clear (paragraph 2). Paragraph 3 lists the mandatory content: provider and authorised representative identity, intended purpose, accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity levels, known risks and foreseeable misuse, performance for specific groups, input data specifications, predetermined changes, the human oversight measures under Article 14, computational and hardware needs, expected lifetime and maintenance, and the logging mechanisms under Article 12. Providers write these instructions; deployers rely on them for Articles 26 and 27. Binds: provider, deployer. Applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I).
docs.m: Chapter III: High-Risk AI Systems · applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I)

docs.t: Article 14: Human Oversight
docs.x: Article 14 requires high-risk AI systems to be designed with human-machine interface tools so that natural persons can effectively oversee them during use, to prevent or minimise risks to health, safety and fundamental rights (paragraphs 1 and 2). Measures must be proportionate to the risks and level of autonomy and are either built in by the provider or specified for the deployer (paragraph 3). Overseers must be able to understand capacities and limitations, resist automation bias, interpret output correctly, decide not to use the system, override it or halt it (paragraph 4). Remote biometric identification under Annex III point 1(a) needs separate verification by at least two persons (paragraph 5). Binds: provider, deployer. Applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I).
docs.m: Chapter III: High-Risk AI Systems · applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I)

docs.t: Article 15: Accuracy, Robustness and Cybersecurity
docs.x: Article 15 requires high-risk AI systems to achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity and to perform consistently throughout their lifecycle (paragraph 1). The Commission encourages benchmarks and measurement methodologies with stakeholders and metrology bodies (paragraph 2), and providers must declare accuracy levels and metrics in the instructions for use (paragraph 3). Robustness against errors, faults and inconsistencies may rely on redundancy, backup or fail-safe plans, and continuously learning systems must control biased feedback loops (paragraph 4). Cybersecurity measures must address data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples, confidentiality attacks and model flaws (paragraph 5), so providers should map these threats into the Article 9 risk register. Binds: provider, commission. Applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I).
docs.m: Chapter III: High-Risk AI Systems · applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I)

docs.t: Article 16: Obligations of Providers of High-Risk AI Systems
docs.x: Article 16 is the provider checklist for high-risk AI systems. Providers must ensure compliance with Section 2, mark the system or its packaging with their name and contact address, run an Article 17 quality management system, keep the Article 18 documentation and Article 19 logs, complete the Article 43 conformity assessment before placing on the market, draw up the Article 47 EU declaration of conformity, affix the CE marking under Article 48, register under Article 49(1), take corrective action under Article 20, demonstrate conformity on reasoned request and meet the accessibility requirements of Directives (EU) 2016/2102 and (EU) 2019/882 (points (a) to (l)). Binds: provider. Applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I).
docs.m: Chapter III: High-Risk AI Systems · applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I)

docs.t: Article 17: Quality Management System
docs.x: Article 17 requires providers of high-risk AI systems to run a documented quality management system with written policies, procedures and instructions covering thirteen areas (paragraph 1): regulatory compliance strategy, design and development controls, examination and testing, technical specifications and standards, data management, the Article 9 risk management system, Article 72 post-market monitoring, Article 73 serious incident reporting, communication with authorities and notified bodies, record-keeping, resource management and an accountability framework. Implementation is proportionate to the provider's size, including SMEs, start-ups and small mid-caps, without lowering protection (paragraph 2). Sectoral quality systems may be integrated (paragraph 3), and financial institutions satisfy most points through internal governance rules (paragraph 4). Binds: provider. Applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I).
docs.m: Chapter III: High-Risk AI Systems · applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I)

docs.t: Article 17: Quality Management System (amended by Regulation 2026/1744)
docs.x: Paragraph 2 now names small mid-caps (SMCs) alongside SMEs and start-ups among the organisations entitled to proportionate implementation.
docs.m: Chapter III: High-Risk AI Systems · applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I)

docs.t: Article 18: Documentation Keeping
docs.x: Article 18 obliges providers to keep, at the disposal of national competent authorities for 10 years after a high-risk AI system is placed on the market or put into service, the Article 11 technical documentation, the Article 17 quality management documentation, changes approved by notified bodies, notified body decisions and documents, and the Article 47 EU declaration of conformity (paragraph 1). Member States set the rules for the documentation when a provider or its authorised representative goes bankrupt or ceases activity before the 10 years end (paragraph 2), and financial institutions keep it under their financial services rules (paragraph 3). Set retention schedules to the 10-year clock from release. Binds: provider. Applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I).
docs.m: Chapter III: High-Risk AI Systems · applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I)

docs.t: Article 19: Automatically Generated Logs
docs.x: Article 19 requires providers of high-risk AI systems to keep the logs their systems generate automatically under Article 12, to the extent the logs are under their control, for a period appropriate to the intended purpose and at least six months unless Union or national law, in particular data protection law, provides otherwise (paragraph 1). Financial institutions keep the logs as part of the documentation required by their financial services rules (paragraph 2). Providers should decide at design time which logs they control, for example in hosted deployments, and set retention accordingly; the matching deployer duty is in Article 26(6). Binds: provider. Applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I).
docs.m: Chapter III: High-Risk AI Systems · applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I)

docs.t: Article 20: Corrective Actions and Duty of Information
docs.x: Article 20 requires providers who consider or have reason to consider that a high-risk AI system they have placed on the market is not in conformity to immediately bring it into conformity, withdraw it, disable it or recall it, and to inform the distributors, deployers, authorised representative and importers concerned (paragraph 1). Where the system presents an Article 79(1) risk and the provider becomes aware of it, the provider must immediately investigate the causes with the reporting deployer and inform the market surveillance authorities and, where applicable, the certifying notified body, describing the non-compliance and the corrective action (paragraph 2). Providers need a recall and notification procedure before release. Binds: provider. Applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I).
docs.m: Chapter III: High-Risk AI Systems · applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I)

docs.t: Article 21: Cooperation with Competent Authorities
docs.x: Article 21 requires providers of high-risk AI systems, on reasoned request from a competent authority, to supply all information and documentation necessary to demonstrate conformity with Section 2 in an official Union language that the requesting Member State can readily understand (paragraph 1) and to give access to the automatically generated logs referred to in Article 12(1) to the extent those logs are under their control (paragraph 2). Information obtained is protected by the confidentiality obligations in Article 78 (paragraph 3). Providers should keep the technical file in a form that can be handed over on request and know which languages their markets require. Binds: provider, authority. Applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I).
docs.m: Chapter III: High-Risk AI Systems · applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I)

docs.t: Article 22: Authorised Representatives of Providers of High-Risk AI Systems
docs.x: Article 22 requires providers established outside the Union to appoint, by written mandate and before placing a high-risk AI system on the Union market, an authorised representative established in the Union (paragraph 1). The representative verifies that the EU declaration of conformity and technical documentation exist and the conformity assessment was carried out, keeps the provider's contact details and documentation copies for 10 years after placing on the market, supplies information to authorities on reasoned request, cooperates on risk mitigation and complies with Article 49(1) registration (paragraph 3). The representative must terminate the mandate and inform the market surveillance authority if the provider breaches the Regulation (paragraph 4). Binds: provider. Applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I).
docs.m: Chapter III: High-Risk AI Systems · applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I)

docs.t: Article 23: Obligations of Importers
docs.x: Article 23 requires importers, before placing a high-risk AI system on the market, to verify that the provider has carried out the Article 43 conformity assessment, drawn up the Annex IV technical documentation, affixed the CE marking, supplied the EU declaration of conformity and instructions for use and appointed an authorised representative under Article 22(1) (paragraph 1). An importer with reason to believe the system is non-conforming must not place it on the market and must report any Article 79(1) risk (paragraph 2). Importers add their own name and address, keep the certificate, instructions and declaration for 10 years and cooperate with authorities (paragraphs 3 to 7). Binds: importer. Applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I).
docs.m: Chapter III: High-Risk AI Systems · applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I)

docs.t: Article 24: Obligations of Distributors
docs.x: Article 24 requires distributors, before making a high-risk AI system available, to verify that it bears the CE marking, is accompanied by the EU declaration of conformity and instructions for use, and that the provider and importer have met their marking duties under Article 16(b) and (c) and Article 23(3) (paragraph 1). A distributor with reason to believe the system does not meet Section 2 must not make it available and must report any Article 79(1) risk (paragraph 2). Distributors protect the system in storage and transport, take or secure corrective action, withdrawal or recall on discovering non-conformity, and cooperate with authorities (paragraphs 3 to 6). Binds: distributor. Applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I).
docs.m: Chapter III: High-Risk AI Systems · applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I)

docs.t: Article 25: Responsibilities Along the AI Value Chain
docs.x: Article 25 makes any distributor, importer, deployer or other third party the provider of a high-risk AI system, with all Article 16 duties, where it puts its name on the system, makes a substantial modification that keeps or renders it high-risk, or changes the intended purpose so that the system becomes high-risk (paragraph 1). The initial provider then ceases to be provider but must supply technical documentation, known limitations and failure modes and targeted technical access, unless it clearly specified that the system was not to become high-risk (paragraph 2). Annex I Section A product manufacturers are the provider (paragraph 3); component suppliers must agree assistance in writing (paragraph 4). Binds: provider, deployer, importer, distributor. Applies from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I).
